cards.phrase: montage sequence over an upbeat song: dawn runs, the calendar filling up, the sweat, and finally arms raised at the top of the steps

cards.name: Soviet montage
cards.desc: Shots chosen to collide, so their meaning comes from the clash between them: marching boots, a screaming face, a runaway pram. Eisenstein thought of editing as an argument.
cards.phrase: Soviet montage on a great stone staircase: a crowd fleeing, a line of soldiers' boots marching down, a baby carriage rolling loose, stark black and white, hard rhythmic cuts

cards.name: Hip-hop montage
cards.desc: A burst of tiny, extreme close-ups, each a few frames long and punched with a sound effect: a pupil dilates, a pill drops, coffee pours. It turns a routine into a ritual or an addiction.
cards.phrase: hip-hop montage: rapid-fire extreme close-ups, each a few frames long, of a key in a lock, coffee pouring, a match striking and a pupil dilating, each hit with a sharp sound

cards.name: Graphic match cut
cards.desc: A cut between two shots whose shapes, positions or movements match exactly, so one object seems to turn into another. The rhyme makes a leap across time or space feel inevitable.
cards.phrase: graphic match cut: a bone tossed into a blue sky spins at the top of its arc and becomes a long white satellite drifting in black space in the same position

cards.name: Jump cut
cards.desc: Cutting between two shots of the same subject from almost the same angle, so they seem to skip forward in time. Once an error, it became the signature of the French New Wave and of YouTube vlogs.
cards.phrase: jump cuts in a single fixed framing of a hotel room: she sits on the bed, then lies across it, then stands at the window, time skipping between each cut

cards.name: Flashback
cards.desc: A jump back to an earlier time, usually signaled by a push in on a face, a dissolve and a change in color or texture. It explains who someone is by showing what happened to them.
cards.phrase: flashback: push in on her face as she remembers, slow dissolve to a warm, faded, grainy image of her as a child on a summer lawn

cards.name: Nonlinear timeline
cards.desc: The story is told out of order: the ending first, chapters shuffled, or scenes running backward. The audience pieces the timeline together, which makes them part of the puzzle.
cards.phrase: tell it as a nonlinear timeline: open on the aftermath, then jump back to the morning, then to a week earlier, with chapter title cards

cards.name: Motivated lighting
cards.desc: Every light on set pretends to come from something in the scene: a window, a lamp, a fridge, a fire. The audience never questions it, so the image feels real.
cards.phrase: motivated lighting: soft daylight from a tall window on the right falls across her face, the side away from the window falls into shadow, no other visible source

cards.name: Practicals
cards.desc: Lamps, neon signs, candles and screens that appear in the shot and actually light it. They make a set feel lived in and give the frame warm points of light.
cards.phrase: lit by practicals in frame: a green banker's lamp on the bar, a red neon beer sign and a string of bulbs, warm pools of light in a dark room

cards.name: Venetian-blind noir
cards.desc: Hard light through venetian blinds throws bars of shadow across a face and wall. It is shorthand for film noir: secrets, guilt and a detective's office at night.
cards.phrase: film noir: hard light through venetian blinds casting diagonal bars of shadow across a detective's face and the wall, cigarette smoke, high-contrast black and white

cards.name: Top light
cards.desc: A single soft light from directly above. Foreheads and shoulders glow while the eyes sink into shadow, so you can't quite read what someone is thinking.
cards.phrase: Gordon Willis top light: one soft source directly overhead, a man at a desk with his eyes lost in shadow, warm amber, underexposed and dark

cards.name: Day for night
cards.desc: Shooting in daylight and darkening and tinting it blue to pass for moonlight. Old westerns did it constantly; it gives a strange, flat, dreamlike night.
cards.phrase: day-for-night: a rider crossing a desert under hard sun, graded deep blue and underexposed to read as moonlit night, crisp shadows

cards.name: Available light only
cards.desc: No film lights at all: only the sun, the sky, fire and whatever the location provides, often caught at the edges of the day. It looks raw and beautiful, and it is hard to schedule.
cards.phrase: available light only: a trapper in a snowy forest at dusk, lit by the cold blue sky and a small campfire, wide lens close to his face, no film lights

cards.name: Candlelight
cards.desc: Faces lit only by candles: warm, soft, flickering, with rich darkness all around. Kubrick shot Barry Lyndon with NASA lenses fast enough to do it for real.
cards.phrase: lit only by candlelight: two figures in 18th-century dress at a card table, warm golden glow on their faces, rich darkness beyond, soft and grainy

cards.name: Volumetric haze
cards.aka: god rays, light shafts, smoke and beams
cards.desc: Haze or smoke in the air makes beams of light visible, so a window or a skylight becomes solid shafts cutting through the room. Instant grandeur.
cards.phrase: volumetric haze in a cavernous warehouse: hard shafts of sunlight slant down from high windows through smoke, a lone silhouette standing in one beam

cards.name: Screen glow
cards.desc: A face lit only by a television, phone or computer: cold, blue and flickering, with the room black around it. It reads as loneliness, insomnia or obsession.
cards.phrase: lit only by the cold blue flicker of a television in a dark living room, a man alone on a sofa, the rest of the room black

cards.name: Red and blue strobes
cards.desc: Alternating red and blue light washing over a face or a street from an unseen police car. It says trouble has arrived, and it pulses even in a still.
cards.phrase: night, red and blue police strobes washing across her face from opposite sides, wet street reflections, a sense of sudden trouble

cards.name: Three-strip Technicolor
cards.desc: The dye-transfer color of Hollywood's golden age: saturated primaries, lipstick reds, emerald greens and skies like enamel. It looks richer than reality on purpose.
cards.phrase: three-strip Technicolor look: hyper-saturated primaries, a ruby-red dress against emerald green and a deep blue sky, lustrous 1950s Hollywood color

cards.name: Two-strip Technicolor
cards.desc: The 1920s and early 30s process that recorded only red and green. No true blues: skies come out teal, faces peachy, and everything has a hand-tinted, antique glow.
cards.phrase: two-strip Technicolor look: only coral reds and sea greens, no true blues, skies rendered teal, soft 1920s glow

cards.name: Matrix green
cards.desc: A sickly green cast laid over everything, used in The Matrix for scenes inside the simulation (the real world is blue). It feels artificial and coded.
cards.phrase: Matrix-green grade: a man in a long black coat and sunglasses in an office corridor, everything tinted a cold digital green, high contrast

cards.name: Amélie grade
cards.aka: warm greens and golds, storybook Paris
cards.desc: Reds and greens pushed hard, blues pulled almost out, and everything warmed to gold. It turns a real city into a fairy tale.
cards.phrase: storybook grade in the spirit of Amélie: saturated emerald greens and cherry reds, blues pulled out, warm golden skin, a whimsical Paris café

cards.name: Fincher yellow-green
cards.desc: Low saturation with a dirty yellow-green cast and inky shadows. Everything looks slightly ill, like a city under sodium lamps that never quite wakes up.
cards.phrase: Fincher-style grade: desaturated, a sickly yellow-green cast, inky shadows, a rain-damp office at night lit by fluorescent tubes

cards.name: Hot yellow filter
cards.desc: A blown-out, saturated yellow wash that Hollywood uses to mean "hot, dusty, somewhere else". Critics call it the Mexico filter, and it's now a cliché worth knowing.
cards.phrase: hot yellow tobacco-filter grade over a dusty border-town street at noon, blown-out sky, heavy heat haze

cards.name: Desaturated war grade
cards.aka: drained color, Saving Private Ryan look
cards.desc: Color drained almost to monochrome, crushed blacks and harsh contrast, often with a shuttered, staccato motion. It makes a war film feel like newsreel and memory.
cards.phrase: desaturated war-film grade, color drained almost to grey, crushed blacks, soldiers in a smoky landing with hard contrast and a newsreel feel

cards.name: Color isolation
cards.desc: A black-and-white film with one thing left in color: a girl's red coat, a goldfish, a single dress. The eye goes straight to it and the meaning lands hard.
cards.phrase: black-and-white film with color isolation: a crowded wartime street in monochrome, one little girl in a red coat the only color in the frame

cards.name: Neon magenta and blue
cards.desc: Faces lit in hot magenta on one side and electric blue on the other, deep black around them. Nicolas Winding Refn made it a signature; music videos made it everywhere.
cards.phrase: neon noir lighting: a face split between hot magenta and electric blue neon, deep glossy blacks, synth-scored stillness

cards.name: Modern black and white
cards.desc: Black and white shot on a modern digital camera: clean, sharp, wide and silvery, with no grain or scratches. It feels timeless rather than old.
cards.phrase: pristine modern digital black and white, a wide deep-focus shot of a family on a beach, silvery tones, enormous detail, no grain

cards.name: Sepia to color
cards.aka: the Oz door, monochrome to color
cards.desc: A film that starts in sepia or black and white and bursts into color when the story crosses into another world, or the other way round.
cards.phrase: a sepia-toned farmhouse doorway swinging open onto a world of saturated Technicolor flowers and a yellow road

cards.aka: silent-era and old TV ratio, fullscreen
cards.desc: Almost square. The shape of silent films and of television until the 2000s. Today it reads as vintage, intimate or claustrophobic.
cards.phrase: 4:3 aspect ratio (1.33:1), a boxy almost-square frame, pillarboxed

cards.name: 1.37:1 Academy
cards.desc: The standard frame of Hollywood's golden age, from 1932 until widescreen arrived in the 1950s. Slightly wider than 4:3, it centers faces and suits close, formal compositions.
cards.phrase: 1.37:1 Academy ratio, classical boxy framing

cards.name: 1.19:1 Movietone
cards.desc: An even squarer frame from the first sound films, when the soundtrack took a slice of the picture. Revived for claustrophobic period pieces.
cards.phrase: 1.19:1 near-square frame, claustrophobic, early-sound-film proportions

cards.name: 1.66:1 European widescreen
cards.desc: The wide ratio European cinema adopted in the 1950s and 60s: wider than Academy, narrower than American widescreen. Common in art films and animation.
cards.phrase: 1.66:1 European widescreen framing

cards.name: 1.85:1 flat
cards.desc: The everyday widescreen of American films, shot with ordinary lenses. Close to a 16:9 TV, so it fills the screen at home.
cards.phrase: 1.85:1 widescreen frame

cards.name: 2.39:1 scope
cards.desc: The wide, letterboxed frame of epics and blockbusters. It gives room for landscapes and lets two faces share the frame with space between them. People call it "cinematic" for a reason.
cards.phrase: 2.39:1 anamorphic widescreen, letterboxed, wide cinematic frame

cards.name: 2.76:1 Ultra Panavision 70
cards.desc: The widest frame in common use: 65mm film squeezed through anamorphic lenses. Revived for a handful of event films that want vast horizons.
cards.phrase: 2.76:1 Ultra Panavision 70, an extremely wide strip of a frame, epic horizon

cards.name: 1.43:1 IMAX
cards.desc: The tall frame of 15-perf 65mm IMAX film, used for a film's biggest moments. On a giant screen it fills your peripheral vision top to bottom.
cards.phrase: 1.43:1 IMAX frame, towering vertical scale, immense detail

cards.name: 9:16 vertical
cards.desc: The phone-native frame of social video and vertical micro-dramas. One person fills it; anything wide has to be told in height instead.
cards.phrase: vertical 9:16 framing for a phone, a single figure filling the height of the frame

cards.name: Changing aspect ratio
cards.desc: A film that changes shape: the frame widens or narrows to mark a new era, a new world or a big moment.
cards.phrase: change the aspect ratio between eras: boxy 1.37:1 for the past, widening to 2.39:1 for the present

cards.name: 65mm / 70mm film
cards.desc: Film twice the width of 35mm. Enormous detail, very fine grain and a depth that feels almost three-dimensional. Reserved for epics and landscapes.
cards.phrase: shot on 65mm film: crisp large-format detail, extremely fine grain, rich deep color, vast landscape

cards.name: 35mm film
cards.desc: The standard gauge of cinema for a century. Gentle grain, soft highlights that roll off rather than clip, and color that still defines "the film look".
cards.phrase: shot on 35mm film: fine organic grain, soft highlight roll-off, warm natural skin tones

cards.name: 16mm film
cards.desc: A smaller, cheaper gauge with visible grain and a soft, intimate feel. Light cameras made it the format of documentaries, indies and handheld realism.
cards.phrase: shot on Super 16mm film: visible chunky grain, muted color, intimate handheld feel

cards.name: Super 8
cards.desc: The tiny home-movie film of the 1960s to 80s. Heavy grain, warm faded color, light leaks and a flickering, rounded frame. Pure nostalgia.
cards.phrase: Super 8 home movie: heavy grain, warm faded color, light leaks, soft focus, rounded flickering frame edges

cards.name: VHS camcorder
cards.aka: home video, analog tape, 80s and 90s video
cards.desc: Analog videotape from a consumer camcorder: soft, smeary color, scan lines, tracking noise and an on-screen date stamp.
cards.phrase: VHS camcorder footage: soft smeared color bleeding sideways, scan lines, a band of tracking noise, a blocky date stamp in the corner

cards.name: Early digital video
cards.aka: MiniDV, standard definition digital, prosumer DV
cards.desc: The first consumer digital camcorders of the late 1990s and 2000s: harsh, over-sharpened, clipped white skies and smeary motion. Dogme 95 and early horror made it an aesthetic.
cards.phrase: early 2000s MiniDV digital video: harsh over-sharpened detail, blown-out white sky, smeary motion, 4:3 standard definition

cards.name: Anamorphic lens
cards.desc: Lenses that squeeze a wide picture onto the film, then unsqueeze it in projection. They leave fingerprints: oval out-of-focus lights, horizontal blue streak flares and gently bending edges.
cards.phrase: shot on anamorphic lenses: oval vertical bokeh, a long horizontal blue streak flare across the frame, 2.39:1, slight edge distortion

cards.name: Silent-era film
cards.desc: Early black-and-white film, often slightly sped up because it was shot at around 16 to 18 frames a second. Flicker, scratches, an iris vignette and theatrical acting.
cards.phrase: silent-era film: flickering scratched black and white, sped-up 18 frames per second motion, iris vignette, 1.33:1, an intertitle card

cards.name: Digital cinema camera
cards.desc: Modern digital cinema cameras: clean, grainless images with huge dynamic range, holding detail in both the sunset and the shadows. The baseline look of most current films and series.
cards.phrase: shot on an ARRI Alexa: clean grainless digital image, wide dynamic range holding the sunset and the shadows, natural skin tones

cards.name: Found footage
cards.desc: The film pretends to be footage recovered from a character's own camera: shaky, badly framed, night-vision green, with an on-screen REC indicator. It feels like evidence.
cards.phrase: found-footage horror: shaky handheld night-vision camcorder, green monochrome, a figure with glowing eyes at the end of a hallway, REC indicator and timestamp

cards.name: Security camera
cards.desc: A fixed, high, wide view with a fisheye bulge, washed-out grey color, a low frame rate and a timestamp. It makes ordinary moments feel like evidence.
cards.phrase: CCTV security camera footage: high corner angle looking down a convenience store, fisheye distortion, grey low-saturation image, timestamp and CAM 03 overlay

cards.name: Film noir
cards.desc: Hard-boiled 1940s and 50s crime films: black and white, night, rain, cigarettes, fedoras and trench coats, and light that cuts faces in half. Everyone has something to hide.
cards.phrase: classic 1940s film noir: a man in a fedora and trench coat under a lone streetlight on a rain-slicked street, hard high-contrast black and white, long shadows

cards.name: Neo-noir
cards.desc: Noir's moral murk carried into color: night cities, neon reflected in wet asphalt, lone drivers and synth scores. The rules are the same, only the light has changed.
cards.phrase: neo-noir: a lone driver in a parked car on a rain-soaked Los Angeles street at night, magenta and cyan neon reflected in the wet asphalt, sodium-orange streetlights

cards.name: Western
cards.desc: Wide frontier landscapes, lone riders, saloons and showdowns at high noon. The space itself is the subject: tiny people against an enormous, indifferent land.
cards.phrase: classic western: a lone rider on horseback crossing a vast desert valley beneath towering red mesas, hard afternoon sun, dust, extreme wide shot

cards.name: Science fiction
cards.desc: Spaceships, future cities and other worlds, from clean white corridors to grimy cargo holds. It is often about scale, loneliness and what technology does to people.
cards.phrase: hard science fiction: a small spacecraft drifting past an enormous ringed gas giant, cold sunlight, deep black space, realistic scale

cards.name: Horror
cards.desc: Darkness you can't see into, long hallways, doors left ajar and a figure that shouldn't be there. The frame leaves empty space on purpose so the audience searches it.
cards.phrase: horror: a terrified woman in the foreground of a dark hallway, unaware of a pale figure standing motionless in the doorway far behind her, cold moonlight

cards.name: Folk horror
cards.desc: Horror in bright daylight: a remote village, flower crowns, smiling locals and an old ritual nobody will explain. The sunshine makes it worse.
cards.phrase: folk horror in bright midsummer daylight: villagers in white with flower crowns dancing around a maypole in a meadow, eerie smiling calm, overexposed pastel

cards.name: Musical
cards.desc: Characters break into song and dance, and the film breaks into theater: spotlights, saturated color, painted skies and choreography designed for the camera.
cards.phrase: movie musical: a dancer mid-twirl in a yellow dress on a hilltop at magic hour, a painted purple sky, a single spotlight following her

cards.name: Heist
cards.desc: A crew assembles, a plan is laid out, and it goes wrong at the worst moment. Look for blueprints, slick suits, slow-motion walks and split-second timing.
cards.phrase: heist film: a crew of five in sharp dark suits walking toward the camera in a line, slow motion, low angle, a casino glowing behind them

cards.name: Romantic comedy
cards.desc: Two people who obviously belong together keep missing each other in a warm, bright, picture-postcard city. Rain, bookstores, autumn leaves and the airport run.
cards.phrase: romantic comedy: a couple sharing a red umbrella on a rainy autumn street in New York, warm shop windows glowing, soft flattering light, a meet-cute

cards.name: War film
cards.desc: Trenches, beaches and ruined towns; desaturated color, smoke, shaky cameras and sudden chaos. The best ones keep the camera at soldier height, where nobody can see far.
cards.phrase: war film: soldiers silhouetted in a muddy trench at night, a flare burning orange overhead through drifting smoke, desaturated palette

cards.name: Road movie
cards.desc: Characters running from something on long empty highways: motels, diners, gas stations and a car that becomes a home. The landscape keeps changing while they don't.
cards.phrase: road movie: a dusty convertible on a long empty desert highway under a huge sky, a lone motel sign in the distance, late afternoon sun

cards.name: Kaiju
cards.desc: A colossal creature rising over a city, shot from street level to sell the scale: tiny people, toppling towers, searchlights and smoke.
cards.phrase: kaiju film: a colossal monster silhouette rising out of the bay behind a city skyline at night, searchlights sweeping through smoke, crowds fleeing in the foreground, shot from street level

cards.name: Wuxia
cards.desc: Chinese martial-arts fantasy: warriors who run up walls and fly across rooftops and treetops, with flowing silk, sword fights and painterly landscapes.
cards.phrase: wuxia: two swordfighters in flowing robes balanced on the swaying tops of a misty bamboo forest, green light filtering through, weightless and graceful

cards.name: Period drama
cards.desc: Historical stories in careful costume and real old houses: corsets, carriages, letters, candlelit dinners and grey English skies. Composition is often painterly and still.
cards.phrase: period drama: a young woman in a Regency empire-waist dress walks across a misty meadow at dawn toward a grand English country house, soft overcast light

cards.name: German Expressionism
cards.desc: Silent German films of the 1920s with painted, tilting sets, jagged shadows and stylized acting. The world looks the way the characters feel: twisted.
cards.phrase: German Expressionist film: a gaunt figure creeping through a crooked painted alley, jagged angled walls, shadows painted onto the set, black and white with a tinted wash

cards.name: Italian Neorealism
cards.desc: Postwar Italian films shot on real streets with non-professional actors, about poverty and ordinary people. Plain, natural, grey and heartbreaking.
cards.phrase: Italian Neorealism: a father and young son walk a bicycle down a crowded postwar Roman street, real locations, natural light, black and white

cards.name: French New Wave
cards.desc: Young critics-turned-directors in late-1950s Paris who broke the rules: handheld cameras on real streets, jump cuts, characters who talk to the camera, cool and playful.
cards.phrase: French New Wave: a cool young couple strolling down a Paris boulevard in 1960, she sells newspapers in a striped shirt, handheld camera, natural light, black and white

cards.name: New Hollywood
cards.desc: American films of the late 60s and 70s made by young directors with real freedom: gritty locations, natural light, long lenses, moral grey areas and downbeat endings.
cards.phrase: New Hollywood 1970s look: a grimy Manhattan street at dusk, yellow cabs and steam from a manhole, grainy warm film stock, long telephoto lens, a loner in an army jacket

cards.name: Dogme 95
cards.desc: A Danish manifesto that banned film lights, music not recorded on set, tripods and special effects. Handheld digital video, real locations and raw emotion.
cards.phrase: Dogme 95 style: shaky handheld digital video of a tense family dinner in a real dining room, available light only, no music, awkward intimate framing

cards.name: Giallo
cards.desc: Lurid Italian murder mysteries of the 60s and 70s: a killer in black leather gloves, saturated red and blue gel light, fashion, mirrors and an operatic score.
cards.phrase: giallo: a black-leather-gloved hand reaching for a doorknob in a stylish apartment lit with saturated red and blue gels, operatic suspense

cards.name: Hong Kong action
cards.desc: 1980s and 90s Hong Kong action: balletic gunfights in slow motion, two guns at once, white doves, churches and honor among killers.
cards.phrase: Hong Kong heroic-bloodshed gunfight: a man in a white suit leaps sideways in slow motion with a pistol in each hand, white doves bursting through a candlelit church

cards.name: Slow cinema
cards.desc: Very long, mostly static takes in which little happens, so you notice light, weather, sound and time itself. Hypnotic if you give in to it.
cards.phrase: slow cinema: a static wide shot held for minutes of a lone figure crossing a misty, wind-blown plain toward a distant farmhouse, muted grey light

cards.name: Mumblecore
cards.desc: Cheap, talky 2000s indies about twenty-somethings and their relationships, shot on digital in real apartments with friends as actors and lots of improvised, overlapping dialogue.
cards.phrase: mumblecore: two twenty-somethings talking awkwardly in a cramped real apartment kitchen at night, flat practical light, handheld digital, improvised feel

cards.name: Kitchen-sink realism
cards.desc: British films about working-class life in industrial towns: terraced houses, rain, pubs and angry young men. Its descendants are Ken Loach and Andrea Arnold.
cards.phrase: British kitchen-sink realism: a young man in a donkey jacket on a wet street of brick terraced houses with smoking chimneys, overcast industrial town, gritty black and white

cards.name: Alfred Hitchcock
cards.desc: Suspense built from what the audience knows and the character doesn't. Precise storyboarded shots, voyeuristic POVs, icy blondes, staircases and ordinary men chased across wide open spaces.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Alfred Hitchcock: a man in a grey suit running across a flat empty prairie as a crop-duster plane swoops low behind him, wide controlled framing, suspense

cards.name: Stanley Kubrick
cards.desc: Cold perfectionism: one-point perspective, wide lenses, slow zooms out, symmetrical corridors, classical music over violence and the Kubrick stare.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Stanley Kubrick: a perfectly symmetrical one-point-perspective hotel corridor with patterned carpet, two identical girls in pale blue dresses standing at the far end, wide lens, unsettling stillness

cards.name: Akira Kurosawa
cards.desc: Epic samurai films with weather as drama: driving rain, wind-whipped banners, mud and fog. Long telephoto lenses compress crowds into a wall of movement; axial cuts punch in.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Akira Kurosawa: samurai with banners charging through driving rain and mud, telephoto compression, wind-whipped flags, black and white

cards.name: Yasujirō Ozu
cards.desc: Quiet family dramas shot with a still camera at the height of someone kneeling on a tatami mat, actors facing almost straight into the lens, and pillow shots between scenes.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Yasujirō Ozu: a static low camera at tatami height, an elderly couple seated on the floor of a Japanese home framed by sliding doors, calm, frontal, gentle

cards.name: Andrei Tarkovsky
cards.desc: Long, slow, spiritual films full of water, fire, wind in grass, levitation and ruined rooms. Shots last minutes; the camera drifts; dreams and memory blur together.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Andrei Tarkovsky: a wooden house burning in a misty meadow, a lone figure standing in the wet grass watching, muted green-grey palette, a slow minutes-long take

cards.name: Steven Spielberg
cards.desc: Wonder and danger for everyone: silhouettes against huge light sources, backlit haze, the awed face, kids on bikes, and long fluid shots that hide their complexity.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Steven Spielberg: a kid on a bicycle silhouetted against a giant full moon over a forest, soft blue night, a sense of wonder

cards.name: Martin Scorsese
cards.desc: Restless energy: long Steadicam tracking shots, slow motion set to a rock song, freeze frames with voice-over, saturated red bars and men who talk too fast.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Martin Scorsese: slow-motion entrance into a crowded bar bathed in red light, a tough guy in a sharp suit, a rock song on the soundtrack, the camera gliding with him

cards.name: David Lynch
cards.desc: Dream logic and dread under a cozy surface: red velvet curtains, zigzag floors, humming lamps, small towns and nightmares. "Lynchian" means wholesome and wrong at once.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of David Lynch: a room of red velvet curtains with a black-and-white zigzag floor, a single art-deco lamp, a figure standing very still, uncanny dream logic

cards.name: David Fincher
cards.desc: Clinical, perfectly locked-off camera, dark rooms, sickly yellow-green color and rain. Every move is motivated and machine-smooth; nothing is left to chance.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of David Fincher: two detectives with flashlights entering a pitch-dark apartment, beams cutting through dust, desaturated yellow-green, locked-off precise framing, rain outside

cards.name: Christopher Nolan
cards.desc: Big-concept puzzles shot practically on IMAX film: folding cities, rotating hallways, ticking scores, cross-cut timelines and cool steel-blue palettes.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Christopher Nolan: a city street folding up and over itself into the sky, two figures in suits standing in the middle, steel-blue grade, IMAX large-format scale

cards.name: Denis Villeneuve
cards.desc: Hushed, enormous science fiction and thrillers: vast brutalist shapes in fog, tiny people, low droning sound and patient, monolithic compositions.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Denis Villeneuve: a colossal dark oval vessel hovering silently over a misty green valley, tiny figures on the ridge below, muted palette, monumental stillness

cards.name: Terrence Malick
cards.desc: Lyrical, drifting films about nature and grace: magic-hour light, wide lenses floating close to people, whispered voice-over, trees, water and hands touching grass.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Terrence Malick: looking up into the canopy of a huge oak at magic hour, the sun flaring through the leaves, a mother lifting a child, floating wide-angle camera

cards.name: Quentin Tarantino
cards.desc: Pop-culture pastiche: chapter titles, long dialogue scenes, trunk shots, crash zooms, bold primary color and sudden stylized violence, all borrowed from grindhouse and kung-fu films.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Quentin Tarantino: a woman in a yellow tracksuit with a katana standing in a snowy Japanese garden lit deep blue, stylized grindhouse composition, a chapter title card

cards.name: Wong Kar-wai
cards.aka: WKW, In the Mood for Love
cards.desc: Romantic longing in saturated Hong Kong color: narrow corridors, rain, cigarette smoke, slow motion, step-printed blur and lovers who never quite touch.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Wong Kar-wai: a woman in a patterned qipao passing a man in a narrow green corridor under a warm lamp, slow motion, rain on the window, saturated longing

cards.name: Wes Anderson
cards.desc: Storybook symmetry: centered compositions, flat frontal staging, pastel palettes, whip pans, overhead inserts, title cards and deadpan characters in uniforms.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Wes Anderson: a perfectly symmetrical pink-and-red hotel lobby, a lobby boy in a purple uniform standing dead center facing the camera, pastel palette, flat frontal composition

cards.name: Sofia Coppola
cards.desc: Soft, pastel loneliness: young women gazing out of hotel and palace windows, natural light, long quiet moments, pop music and beautiful boredom.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Sofia Coppola: a young woman in a pink sweater sitting on a hotel windowsill looking out over Tokyo at dusk, soft pastel light, quiet loneliness

cards.name: Bong Joon-ho
cards.desc: Genre films that switch tone mid-scene (comedy, thriller, horror, satire) with class staged vertically: the rich up the stairs, the poor below, and rain flowing down between them.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Bong Joon-ho: a family running down an endless stone staircase through a hillside city in torrential night rain, water cascading past them, framed to show high and low

cards.name: Spike Lee
cards.desc: Bold, political and stylized: Dutch angles, characters talking straight to camera, saturated heat, the double-dolly float and a neighborhood as a whole world.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Spike Lee: a Dutch-angle close-up of a man on a Brooklyn stoop talking straight into the lens on the hottest day of the summer, saturated red and orange heat

cards.name: Jordan Peele
cards.desc: Horror built on social unease: everyday settings that turn uncanny, faces in tight close-up with tears or frozen smiles, and surreal voids like the Sunken Place.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Jordan Peele: a man floating and falling slowly through an endless black void, a small glowing screen of the real world far above him, uncanny social-horror stillness

cards.name: Agnès Varda
cards.aka: the grandmother of the New Wave
cards.desc: Playful, personal films and essays mixing documentary and fiction: beaches, mirrors, potatoes, cats and the director herself on camera, curious about everyone.
cards.phrase: in the spirit of Agnès Varda: a row of old mirrors standing upright on a sunny beach, each reflecting a slice of sea and sky, playful and personal, bright natural light

cards.name: Roger Deakins
cards.desc: Simple, bold compositions built around one strong source: silhouettes against walls of light, colored haze, and perfect restraint. Every frame reads in a glance.
cards.phrase: lit like Roger Deakins: two figures fighting in pure silhouette against a vast glowing blue digital billboard in a dark skyscraper at night, single source, minimal

cards.name: Emmanuel Lubezki
cards.desc: Natural light, wide lenses inches from the actors and impossibly long, floating takes. The camera breathes with the characters and the world feels physically present.
cards.phrase: shot like Emmanuel Lubezki: an ultra-wide lens inches from a man's face as his breath fogs in the cold blue dusk of a vast forest, natural light only, one floating continuous take

cards.name: Vittorio Storaro
cards.desc: Bold, symbolic color as emotion: blazing oranges, deep reds and blues, and light that moves across faces during a scene. Painterly and operatic.
cards.phrase: lit like Vittorio Storaro: helicopters silhouetted over a jungle through billowing orange smoke at sunset, saturated symbolic color, operatic

cards.name: Gordon Willis
cards.desc: Daring underexposure and top light (The Godfather), and luminous black-and-white city panoramas (Manhattan). He trusted darkness more than anyone before him.
cards.phrase: shot like Gordon Willis: a couple on a bench beneath the Queensboro Bridge at dawn, silvery widescreen black and white, silhouettes against the river

cards.name: Hoyte van Hoytema
cards.desc: Large-format film used for intimate realism: IMAX cameras handheld, natural light, real locations and enormous landscapes that make people feel tiny and exposed.
cards.phrase: shot like Hoyte van Hoytema on IMAX film: a tiny astronaut standing in shallow water on an endless ocean planet as a mountainous wave rises on the horizon, natural light, tall large-format frame

cards.name: Janusz Kamiński
cards.desc: Spielberg's cinematographer since Schindler's List: blown-out white windows, heavy backlit haze, desaturated or bleach-bypassed color and shuttered, staccato motion.
cards.phrase: lit like Janusz Kamiński: silhouetted figures in a smoky room against windows blown out to pure white, heavy backlit haze, desaturated bleach-bypass color

cards.name: Bradford Young
cards.desc: Daringly underexposed, soft and warm images where faces glow out of rich darkness. He lights dark skin with love and lets the shadows hold most of the frame.
cards.phrase: shot like Bradford Young: a woman's face emerging softly out of deep warm darkness, lit by a dim window to the side, underexposed, rich luminous skin, most of the frame in shadow

cards.name: Greig Fraser
cards.desc: Moody, textured digital images built from silhouettes, harsh single sources and colored haze, often on custom-detuned lenses for a slightly imperfect, analog feel.
cards.phrase: shot like Greig Fraser: a caped silhouette in heavy rain lit only by a red emergency flare, thick haze, soft detuned lens, dark textured image

cards.name: Sven Nykvist
cards.desc: Simple, soft, natural light, often a single bounced source, and long close-ups of faces. His work with Ingmar Bergman made the human face the main landscape of cinema.
cards.phrase: lit like Sven Nykvist: two women's faces close together in the frame, one in profile and one facing the camera, soft natural northern light, minimal grey background, black and white

cards.name: James Laxton
cards.desc: Barry Jenkins' cinematographer: saturated, dreamlike color on rich dark skin, faces looking straight into the lens, Miami teals and purples, and the sea at night.
cards.phrase: shot like James Laxton: a young man on a beach at night looking straight into the lens, his dark skin glowing in saturated blue and violet moonlight, teal ocean behind, intimate and lush

cards.name: Linear
cards.desc: The same speed from start to finish, with an instant start and stop. Feels mechanical and robotic for objects, but right for things that never stop, like spinners, marquees and progress that tracks time.
cards.phrase: linear timing (constant speed) for continuous loops like spinners and tickers

cards.name: Ease-out
cards.desc: Starts fast and slows into its resting place, like a sliding object meeting friction. The workhorse for anything entering the screen: it responds instantly and lands gently.
cards.phrase: ease-out (decelerate) easing for things entering the screen, so they respond fast and settle gently

cards.name: Ease-in
cards.desc: Starts slow and speeds up as it leaves. Used for things exiting the screen, since the slow start shows where they go and the fast finish gets them out of the way. As an entrance it feels sluggish.
cards.phrase: ease-in (accelerate) easing on exits, so elements gather speed as they leave

cards.name: Ease-in-out
cards.desc: Slow at both ends and fastest in the middle. Natural for objects that move from one resting place to another on screen, like a slider thumb or a camera move between two framings.
cards.phrase: ease-in-out (S-curve) easing for moves between two resting positions on screen

cards.name: CSS "ease"
cards.desc: The curve browsers use if you name none: a quick start and a long, soft landing. A fine default, though a stronger ease-out usually feels more polished.
cards.phrase: the default CSS ease curve, cubic-bezier(.25,.1,.25,1)

cards.name: Steps
cards.desc: Jumps between a fixed number of positions with no in-betweens. Used for sprite-sheet animation, typewriter text, ticking clocks and deliberately choppy, handmade motion.
cards.phrase: stepped timing (steps) with no in-betweens, for a sprite-sheet or ticking-clock feel

cards.name: Quart out
cards.desc: A much stronger deceleration than plain ease-out: almost all the movement happens in the first third, then a long, quiet settle. Feels crisp and expensive.
cards.phrase: a strong ease-out like easeOutQuart, cubic-bezier(.25,1,.5,1)

cards.name: Expo out
cards.desc: The most dramatic common ease-out: a near-instant jump, then a very long glide into place. The signature of premium product sites and Apple-style reveals.
cards.phrase: an expo ease-out, cubic-bezier(.16,1,.3,1): a fast start and a long, silky settle

cards.name: Expo in
cards.desc: Barely moves, then rockets away. Good for things that launch or get sucked out of frame.
cards.phrase: an expo ease-in, cubic-bezier(.7,0,.84,0), so it barely moves and then launches away

cards.name: Circ in-out
cards.desc: A steep S-curve: long slow ends and a snap through the middle. Reads as decisive and cinematic, good for big transitions between sections.
cards.phrase: a hard S-curve like easeInOutCirc, cubic-bezier(.85,0,.15,1), for decisive section changes

cards.name: Back out
cards.desc: Goes a little past the target and settles back. Adds playful energy to pop-ups, badges and buttons without a full bounce.
cards.phrase: a back-out easing that overshoots slightly and settles, cubic-bezier(.34,1.56,.64,1)

cards.name: Back in
cards.desc: Pulls back slightly before leaving, like winding up a throw. The curve version of the anticipation principle.
cards.phrase: a back-in easing that pulls back slightly before moving off, cubic-bezier(.36,0,.66,-.56)

cards.name: Back in-out
cards.desc: Winds up, moves, overshoots and settles. Cartoony and full of character; use it on one hero element, not everywhere.
cards.phrase: an anticipate-and-overshoot easing, cubic-bezier(.68,-.6,.32,1.6), on the hero element only

cards.name: Material standard
cards.desc: Google's house curve for things moving within the screen: quick to start, long to settle. A safe, modern default for app UI.
cards.phrase: Material 3 standard easing, cubic-bezier(.2,0,0,1), for on-screen moves

cards.name: Emphasized decelerate
cards.desc: An extreme deceleration for elements entering with importance, like a full-screen sheet or a hero card. Pair it with emphasized accelerate for the exit.
cards.phrase: Material emphasized decelerate, cubic-bezier(.05,.7,.1,1), for important entrances; emphasized accelerate, cubic-bezier(.3,0,.8,.15), for their exits

cards.name: Bouncy spring
cards.desc: A spring with low damping overshoots and oscillates a few times before settling. Lively and toy-like; use it where delight matters more than speed.
cards.phrase: a bouncy spring (stiffness about 300, damping about 10) that overshoots and wobbles before settling

cards.name: Critically damped spring
cards.desc: A spring tuned to arrive as fast as possible with no overshoot at all. The default feel of iOS sheets and gestures: smooth, physical and never wobbly.
cards.phrase: a critically damped spring (damping ratio 1, no overshoot) so it arrives quickly and settles without bouncing

cards.name: Gentle spring
cards.desc: Low stiffness makes the spring slow and floaty, with one soft overshoot. Calm, relaxed and a little luxurious.
cards.phrase: a gentle, low-stiffness spring (stiffness about 80) with one soft overshoot, calm and floaty

cards.name: Snappy spring
cards.desc: High stiffness and enough damping for a tiny overshoot. Quick and responsive, ideal for toggles, taps and drag releases.
cards.phrase: a stiff, snappy spring (stiffness about 500, damping about 28) with a barely visible overshoot

cards.name: Bounce
cards.desc: Hits the target and rebounds in shrinking hops, like a ball dropped on the floor. Very cartoony; use it for one playful landing.
cards.phrase: a bounce-out easing that lands and rebounds in two or three shrinking hops

cards.name: Elastic
cards.desc: Snaps past the target and vibrates like a plucked rubber band. Loud and springy; good for a celebratory pop.
cards.phrase: an elastic-out easing that snaps past the target and vibrates into place

cards.name: Inertia
cards.desc: After a flick, the element keeps moving and slows down on its own, as if sliding on ice. It is how scroll views and carousels coast after you let go.
cards.phrase: momentum after release: the element keeps the flick velocity and decays smoothly to a stop

cards.name: Rubber banding
cards.desc: Dragging past the edge meets increasing resistance, and letting go springs back. Tells you there is nothing more without a hard stop.
cards.phrase: rubber-band resistance when dragged past the edge, springing back on release

cards.name: Micro duration
cards.desc: Short enough to feel instant but still visible. For small state changes like a button press, a checkbox or a color change on hover.
cards.phrase: micro durations of 100 to 150ms for small state changes like hovers, presses and toggles

cards.name: Standard duration
cards.desc: The default range for most interface motion: menus, dropdowns, tabs and small panels. Long enough to follow, short enough never to make people wait.
cards.phrase: standard durations of 200 to 300ms for menus, tabs and panels

cards.name: Long duration
cards.desc: For large, full-screen or meaningful moves, like a page transition, a hero reveal or an onboarding moment. Past about 700ms, UI starts to feel slow.
cards.phrase: longer durations of 400 to 600ms only for full-screen transitions and hero moments

cards.name: Duration scales with size
cards.desc: Bigger moves and bigger elements get more time; small ones get less. A tooltip and a full-screen sheet should not share one duration.
cards.phrase: scale duration with distance and size: about 150ms for small elements, up to 500ms for full-screen moves

cards.name: Stagger
cards.desc: A list of items starts animating one after another with a small fixed delay between them, so the eye reads the order. Keep the gap at 30 to 80ms or the last item arrives too late.
cards.phrase: stagger the list items 50ms apart as they fade and rise in

cards.name: Overlap
cards.desc: Each move starts before the previous one finishes, so a sequence flows as one gesture instead of ticking through steps.
cards.phrase: overlap the moves so each starts before the last finishes, flowing as one gesture

cards.name: Choreography
cards.desc: Arranging several moves so the container arrives first, then its title, then its contents. The order tells people what matters and where to look.
cards.phrase: choreograph the reveal: the card scales in first, then the title, then the items stagger in

cards.name: Enter slow, exit fast
cards.desc: Entrances get a little more time and an ease-out; exits are quicker with an ease-in, because once something is dismissed nobody wants to watch it leave.
cards.phrase: asymmetric timing: enter over 300ms with ease-out, exit over 200ms with ease-in

cards.name: Hold
cards.desc: A deliberate pause between moves gives the viewer time to register what changed. Motion without holds feels frantic; a held beat makes the next move land.
cards.phrase: add short holds (a beat of 300 to 500ms) between moves so each change registers

cards.name: Reduced motion
cards.desc: Some people get dizzy or sick from large movement and turn on a system setting to reduce it. Respecting it means swapping slides, zooms and parallax for simple fades, not removing feedback entirely.
cards.phrase: respect prefers-reduced-motion: replace slides, zooms and parallax with short crossfades

cards.name: Squash and stretch
cards.desc: Objects flatten on impact and stretch when moving fast, while keeping the same volume. It is the single biggest cue that something is soft, alive or has weight.
cards.phrase: squash and stretch: the shape stretches when moving fast and squashes on impact, keeping its volume

cards.name: Anticipation
cards.desc: A small move in the opposite direction before the main action: a crouch before a jump, a pull back before a throw. It tells the viewer what is about to happen.
cards.phrase: anticipation: a small crouch or pull-back in the opposite direction before the main move

cards.name: Staging
cards.desc: Presenting one idea at a time so it is unmistakable: one thing moves while everything else holds still, dims or gets out of the way.
cards.phrase: clear staging: only the key element moves while everything else holds still and dims

cards.name: Pose to pose
cards.aka: keyframes and in-betweens, vs. straight ahead
cards.desc: Plan the key poses first, then fill the frames between. Its opposite, straight-ahead animation, draws frame after frame in order and suits fire, water and chaos. Software keyframing is pose to pose.
cards.phrase: pose-to-pose animation with clear key poses and smooth in-betweens

cards.name: Follow-through and overlap
cards.desc: When the main body stops, the loose parts (hair, a tail, a scarf, a card's shadow) keep going and settle a moment later. Parts move at slightly different times instead of all at once.
cards.phrase: follow-through and overlapping action: loose parts lag behind the main body and settle after it stops

cards.name: Slow in and slow out
cards.aka: ease in and ease out, cushioning
cards.desc: Real objects need time to speed up and slow down, so animators put more drawings near the start and end of a move. Easing curves are this principle in software.
cards.phrase: slow in and slow out: more frames near the start and end of each move, fewer in the middle

cards.name: Arcs
cards.desc: Living things and thrown objects move along curves, not straight lines. Animating along an arc instead of a straight path is the quickest way to make motion feel natural.
cards.phrase: move along gentle arcs instead of straight lines, as living things do

cards.name: Secondary action
cards.desc: A smaller motion that supports the main one and adds personality: a character walks while swinging its arms and its antenna bobs. It should never steal focus from the main action.
cards.phrase: add a small secondary action, like an antenna bob or an icon wiggle, that supports the main move without stealing focus

cards.name: Timing
cards.aka: number of frames, weight through speed
cards.desc: How many frames an action takes decides how heavy, large or emotional it feels. Same distance, different timing: the fast one reads as light or excited, the slow one as heavy or calm.
cards.phrase: use timing to show weight: light things move quickly, heavy things take longer to start and stop

cards.name: Exaggeration
cards.aka: push the pose, caricature of motion
cards.desc: Pushing a motion beyond realism so it reads clearly and with more feeling. Not distortion for its own sake, but a bigger squash, a longer wind-up or a higher jump.
cards.phrase: exaggerate the motion: a bigger squash, a longer wind-up and a higher arc than realism would allow

cards.name: Solid drawing
cards.desc: Drawing or modeling things as solid forms with weight and volume, so they turn convincingly in space instead of looking like flat cutouts.
cards.phrase: solid, volumetric forms that turn convincingly in space, with consistent perspective and light

cards.name: Appeal
cards.desc: The quality that makes something pleasant to watch: clear shapes, a readable silhouette and a bit of life even at rest. A blinking, breathing mascot has it; a static clip-art one does not.
cards.phrase: give it appeal: simple readable shapes, a clear silhouette and small signs of life like blinking and breathing

cards.name: Keyframes and tweening
cards.desc: You set the important values at a few moments (keyframes) and the software fills in the frames between them (tweening). Nearly all digital animation, CSS included, works this way.
cards.phrase: keyframe the key poses and let the tool interpolate between them with eased tweens

cards.name: Overshoot and settle
cards.desc: The element goes slightly past its final position and eases back into place. A small dose makes UI feel physical; too much feels bouncy.
cards.phrase: a small overshoot and settle as each panel lands

cards.name: Smear frame
cards.desc: A single distorted, stretched frame drawn in the middle of a very fast move, so the eye reads speed instead of a jump. A stylish alternative to motion blur in 2D animation.
cards.phrase: use smear frames on the fastest moves: one stretched, streaky frame instead of motion blur

cards.name: Motion blur
cards.desc: The blur along the direction of travel that a real camera records on a fast object. It makes motion read as smooth and filmic; without it, fast motion strobes.
cards.phrase: natural directional motion blur on fast-moving elements, like a 180-degree film shutter

cards.name: Moving hold
cards.desc: Even when a character or object is "still", a tiny amount of motion keeps it alive: breathing, a slow drift, a blink. A dead-still hold looks like the animation froze.
cards.phrase: a subtle moving hold: when at rest, keep a slow breathing scale and gentle drift so it never looks frozen

cards.name: On twos
cards.aka: animating on twos, limited animation, low frame rate
cards.desc: Holding each drawing for two frames (12 per second) instead of one (24). Choppier but more graphic and hand-made; much classic and modern 2D animation is on twos, and on threes or fours for stylized moments.
cards.phrase: animate on twos (12 drawings per second) for a choppy, hand-drawn feel

cards.name: Weight
cards.desc: How heavy something feels comes from how it starts, stops and lands. Heavy things accelerate slowly, hit hard and shake the world; light things drift, flutter and barely land.
cards.phrase: make it feel heavy: slow to start, a hard landing and a small screen shake on impact

cards.name: Cycle
cards.desc: A short sequence that ends where it starts so it can repeat forever, like a walk, a run, a flag waving or a wheel turning. Most game and background animation is built from cycles.
cards.phrase: a seamless cycle that ends exactly where it starts, like a walk cycle, so it loops forever

cards.name: Motion path
cards.aka: path animation, follow path, orient to path
cards.desc: An element travels along a drawn curve and turns to face its direction of travel, like a paper plane looping across the screen.
cards.phrase: animate along a curved motion path, auto-oriented so it turns to face the direction of travel

cards.name: Shape morph
cards.desc: One shape smoothly turns into another: a play icon into a pause icon, a square into a circle, a button into a panel. Keeps continuity so people see that it is the same thing changing.
cards.phrase: morph the shape smoothly from one form to the next instead of swapping it

cards.name: Fade
cards.desc: The new content simply appears by fading in over the old. The quietest transition; safe for content changes that have no spatial relationship.
cards.phrase: a simple fade-in (opacity 0 to 1 over 200ms) for content changes

cards.name: Crossfade
cards.desc: The old content fades out while the new fades in, overlapping. Material's "fade through" fades out first and then in, so the two never blend into mush.
cards.phrase: a fade-through: the old view fades out over 90ms, then the new one fades and scales in from 92 percent over 210ms

cards.name: Push
cards.desc: The new screen slides in from the right while the old one slides a shorter distance left, as if on a strip. The standard way to go deeper in a hierarchy on phones; back reverses it.
cards.phrase: a push navigation transition: the new screen slides in from the right while the old one shifts left by a third with a slight dim

cards.name: Cover
cards.aka: modal slide-up, sheet present, slide over
cards.desc: The new layer slides up over the current one, which stays put and dims behind. Signals a temporary task you will dismiss to return to where you were.
cards.phrase: present it as a cover: the new layer slides up from the bottom over the dimmed current screen

cards.name: Reveal
cards.desc: The top layer slides away to uncover what was already underneath. The reverse of cover, used for dismissing a sheet or swiping a card off a stack.
cards.phrase: an uncover transition: the top layer slides away to reveal the screen already underneath

cards.name: Zoom
cards.aka: scale transition, zoom through, depth transition
cards.desc: The old screen scales up and fades as if you are moving through it, and the new one scales in from slightly smaller. Suggests going deeper on the Z axis.
cards.phrase: a zoom transition: the old view scales up to 110 percent and fades while the new one scales in from 90 percent

cards.name: Shared element
cards.aka: hero transition, magic move, matched geometry
cards.desc: An element that exists on both screens, like a thumbnail, flies and grows into its new position while the rest fades around it. Tells people exactly what they tapped and where it went.
cards.phrase: a shared-element transition: the tapped thumbnail grows and moves into the detail header while the rest crossfades

cards.name: Container transform
cards.desc: A card or button grows to become the whole next screen, morphing its corners, color and content on the way. Keeps a strong sense that the new screen came out of what you tapped.
cards.phrase: a container transform: the tapped card expands, morphing its shape and color, into the full detail screen

cards.name: Card flip
cards.desc: The element turns over in 3D to show its back. Natural for two-sided things like cards, tickets or settings behind a widget.
cards.phrase: a 3D card flip around the vertical axis with perspective, revealing the back side

cards.name: Circular reveal
cards.desc: The new view grows out of the tap point as an expanding circle. Ties the change directly to the spot that caused it.
cards.phrase: a circular reveal: the new view expands from the tap point as a growing circle (clip-path)

cards.name: Expand and collapse
cards.desc: A row grows to show more and the rows below slide down to make room, instead of jumping. Keeps context while adding detail.
cards.phrase: expand the row in place, animating its height while the content below slides down smoothly

cards.name: Directional tab slide
cards.desc: Switching tabs slides the content in the direction of the tab you picked, and the underline glides to it. Spatially consistent: tabs to the right are "to the right".
cards.phrase: switching tabs slides the content in the direction of the chosen tab while the indicator glides under it

cards.name: Dialog pop
cards.desc: A dark scrim fades over the page while the dialog scales up from about 90 percent with a slight overshoot. Focus moves to the dialog without a jarring jump.
cards.phrase: the dialog scales in from 90 percent with a slight overshoot while a dark scrim fades in behind it

cards.name: Hard cut
cards.desc: One shot simply replaces the next on a single frame. Invisible when well placed, and by far the most common edit in film.
cards.phrase: hard cuts between shots, no transitions

cards.name: Match cut
cards.desc: A cut between two shots that share a shape, motion or composition, so one seems to turn into the other. A setting sun cuts to a rising moon in the same spot.
cards.phrase: a match cut: the sun at frame center cuts to the moon in exactly the same position and size

cards.name: Jump cut
cards.desc: Cutting within the same shot so the subject jumps forward in time. Feels restless, modern or comic, and compresses time; standard in vlogs and the French New Wave.
cards.phrase: jump cuts within the same framing to compress time, the subject popping to new positions

cards.name: Smash cut
cards.desc: An abrupt cut from a quiet moment to a loud, jarring one (or the reverse), for shock or comedy. The contrast is the point.
cards.phrase: a smash cut from the calm, quiet shot straight to a loud, chaotic one with no warning

cards.name: J-cut and L-cut
cards.aka: split edit, audio lead, audio lag
cards.desc: Sound and picture change at different moments. In a J-cut you hear the next shot before you see it; in an L-cut the sound of the last shot carries over the new picture. Makes edits feel smooth and conversational.
cards.phrase: use J-cuts so the next scene's sound starts a beat before its picture

cards.name: Dissolve
cards.desc: One shot gradually blends into the next. Suggests the passing of time, a change of place or a dreamy, reflective mood. Overused, it feels like a wedding video.
cards.phrase: a slow cross dissolve between the two shots to suggest time passing

cards.name: Fade to black
cards.aka: fade out, fade in, dip to black
cards.desc: The picture fades to black, holds, then fades up on the next scene. A strong full stop: the end of a chapter, a death, or the end of the film.
cards.phrase: fade to black, hold a beat, then fade up on the next scene

cards.name: Dip to white
cards.desc: Like a fade to black but through white. Reads as memory, a flashback, an explosion of light or a spiritual moment.
cards.phrase: dip to white between the shots, like a flash of memory

cards.name: Wipe
cards.desc: The new shot pushes across the frame behind a moving edge. Deliberately old-fashioned and playful; Star Wars made it a signature.
cards.phrase: a hard-edged horizontal wipe from left to right into the next shot

cards.name: Iris
cards.aka: iris out, iris in, circle wipe
cards.desc: The picture shrinks to a circle on one detail and closes to black, or opens from one. Pure silent-film and cartoon nostalgia, often used as a wink.
cards.phrase: an iris out: the frame closes to a shrinking circle around the subject, then to black

cards.name: Whip-pan transition
cards.desc: The camera whips so fast that the frame becomes a blur, and the next shot whips in from the same blur. Energetic; Edgar Wright and travel videos love it.
cards.phrase: a whip-pan transition: both shots blur sideways through a fast swish

cards.name: Hidden cut
cards.desc: The cut is hidden under a moment when the frame is filled by something dark or blurred, like a passing person or a pillar, to fake a single continuous take.
cards.phrase: hide the cut under a dark foreground object passing the lens, so it reads as one continuous take

cards.name: Zoom transition
cards.desc: The camera zooms hard into the first shot with a radial blur and lands, mid-zoom, inside the next. Popular in reels, vlogs and trailers.
cards.phrase: a zoom transition: punch hard into the first shot with zoom blur and land in the next shot mid-zoom

cards.name: Flash and light leak
cards.aka: flash frame, light leak, film burn
cards.desc: A burst of warm light or a white flash covers the cut, like light leaking onto film or a camera flash. Nostalgic, warm and a little analog.
cards.phrase: cover the cut with a warm orange light leak, like light bleeding onto film

cards.name: Glitch transition
cards.desc: A few frames of slices, color splits and jitter as the picture changes, as if the signal broke. Techy, edgy and electronic.
cards.phrase: a short glitch transition with RGB split and horizontal slice jitter at the cut

cards.name: Press
cards.aka: tap scale, pressed state, button squish
cards.desc: The button shrinks a few percent while pressed and springs back on release, like a physical key. The most basic tactile feedback.
cards.phrase: buttons scale to 96 percent while pressed and spring back on release

cards.name: Hover lift
cards.desc: On hover, a card rises slightly and its shadow grows, inviting a click. Desktop only, so never hide essential information behind it.
cards.phrase: cards lift 4px with a larger, softer shadow on hover over 150ms

cards.name: Ripple
cards.desc: A circle of color spreads out from the exact point you touched and fades. Material Design's signature feedback.
cards.phrase: a Material-style ripple spreading from the touch point and fading out

cards.name: Toggle switch
cards.desc: The knob slides across with a small spring while the track changes color. A stretchy knob mid-slide adds a nice tactile touch.
cards.phrase: the toggle knob slides with a snappy spring, stretching slightly mid-move, while the track fades to the accent color

cards.name: Check draw
cards.desc: The box fills and the checkmark draws itself in one quick stroke. A tiny moment of satisfaction on to-do lists and forms.
cards.phrase: when checked, the box fills and the checkmark draws itself in a quick stroke

cards.name: Like burst
cards.desc: The heart pops bigger, fills with color and throws off a ring of tiny particles. Rewarding enough that people tap it just to see it.
cards.phrase: on like, the heart pops to 120 percent with a spring, fills red and bursts a ring of small particles

cards.name: Shake
cards.desc: A field shakes quickly side to side, like a head saying no, when input is wrong. Pair it with a clear message, since the shake alone says nothing about what went wrong.
cards.phrase: on an error, shake the field side to side three times over 400ms and show a red message below

cards.name: Success check
cards.desc: A circle draws itself around, then a checkmark ticks in, often with a small scale pop. The universal "it worked".
cards.phrase: a success state: a circle draws around, then a checkmark ticks in with a small pop

cards.name: Toast
cards.desc: A small message slides up from the edge, waits a few seconds and slides away on its own. Good for confirming an action without interrupting.
cards.phrase: a toast slides up from the bottom with a spring, stays four seconds and slides back down

cards.name: Label swap
cards.desc: The button's own label slides out and a confirmation like "Copied" slides in, then reverts. Feedback right where you were looking.
cards.phrase: after copying, the button label slides up and out as "Copied ✓" slides in, reverting after 1.5 seconds

cards.name: Tooltip
cards.desc: A small label fades in and nudges toward its target after a short hover delay, and leaves faster than it came. The delay prevents flicker as the cursor passes by.
cards.phrase: tooltips appear after a 300ms hover delay, fading and sliding 4px toward the target, and vanish instantly on leave

cards.name: Badge pop
cards.desc: A notification badge pops in with an overshoot, and its number bumps when it changes. Draws the eye without a sound or a modal.
cards.phrase: the notification badge pops in with an overshoot and bumps each time the count changes

cards.name: Spinner
cards.desc: An endlessly rotating arc for short, unknown waits. The arc that grows and shrinks as it spins feels less mechanical than a plain rotating ring.
cards.phrase: a spinner whose arc grows and shrinks as it rotates, for short unknown waits

cards.name: Typing dots
cards.aka: typing indicator, bouncing dots, ellipsis loader
cards.desc: Three dots rise and fall one after another. In chat it means someone is typing; elsewhere it is a friendly, low-key loader.
cards.phrase: a typing indicator of three dots bouncing in sequence inside a chat bubble

cards.name: Skeleton shimmer
cards.aka: skeleton screen, placeholder shimmer, ghost loading
cards.desc: Grey shapes in the layout of the coming content, with a soft highlight sweeping across. Feels faster than a spinner because the page seems to be already arriving.
cards.phrase: skeleton placeholders in the shape of the real content with a soft shimmer sweeping left to right

cards.name: Progress bar
cards.desc: A bar that fills to show how much is done. When the length is known, it is always better than a spinner. Slightly speeding up near the end makes it feel faster.
cards.phrase: a determinate progress bar with a percent label, easing slightly faster toward the end

cards.name: Indeterminate bar
cards.desc: A segment that keeps sliding along the track when progress cannot be measured. Common as a thin bar at the very top of a page during navigation.
cards.phrase: a thin indeterminate loading bar along the top edge, a segment sliding across repeatedly

cards.name: Pull to refresh
cards.desc: Dragging the list down past the top reveals a spinner that fills as you pull; letting go starts the refresh and the list springs back when done.
cards.phrase: pull to refresh: the list drags down to reveal a spinner that fills with the pull, then springs back after loading

cards.name: Number roll
cards.desc: Numbers roll up to their value like an odometer instead of appearing. Draws attention to a changing total and makes it feel earned.
cards.phrase: numbers roll up to their new value digit by digit, like an odometer, with an expo ease-out

cards.name: Stateful button
cards.desc: The button itself shows the whole journey: it shrinks into a spinner while working, then turns into a checkmark. People never have to look away from what they tapped.
cards.phrase: on submit, the button morphs into a circular spinner, then into a green checkmark when done

cards.name: Drag and drop
cards.desc: The item lifts as you grab it (bigger, tilted, with a deep shadow), follows the pointer, and settles into its new spot with a spring. The drop zone highlights when you are over it.
cards.phrase: when dragged, the card lifts with a larger shadow and slight tilt, the drop zone highlights, and it springs into place on release

cards.name: Reorder
cards.desc: As one row is dragged, the others slide out of its way to show where it will land. Nothing jumps; every row moves to its new place.
cards.phrase: while reordering, the other rows slide smoothly out of the way to open a gap where the dragged row will land

cards.name: Swipe to dismiss
cards.desc: The item follows a sideways swipe, fades as it travels, and flies off once past a threshold. The rest of the list closes the gap.
cards.phrase: swipe to dismiss: the item follows the finger, fades past the threshold and flies off, then the list closes the gap

cards.name: Swipe actions
cards.desc: Swiping a row sideways slides it over to reveal buttons hidden underneath, like Archive or Delete. A full swipe can trigger the action directly.
cards.phrase: swiping a row left reveals Archive and Delete actions underneath, snapping open with a spring

cards.name: Pinch to zoom
cards.desc: Two fingers spread to scale content around the point between them. On release it eases to a sensible zoom level and springs back if pushed too far.
cards.phrase: pinch to zoom around the fingers' midpoint, easing to the nearest zoom level and rubber-banding past the limits

cards.name: Bottom sheet detents
cards.desc: A sheet that can be dragged between set heights (peek, half, full) and snaps to the nearest one with a spring. Map apps use it to keep the map visible while browsing results.
cards.phrase: a draggable bottom sheet with peek, half and full detents, snapping to the nearest one with a spring

cards.name: Carousel snap
cards.desc: Cards slide with your swipe and snap so one sits neatly in place, with the next peeking in to show there is more. Pager dots follow along.
cards.phrase: a swipeable carousel that snaps each card to center, with the next card peeking and pager dots tracking

cards.name: Long-press menu
cards.aka: context menu bloom, press and hold
cards.desc: Holding a finger down makes the item shrink slightly, then lift as a menu blooms out of it. The growing press tells you something is about to happen.
cards.phrase: long-press: the item shrinks slightly while held, then lifts and a context menu blooms out from it

cards.name: Parallax
cards.desc: Background layers scroll slower than the foreground, which creates a sense of depth like looking out of a train window.
cards.phrase: subtle parallax: the background image scrolls at about 40 percent of the content's speed

cards.name: Scroll reveal
cards.aka: fade up on scroll, reveal on enter, AOS
cards.desc: Blocks fade and rise slightly as they enter the viewport. Gives a long page a gentle rhythm. Keep the move small (about 20px) and only animate once.
cards.phrase: blocks fade in and rise 20px as they scroll into view, once only, with a 60ms stagger within each row

cards.name: Pinned section
cards.desc: A section sticks in place while you keep scrolling, and the scroll drives what happens inside it, like images swapping or a product turning. Then it releases and the page moves on.
cards.phrase: pin the feature section while scrolling drives three steps inside it, then release

cards.name: Scrollytelling
cards.aka: scroll-driven story, steps and sticky graphic
cards.desc: Text steps scroll by on one side while a pinned graphic on the other side changes with each step. The New York Times and The Pudding made it the standard for data stories.
cards.phrase: scrollytelling: text steps scroll past while a sticky chart beside them updates at each step

cards.name: Scroll progress
cards.desc: A thin bar at the top fills as you read down the page, so you know how much is left. Simple and useful on long articles.
cards.phrase: a thin reading-progress bar at the top that fills as the page scrolls

cards.name: Horizontal scroll section
cards.desc: Scrolling down moves a row of panels sideways while the section is pinned, like flipping through a gallery. Fun, but give it an obvious end.
cards.phrase: a pinned section where scrolling down moves a row of panels horizontally, then releases

cards.name: Scroll-linked zoom
cards.aka: expanding hero, image grows on scroll
cards.desc: A framed image grows to fill the whole screen as you scroll, as if you are walking into it. A dramatic way to open a story.
cards.phrase: as the page scrolls, the inset hero image expands to full-bleed, its corners squaring off

cards.name: Scroll text highlight
cards.desc: A large paragraph starts faded and each word fills in as you scroll, so reading pace follows scrolling. A popular storytelling device on product sites.
cards.phrase: a large statement where each word fills from 20 percent to full opacity as the page scrolls

cards.name: Shrinking header
cards.aka: condensing header, compact nav on scroll
cards.desc: A tall header with a big title condenses into a slim bar as you scroll, and the title shrinks into it. Saves space while keeping your place.
cards.phrase: a large header that condenses into a slim sticky bar on scroll, the title shrinking into it

cards.name: Marquee
cards.desc: A band of text or logos sliding endlessly at a constant speed. Loud and energetic in big type; calm as a slow logo strip.
cards.phrase: an infinite marquee band of large text scrolling left at a steady linear speed

cards.name: Full-page snap
cards.desc: Each scroll moves exactly one full-screen section and snaps to it, like flipping slides. Good for short story-like pages; frustrating for long reading.
cards.phrase: full-screen sections that snap one at a time on scroll

cards.name: Cursor follower
cards.desc: A circle that trails the pointer with a little lag and grows over clickable things. Common on creative portfolios; easy to overdo.
cards.phrase: a soft circular cursor follower that trails the pointer with lag and grows over links

cards.name: Magnetic button
cards.desc: As the pointer comes near, the button leans toward it as if magnetized, then snaps back when the pointer leaves. A playful touch for one key button.
cards.phrase: a magnetic button that leans toward the nearby cursor and springs back when it leaves

cards.name: 3D hover tilt
cards.aka: tilt card, parallax tilt, holo card
cards.desc: A card rotates slightly in 3D to face the pointer, with a glare that slides across it. Feels physical, like turning a trading card in your hand.
cards.phrase: cards tilt up to 10 degrees in 3D toward the cursor, with a soft glare sliding across the surface

cards.name: Hover spotlight
cards.desc: A soft glow follows the pointer across a dark grid of cards and lights up the borders it passes. A favorite on developer-tool landing pages.
cards.phrase: a soft radial spotlight follows the cursor across dark cards, lighting up the borders it passes

cards.name: Locked-off shot
cards.aka: static shot, tripod shot, locked camera
cards.desc: The camera does not move at all; only the world inside the frame does. Calm, observational and painterly. For image-to-video it is the most reliable way to keep a still image intact.
cards.phrase: a locked-off static camera; only the clouds and grass move

cards.name: Pan
cards.aka: pan left, pan right, horizontal pan
cards.desc: The camera turns left or right on a fixed tripod, sweeping across the scene. No parallax, since the camera does not change position. Reveals a landscape or follows a subject across the frame.
cards.phrase: a slow pan right across the landscape from a fixed tripod

cards.name: Tilt
cards.desc: The camera pivots up or down from a fixed point. Tilting up from feet to face, or from ground to sky, makes a reveal; tilting down can make a subject feel small.
cards.phrase: a slow tilt up from the ground to the sky

cards.name: Zoom
cards.aka: zoom in, zoom out, lens zoom
cards.desc: The lens changes focal length to magnify the scene; the camera itself stays put. Everything scales together with no parallax, which looks more artificial than a dolly, and more 1970s.
cards.phrase: a slow optical zoom in on the figure, the camera itself not moving

cards.name: Dolly in
cards.aka: push in, track in, move in
cards.desc: The camera physically moves toward the subject. Unlike a zoom, near things grow faster than far ones, so the space opens up around you. The classic way to build intensity or intimacy.
cards.phrase: the camera dollies in toward the figure; the foreground slides out of frame while the mountains barely grow

cards.name: Dolly out
cards.aka: pull out, track out, move back
cards.desc: The camera moves backward away from the subject, revealing more of the surroundings and leaving the subject smaller. Feels like leaving, loneliness or an ending.
cards.phrase: the camera dollies slowly back, leaving the figure small in the wide landscape

cards.name: Truck
cards.aka: tracking shot sideways, crab, lateral dolly
cards.desc: The camera slides sideways, parallel to the scene. Near objects pass quickly and far ones slowly, which gives strong depth. Often done on rails or a slider.
cards.phrase: the camera trucks left on a slider, with strong parallax between the foreground grass and the distant mountains

cards.name: Pedestal
cards.desc: The whole camera rises or lowers vertically without tilting. Near objects shift more than far ones. Smaller and subtler than a crane.
cards.phrase: the camera pedestals up slowly, rising vertically without tilting

cards.name: Roll
cards.aka: Dutch angle, canted frame, barrel roll
cards.desc: The camera rotates around the lens axis so the horizon tilts. Held, it is a Dutch angle that signals unease; in motion it disorients.
cards.phrase: the camera slowly rolls into a 12-degree Dutch angle, the horizon tilting

cards.name: Slow push-in
cards.desc: A barely perceptible dolly toward the subject over the whole shot. Builds tension or significance without the viewer noticing the camera at all. The safest move for animating a still image.
cards.phrase: a very slow, steady push-in over the whole shot, barely perceptible

cards.name: Pull-back reveal
cards.desc: Starts tight on a detail and pulls back to reveal the surprising wider context. A storytelling move: the punchline is what was just outside the frame.
cards.phrase: start tight on the figure and pull back to reveal the vast empty landscape around them

cards.name: Dolly zoom
cards.desc: The camera dollies one way while the lens zooms the other, so the subject stays the same size but the background stretches or swells behind them. Pure dread or revelation.
cards.phrase: a dolly zoom: the figure stays the same size while the background swells and warps behind them

cards.name: Orbit
cards.desc: The camera circles around the subject, keeping it centered while the background sweeps behind. Heroic and dramatic; a slow half-orbit is a staple of product and music videos.
cards.phrase: a slow orbit around the figure, keeping them centered as the background sweeps behind

cards.name: Crane up
cards.aka: jib shot, boom up, rising reveal
cards.desc: The camera rises high on a crane or jib, lifting over the foreground to reveal the whole scene. Grand and expansive; a classic opening or closing shot.
cards.phrase: a crane shot rising over the foreground to reveal the full landscape below

cards.name: Tracking shot
cards.desc: The camera moves alongside a moving subject and keeps pace, so the subject stays in place while the world streams past behind. Immersive and kinetic.
cards.phrase: a tracking shot keeping pace beside the walking figure as the landscape streams past

cards.name: Whip pan
cards.desc: A pan so fast the image smears into blur, snapping from one subject to another. Comic timing, energy or a transition.
cards.phrase: a whip pan: the camera snaps sideways so fast the frame blurs, landing on the next subject

cards.name: Crash zoom
cards.desc: A sudden, very fast zoom into a face or detail. Instant comic emphasis or shock, straight out of kung-fu films and reality TV.
cards.phrase: a sudden crash zoom straight in on the figure

cards.name: Rack focus
cards.desc: The focus shifts from something near to something far (or back), guiding the eye between them without moving the camera.
