cards.phrase: a Wear OS list using TransformingLazyColumn inside ScreenScaffold (shared rememberTransformingLazyColumnState for the curved ScrollIndicator), each item with Modifier.transformedHeight(this, transformationSpec) and transformation = SurfaceTransformation(transformationSpec), full-width pill Buttons, a ListHeader, curved TimeText at the top and rotary crown scrolling

cards.name: Tiles
cards.desc: Full-screen glanceable cards people reach by swiping sideways from the watch face. Each shows one thing at a glance, like today's water count or the next meeting, laid out in a title slot, a main slot and a bottom slot with one action.
cards.phrase: a Wear OS tile built with TileService and ProtoLayout Material 3 primaryLayout: an icon and short title in titleSlot, one large glanceable value with a circular progress arc in mainSlot, and an edge button action (textEdgeButton or iconEdgeButton) in bottomSlot, using dynamic system colors and refreshing on a freshness interval

cards.name: Wavy progress and the round screen
cards.aka: circular progress, bezel progress, edge progress ring
cards.desc: On a round watch, progress runs as a ring around the edge of the screen or around a central button instead of a straight bar. Material 3 Expressive gives the filled part a gentle wave while it moves, and leaves a gap at the top for the time.
cards.phrase: round-screen progress for Wear OS: a full-screen CircularProgressIndicator along the bezel with a gap at the top for curved TimeText, or a smaller ring around the play/pause button for media, with the expressive wavy style while playing; use SegmentedCircularProgressIndicator for step goals, and keep the key number large in the center

cards.name: Windows, volumes and immersive spaces
cards.aka: WindowGroup, volumetric window, ImmersiveSpace, Shared Space and Full Space
cards.desc: Apps start as flat glass windows that sit beside other apps. A volume is a bounded 3D box for an object people can walk around, and an immersive space takes over the surroundings, from partly to fully.
cards.phrase: a visionOS app that starts in a glass window (WindowGroup), opens a 3D model in a volume (.windowStyle(.volumetric) with a RealityView), and offers an ImmersiveSpace (.immersionStyle(.mixed, .progressive, .full)) opened with openImmersiveSpace for focused moments

cards.name: Ornaments
cards.aka: toolbar ornament, tab bar ornament, attached accessory view
cards.desc: Controls that float just outside a window's edge, slightly in front of it, so they never cover the content. The tab bar becomes a vertical strip on the leading side that expands to show labels when you look at it, and toolbars sit along the bottom edge.
cards.phrase: visionOS ornaments: a TabView that renders as the vertical tab bar ornament on the window's leading edge, and the main controls in a bottom ornament (.toolbar with ToolbarItem(placement: .bottomOrnament), or .ornament(attachmentAnchor: .scene(.bottom))) overlapping the window edge

cards.name: Look-to-highlight and indirect pinch
cards.aka: hover effect, gaze and pinch, indirect gesture, hoverEffect
cards.desc: Whatever the person looks at gently brightens, so they know what a pinch will hit. They tap by pinching thumb and finger together with the hand resting anywhere, and the app never learns where the eyes are until they pinch.
cards.phrase: every interactive element uses system buttons or .hoverEffect() (with .contentShape for the hit area) so it highlights when looked at, targets at least 60 pt with spacing between them, actions on the standard tap gesture (indirect pinch), and no custom gaze tracking since eye position is private

cards.name: Glass windows that adapt to the room
cards.aka: visionOS glass material, glassBackgroundEffect, spatial glass
cards.desc: visionOS windows are made of a glass material that lets the room show through and picks up its light and color, so an app looks right in a bright kitchen or a dim living room. Text is white with vibrant secondary colors, and there are no light or dark modes.
cards.phrase: visionOS windows on the system glass material (.glassBackgroundEffect()), white primary text with vibrant secondary styles (.secondary, .tertiary), no opaque or solid-color backgrounds, so the window picks up the light and color of the room around it

cards.name: Menu bar and app menus
cards.aka: main menu, application menu, NSMenu, menu strip (Windows)
cards.desc: The row of text menus (File, Edit, View, Window, Help) at the top of the screen on macOS, or at the top of the window on Windows and Linux. Every command lives in it, with its keyboard shortcut on the right.
cards.phrase: a complete native menu bar (File, Edit, View, Window, Help) with the standard items, shortcuts right-aligned, checkmarks on toggles and unavailable items grayed out (SwiftUI .commands / Electron Menu.setApplicationMenu)

cards.name: Unified toolbar
cards.aka: title bar toolbar, NSToolbar, command bar (Windows)
cards.desc: The window title and the most used actions share one strip at the top: window controls, a title, icon buttons and a search field all on the same row. It saves height and makes the window read as one surface.
cards.phrase: a unified title bar and toolbar in one row: window controls, sidebar toggle, title with a subtitle, then a few icon-only toolbar buttons and a search field on the right (SwiftUI .toolbar + .searchable, .windowToolbarStyle(.unified))

cards.name: Three-pane layout
cards.aka: source list + list + detail, master-detail, NavigationSplitView
cards.desc: A sidebar of sources on the left, a list of items in the middle, and the selected item in full on the right. You work left to right: pick a folder, pick an item, read it.
cards.phrase: a three-pane layout: a collapsible sidebar of sources with unread counts, a scrollable list of items showing title, preview and time, and a detail pane for the selected item, with dividers you can drag to resize (SwiftUI NavigationSplitView with sidebar, content and detail columns)

cards.name: Inspector panel
cards.aka: properties panel, attributes inspector, right sidebar
cards.desc: A panel on the right that shows and edits the properties of whatever is selected: size, position, color, options. It changes with the selection and can be hidden to give the canvas more room.
cards.phrase: a collapsible inspector panel on the right showing the selected object's properties in labeled sections (Layout, Fill, Opacity) with compact numeric fields and sliders that update the canvas live (SwiftUI .inspector(isPresented:))

cards.name: Menu bar extra
cards.aka: tray app, status item, menu bar app, system tray icon (Windows), NSStatusItem
cards.desc: An app that lives as a small icon in the menu bar or system tray and opens a compact panel when clicked, often with no main window at all. It runs in the background and stays one click away.
cards.phrase: a menu bar extra with no Dock icon: a monochrome template icon that opens a small panel with status at the top, a few recent items, a pause toggle, and Open and Quit at the bottom (SwiftUI MenuBarExtra with .menuBarExtraStyle(.window), LSUIElement = YES)

cards.name: Keyboard launcher
cards.aka: Spotlight-style search, command bar, quick switcher, command palette
cards.desc: A floating search box opened by a global shortcut that finds apps, files and commands as you type. Arrow keys move through results, Return runs the selected one, and it disappears when you are done.
cards.phrase: a keyboard launcher: a floating centered panel opened by a global hotkey, a large search field, results grouped by type with icons and the matched letters bold, the first result preselected, ↑↓ to move, Return to run, ⌘K for more actions on the selection, Esc to dismiss

cards.name: Document tabs and windows
cards.desc: Each open document gets its own tab or window, and tabs can be dragged out into a new window or merged back. People can put two documents side by side.
cards.phrase: a document-based app with native window tabs: each document opens in a tab, tabs reorder by dragging, a tab dragged out becomes its own window and can be merged back, ⌘T opens a new tab and ⌘W closes one (SwiftUI DocumentGroup / NSWindow.tabbingMode)

cards.name: Context menu
cards.aka: right-click menu, shortcut menu, secondary-click menu
cards.desc: A menu that opens at the pointer on right-click with the actions for the thing under it. It repeats the common menu bar commands and shows their shortcuts, so people learn them over time.
cards.phrase: right-click context menus on every item with the relevant actions grouped by separators, shortcuts right-aligned, submenus marked with ›, and destructive actions last in red (SwiftUI .contextMenu)

cards.name: Settings window
cards.desc: A separate small window opened with ⌘, (Ctrl+, on Windows) that has a row of icon tabs across the top and a short form of labeled options below. Changes apply right away, with no Save button.
cards.phrase: a native Settings window opened with ⌘, : icon tabs in the toolbar (General, Accounts, Appearance, Advanced), a centered form with right-aligned labels, and every change applied instantly without a Save button (SwiftUI Settings scene with a TabView of Forms)

cards.name: Status bar
cards.aka: footer bar, status strip, IDE status bar
cards.desc: A thin strip along the bottom of the window with small clickable readouts: branch, errors, cursor position, encoding, language, sync state. Each item opens the thing it describes.
cards.phrase: a thin status bar along the bottom of the window: workspace state on the left (branch, sync, error and warning counts), current-file details on the right (line and column, encoding, language), each item clickable with a tooltip

cards.name: Drag and drop
cards.aka: DnD, drag to move, drag to copy
cards.desc: Pick up items with the mouse and drop them somewhere else: onto a folder, into another app, or into a new position in a list. A ghost of the items follows the pointer with a count badge, and the target lights up.
cards.phrase: drag and drop for moving items: a semi-transparent drag preview with a count badge, a highlighted drop target, an insertion line when reordering, a green + badge when Option copies instead of moves, and files from other apps accepted (SwiftUI .draggable / .dropDestination)

cards.name: Windows custom title bar
cards.aka: extended title bar, Mica title bar, tall title bar with search
cards.desc: The app draws its own content into the title bar of a Windows 11 window: a back button, the app icon and title, a search box in the middle and an account picture, while keeping the standard minimize, maximize and close buttons. The whole window sits on Mica, a material faintly tinted by the desktop wallpaper.
cards.phrase: a Windows 11 custom title bar with the WinUI 3 TitleBar control (Windows App SDK 1.7): ExtendsContentIntoTitleBar = true, SetTitleBar(titleBar), back button, app icon, title and subtitle, an AutoSuggestBox in the Content slot for search, the account PersonPicture in the RightHeader, standard caption buttons, the empty areas left as drag regions, and Window.SystemBackdrop = new MicaBackdrop()

cards.name: Windows NavigationView, InfoBar and TeachingTip
cards.aka: left nav pane, hamburger pane, info bar, coach mark, teaching tip
cards.desc: The standard Windows app frame: a collapsible pane of top-level pages on the left with a small accent pill on the current one and Settings pinned at the bottom. An InfoBar is a colored strip inside the page for a status that needs attention, and a TeachingTip is a small callout that points at a control to introduce it.
cards.phrase: a WinUI 3 app shell: NavigationView with PaneDisplayMode="Auto" (Left when wide, LeftCompact or LeftMinimal when narrow), NavigationViewItems with icons and an InfoBadge count, IsSettingsVisible for the built-in Settings item; an InfoBar at the top of the page (Severity="Warning", Title, Message, an ActionButton, IsClosable) for app status; and a TeachingTip with Target set to a new toolbar button, Title, Subtitle and a close button, shown once

cards.name: GNOME header bar and adaptive split view
cards.aka: libadwaita split view, headerbar, CSD title bar, sidebar layout
cards.desc: A GNOME app has no separate title bar or menu bar: each pane gets a flat header bar with its own buttons, the sidebar and content sit side by side, and when the window gets narrow the two collapse into pages you move between with a back button. Toggle groups switch modes and toasts confirm actions with Undo.
cards.phrase: a GTK 4 / libadwaita 1.7 layout: AdwNavigationSplitView with an AdwToolbarView and AdwHeaderBar in each pane, the sidebar as a navigation-sidebar list, an AdwBreakpoint (max-width: 400sp) setting collapsed = true so it becomes a single page with a back button, an AdwToggleGroup in the content header bar to switch Edit and Preview, and AdwToastOverlay toasts with an Undo button

cards.name: macOS inset glass sidebar and sheets
cards.aka: Liquid Glass sidebar, floating sidebar, background extension, window-attached sheet
cards.desc: In macOS Tahoe the sidebar floats as a pane of Liquid Glass inset from the window edges, and the content can extend behind it, mirrored and blurred, so a photo or map seems to run under the glass. Sheets stay attached to their window and block only that window, not the whole app.
cards.phrase: a macOS 26 (Tahoe) window with SwiftUI NavigationSplitView: the system inset Liquid Glass sidebar with traffic lights inside it, the detail's hero image using .backgroundExtensionEffect() so it extends mirrored and blurred under the sidebar, toolbar items in glass capsules over the content, and window-attached sheets via .sheet with capsule Cancel and default buttons; no custom sidebar background

cards.name: Native Mac app
cards.aka: Mac-assed Mac app, AppKit look, macOS HIG
cards.desc: Follows macOS conventions closely: a translucent sidebar, a unified toolbar, SF Pro at 13pt, small controls, the system accent color, and a full menu bar with shortcuts. It feels like Apple made it, not like a website in a window.
cards.phrase: a native Mac app feel: SwiftUI or AppKit with standard controls only, a translucent sidebar (NavigationSplitView), unified toolbar, SF Pro at system sizes, the system accent color, a full menu bar with shortcuts, light and dark mode, Liquid Glass on macOS 26, and no web-style custom chrome

cards.name: Windows 11 / WinUI
cards.aka: Fluent on Windows, WinUI 3, Mica and Acrylic
cards.desc: The Windows 11 look: a Mica window background faintly tinted by the wallpaper, a NavigationView on the left with a small accent pill on the selected item, rounded cards, Segoe UI Variable, and Acrylic blur on menus and flyouts.
cards.phrase: a native Windows 11 app: WinUI 3 (Windows App SDK) with a Mica backdrop (MicaBackdrop), NavigationView on the left, settings grouped in rounded cards (SettingsCard from the Windows Community Toolkit), Segoe UI Variable, the system accent color, Acrylic on flyouts, and an extended title bar with standard caption buttons

cards.name: GNOME / libadwaita
cards.desc: The modern GNOME look: one header bar with flat buttons and a centered title, rounded windows, boxed lists of settings rows on a soft gray background, pill-shaped blue buttons, and toasts at the bottom.
cards.phrase: a GNOME app built with GTK 4 and libadwaita: AdwHeaderBar with flat buttons and a centered title, AdwPreferencesGroup boxed lists of AdwActionRow and AdwSwitchRow, a pill-shaped suggested-action button, AdwToast for confirmations with Undo, following the GNOME HIG

cards.name: Pro app dark UI
cards.aka: pro tools look, dense dark interface, editor UI
cards.desc: A dark, neutral gray interface packed with small panels, numeric fields, timelines and meters, so the content (video, audio, 3D) is the brightest thing on screen. Color is saved for selection, state and the playhead.
cards.phrase: a pro-app dark UI: neutral dark grays (not pure black), dense dockable panels with 11–12px labels, scrubbable numeric fields, one accent color for selection and a red playhead, the content viewer as the brightest element, and a keyboard shortcut for every action

cards.name: Streaming response with stop button
cards.aka: token streaming, typewriter output, stop generating
cards.desc: The answer appears word by word as the model writes it, Markdown and all, and the send button becomes a Stop button until it finishes. If you scroll up, the view stops following and a jump-to-latest arrow appears.
cards.phrase: stream the reply token by token and render Markdown as it arrives, with a soft caret at the end; while streaming, the send button turns into a square Stop button (Esc also stops) and a stopped reply keeps its partial text; auto-scroll only while the user is at the bottom, otherwise show a round "jump to latest" arrow

cards.name: Prompt starters and follow-up chips
cards.aka: suggested prompts, conversation starters, suggestion chips, related questions
cards.desc: An empty chat offers a few ready-made prompts so people know what the assistant is good at. After each answer, chips suggest the likely next question in one tap.
cards.phrase: an empty state with a short greeting and 3 to 4 prompt starter cards specific to this product (a tap fills and sends the prompt), plus 2 to 3 follow-up suggestion chips under each finished answer, generated from the answer and hidden while streaming

cards.name: Context chips and attachments
cards.aka: @-mentions, context pills, attachments tray, add context
cards.desc: Files, images, docs and connected sources you add to a message show as small removable chips inside the composer. Typing @ opens a picker to pull in a file, a doc or a person without leaving the keyboard.
cards.phrase: a composer with an attachments row of removable chips (file icon, name, ✕; images as thumbnails) above the text, a paperclip button and drag-and-drop to add files, and an @-mention popover that filters files, docs and connected sources as you type, inserting the choice as an inline chip

cards.name: Model and mode picker
cards.aka: model switcher, mode toggles, tools menu, Think / Research / Plan mode
cards.desc: Controls in the composer that choose which model answers and how hard it works: a model menu, plus toggles like extended thinking, deep research or plan mode. The current choice stays visible so people know what they are talking to.
cards.phrase: a model picker as a compact dropdown in the composer's bottom-right showing the current model name, opening a menu with each model's one-line strength and a check on the active one; mode toggles (Think, Research, Plan) as pill buttons beside the + menu that light up when on and persist per chat

cards.name: Regenerate, edit and branch
cards.aka: retry, edit message, branching conversation, response versions
cards.desc: People can retry an answer or edit an earlier message, and each attempt becomes a new branch instead of overwriting the old one. A small "‹ 2 / 3 ›" pager under the message flips between versions.
cards.phrase: edit-and-branch history: a pencil on each user message opens it inline with Cancel / Save, retry on each reply, and every edit or retry creates a sibling branch shown with a "‹ 2 / 3 ›" pager under the message; switching branches swaps everything below it

cards.name: Voice mode
cards.desc: A hands-free conversation: a glowing orb or waveform reacts to who is speaking, a live transcript scrolls underneath, and big buttons mute or end the call. People can interrupt the model mid-sentence.
cards.phrase: a full-screen voice mode: a centered animated orb that pulses with the user's mic level and ripples while the model speaks, a live two-speaker transcript below with the current words highlighted, barge-in to interrupt, and large round Mute, captions and red End buttons at the bottom

cards.name: Reasoning disclosure
cards.aka: thinking block, "Thought for 12s", chain of thought, reasoning summary
cards.desc: While the model thinks, a shimmering "Thinking…" line shows it is working; when it finishes, the line becomes "Thought for 12s" and collapses. Opening it reveals the reasoning or a summary of it in muted text.
cards.phrase: a reasoning disclosure above each answer: a shimmering "Thinking…" label with elapsed time while it reasons, which collapses to "Thought for 12s ›" when the answer starts; expanding shows the reasoning summary in smaller muted text with a left rule, never mixed into the answer

cards.name: Agent trace
cards.aka: tool-call timeline, activity log, steps view, run trace
cards.desc: A vertical timeline of everything the agent did: each tool call is a row with an icon, a one-line summary and a status, and any row expands to show its input and output. The running step shimmers; finished steps get a check.
cards.phrase: an agent trace: a vertical timeline of tool calls, each row an icon, a short human summary ("Read checkout.ts", "Ran npm test · 2 failed"), duration and a status mark (spinner, ✓, ✗); rows expand to show the exact input and output in monospace; the current step shimmers, and a header shows step count, elapsed time and a Stop button

cards.name: Plan with live checklist
cards.aka: to-do list, task plan, agent plan, plan mode
cards.desc: Before or while it works, the agent writes its plan as a checklist and ticks items off live: done items are struck through, the current one is bold, the rest wait. People can read the plan and correct it before work starts.
cards.phrase: a live plan checklist the agent writes first and updates as it goes: ☒ done items struck through and dimmed, the in-progress item bold with a spinner, ☐ pending items plain, a "3 of 5" count; in plan mode the agent stops after writing the plan and asks for approval before editing anything

cards.name: Approval gate
cards.aka: human in the loop, permission prompt, tool confirmation, ask before acting
cards.desc: The agent pauses before a risky or irreversible action and shows exactly what it wants to do, with Allow once, Always allow and Deny. Saying no lets you tell it what to do instead.
cards.phrase: an approval gate before side-effecting tool calls: an inline card naming the tool and the exact action (recipient, command or amount in monospace), with Deny, Allow once and Always allow for this tool; the agent waits without timing out, Deny asks "what should I do instead?", and "always" rules are listed and revocable in settings

cards.name: Checkpoints and restore
cards.aka: rewind, restore checkpoint, undo agent changes, time travel
cards.desc: The app snapshots files and conversation before each agent turn, so you can jump back to any earlier message and undo everything the agent did after it. Restoring asks first and says how many files will change.
cards.phrase: automatic checkpoints before each agent turn: a "Restore checkpoint" button on hover between messages, a confirm popover listing the files that will revert ("Restore 3 files and drop 2 messages?"), options to restore code only, chat only or both, and a toast with Redo after restoring

cards.name: Background agent task
cards.aka: async agent, cloud task, long-running job, agent inbox
cards.desc: Long jobs run on their own while you do something else: a task list shows each one's status and progress, and a notification arrives when it finishes or needs input. Results wait as a reviewable result, like a pull request.
cards.phrase: background agent tasks: a task list with a status for each (Queued, Running with a progress bar and current step, Needs input, Ready to review), safe to close the app, plus a push notification and an in-app badge when a task finishes or needs a decision; opening a finished task shows its summary and diff to review

cards.name: Inline citations and sources
cards.aka: footnotes, source chips, grounding, references panel
cards.desc: Numbered markers sit right after the claims they support, and hovering one previews the source. A sources list or side panel collects every page, file or doc used, so people can check the answer themselves.
cards.phrase: inline citations: small numbered pills right after each supported sentence, a hover card previewing the source (favicon, site, title, quoted snippet), and a Sources panel listing every source in order with favicon and domain; uncited claims stay visually plain, never get a fake marker

cards.name: Message actions and feedback
cards.aka: copy / thumbs / retry, response actions, rate this answer
cards.desc: A quiet row of icons under each answer: copy, thumbs up, thumbs down, retry, share. A thumbs down opens a short form with reason chips, which is how teams learn what went wrong.
cards.phrase: message actions under each finished reply: icon buttons for copy (with a "Copied" confirmation), thumbs up, thumbs down, retry and more, hidden while streaming; thumbs down opens a small sheet with reason chips (Inaccurate, Didn't follow instructions, Too long, Unsafe) and an optional comment, logged with the message id

cards.name: Usage and context meters
cards.aka: context window indicator, token meter, rate-limit warning, quota bar
cards.desc: Meters show how full the conversation's context is and how much of the plan's usage is left, and a banner warns before a limit hits, with when it resets. No one should be cut off mid-task by surprise.
cards.phrase: usage and context meters: a small ring in the composer showing context used (tooltip "124k of 200k tokens"), a usage popover with bars for the current session and the week with reset times, and an amber banner above the composer at 80% ("You're close to your limit, resets at 3:00 PM") that offers the next step instead of only blocking

cards.name: Memory and incognito chat
cards.aka: saved memories, personalization, temporary chat, private mode
cards.desc: When the assistant saves something about you, a small "Memory updated" note appears in the chat and links to a page where you can see and delete it. An incognito or temporary chat switch starts a conversation that is not saved or remembered.
cards.phrase: visible memory: an inline "Memory updated" chip when something is saved (tap to view or forget it), a Memory settings page listing every saved fact with delete, and an incognito toggle in the chat header that switches to a visibly different dark, ghost-icon chat that is not saved to history or memory

cards.name: AI disclosure and confidence cues
cards.aka: AI label, sparkle badge, caveat line, "AI can make mistakes", uncertainty highlighting
cards.desc: Generated content is labeled as AI where it appears, a one-line caveat says it can be wrong, and shaky parts are marked so people know what to double-check. Inside a normal product screen, it keeps AI output from passing as fact.
cards.phrase: AI disclosure: an "AI summary" label with a sparkle on every generated block, a muted one-line caveat ("AI can make mistakes. Check important info."), low-confidence or unsourced phrases with an amber dotted underline and a tooltip saying why, and Use / Edit / Dismiss actions so a person decides

cards.name: Artifact / canvas side panel
cards.aka: artifacts, canvas, side-by-side editor, preview pane
cards.desc: Substantial output, like a document, an app or a diagram, opens in a panel beside the chat instead of inside the message. You keep chatting on the left while the panel updates, with Preview and Code tabs, versions and a share button.
cards.phrase: an artifact side panel: when the reply produces a document, app or diagram, open it in a resizable right panel (chat stays on the left, about 40%) with a title, version switcher, Preview / Code tabs, Copy and Publish buttons; follow-up messages update the artifact in place as a new version, and the chat shows a small card that reopens it

cards.name: Generative UI components
cards.aka: gen UI, tool UI, rich responses, widgets in chat, A2UI / MCP-UI
cards.desc: The model answers with a real, interactive component instead of a paragraph: a chart, a form, a booking card. It ranges from controlled (the model picks one of your prebuilt components), to declarative (it writes a spec your renderer draws), to open-ended (it writes the UI code itself).
cards.phrase: generative UI in the chat: the model calls tools whose results render as real components (controlled: a fixed set of typed components like WeatherCard or FlightOptions with props from the tool result; declarative: a JSON spec drawn by our renderer with our design tokens; open-ended: sandboxed HTML in an iframe only for one-off visuals), each with a loading skeleton and a text fallback

cards.name: Inline AI actions on selection
cards.aka: Cmd-K edit, AI toolbar, Ask AI on selection, quick actions, rewrite
cards.desc: Select text or code and a small toolbar offers AI actions right there: improve, shorten, translate, or a free-text instruction. The result replaces the selection as a preview you accept or discard, so you never leave the document.
cards.phrase: inline AI on selection: selecting text shows a floating toolbar with an "Ask AI" input and quick actions (Improve, Shorten, Fix grammar, Translate); Cmd-K opens the same input at the cursor; the result streams in place as a highlighted suggestion with Accept, Discard and Try again, and Esc cancels

cards.name: Ghost-text autocomplete
cards.aka: inline suggestion, tab completion, ghost text, copilot completion
cards.desc: As you type, the model's guess for what comes next appears in faded gray text after the cursor. Tab accepts it, keep typing to ignore it; some tools also predict your next edit elsewhere in the file.
cards.phrase: ghost-text suggestions: after a short typing pause, show the predicted continuation in faded gray italic inline after the cursor (multi-line allowed), Tab to accept all, Cmd-→ to accept word by word, Esc or keep typing to dismiss, with a small "Tab to accept" hint the first few times

cards.name: Diff review of AI edits
cards.aka: accept / reject changes, review changes, keep / undo, suggested edits
cards.desc: AI edits arrive as a diff instead of overwriting your work: removed lines in red, added lines in green, with Accept and Reject on each change and Accept all at the top. Nothing is kept until you say so.
cards.phrase: AI edits as a reviewable diff: red removed and green added lines inline in the editor, Accept / Reject buttons on each hunk (with shortcuts), a bar at the top with "3 files changed, 2 of 5 hunks reviewed", Accept all / Reject all, and arrows to jump between hunks; nothing is written until accepted

cards.name: Onboarding
cards.aka: welcome flow, first-run experience, intro carousel
cards.desc: The first few screens a new person sees: what the app does, an optional question or two to personalize it, then straight into the product. Good onboarding is short and skippable.
cards.phrase: a short onboarding flow: at most 3 screens with page dots, a Skip link on every screen, one personalization question with selectable chips, and a single primary Continue button; ask for sign-in and permissions only when first needed, not up front

cards.name: Sign-in
cards.aka: login screen, auth screen, passkeys, social login, passwordless
cards.desc: The screen where people prove who they are. Modern sign-in leads with passkeys and platform buttons (Sign in with Apple, Google) and offers a one-time email link or code instead of a password.
cards.phrase: a sign-in screen that leads with passkeys (WebAuthn / ASAuthorizationController / Credential Manager), then Sign in with Apple and Continue with Google buttons in their official styles, then an email field that sends a magic link or 6-digit code; no password field, autofill hints set on every input

cards.name: Permission priming
cards.desc: Your own screen that explains why you need notifications, location or the camera, shown right before the system prompt. The system dialog can usually be shown only once, so the primer protects that one chance.
cards.phrase: permission priming: ask in context, when the feature is first used, with an in-app screen that shows the benefit in one sentence, a primary "Turn on" button that triggers the system prompt and a "Not now" that skips it; if denied, show a later inline hint that deep-links to Settings

cards.name: Settings screen
cards.desc: A list of grouped options, each a row with a label, an optional one-line explanation and a control on the right (toggle, value, or chevron to a sub-page). On iOS it's an inset grouped list; on the web, a sidebar of sections with forms that save as you go.
cards.phrase: a settings screen: options grouped under short section headers, one row per option with label, optional helper text and a right-aligned control (toggle, current value, or chevron); toggles save instantly with no Save button; inset grouped List on iOS, preference rows on Android, left section sidebar on desktop web

cards.name: Search screen
cards.aka: search with recents, search suggestions, typeahead, autocomplete
cards.desc: Tapping the search field opens a focused screen that shows your recent searches and suggestions before you type, then live results as you type. Each recent can be removed, and Cancel puts you back where you were.
cards.phrase: a dedicated search screen: focused field with Cancel, recent searches (each removable with ✕, plus Clear all) and suggestion chips before typing, live debounced results while typing, and a "No results for …" state with spelling suggestions (SwiftUI .searchable with .searchSuggestions, Material 3 SearchBar on Android, combobox ARIA pattern on web)

cards.name: Checkout
cards.desc: A long task split into a few short steps with a progress indicator, so people always know where they are and how much is left. An order summary stays visible beside the form.
cards.phrase: a multi-step checkout: a stepper showing completed, current and upcoming steps, one topic per step, a sticky order summary beside the form on desktop (collapsible at the top on mobile), Back without losing input, inline validation on blur, and Apple Pay / Google Pay express buttons above the form

cards.name: Paywall
cards.aka: upgrade screen, subscription screen, pricing sheet, upsell
cards.desc: The screen that asks for money: what you get, two or three plans with the recommended one preselected, the trial terms in plain words, and a clear way out. App stores require visible pricing, a restore button and terms links.
cards.phrase: a paywall: close ✕ always visible, 3 to 4 benefit lines with checkmarks, yearly and monthly plan cards with yearly preselected and a "Save 45%" badge, a primary trial button, the exact price and renewal terms under it, and Restore Purchases / Terms / Privacy links (StoreKit 2 SubscriptionStoreView on iOS, Google Play Billing on Android)

cards.name: Feed
cards.aka: timeline, stream, activity feed, infinite scroll
cards.desc: A vertical stream of posts or updates, newest or most relevant first, that loads more as you scroll. New items wait behind a "new posts" pill instead of shoving the content you are reading.
cards.phrase: a feed of post cards (avatar, name, timestamp, text, optional media, action row), infinite scroll with a skeleton for the next page, pull-to-refresh on mobile, and a floating "↑ 4 new posts" pill instead of inserting new items above the reading position (LazyColumn / List / virtualized list)

cards.name: Detail page
cards.aka: product page, item view, PDP, show page
cards.desc: Everything about one thing: big media at the top or left, then the name, key facts, the main action, and longer details folded into sections below. On phones the main action often sticks to the bottom of the screen.
cards.phrase: a detail page: large media gallery with thumbnails, title, price and rating up top, option pickers (color swatches, size chips), one prominent primary action that stays visible (sticky bottom bar on mobile, right column on desktop), and long content (details, shipping, reviews) in collapsible sections

cards.name: Chat / messaging
cards.aka: conversation view, message thread, DM screen
cards.desc: A conversation as bubbles: theirs on the left, yours on the right in the accent color, grouped by sender with timestamps between bursts. A composer stays pinned above the keyboard, and the view starts scrolled to the newest message.
cards.phrase: a chat thread: incoming bubbles left in gray, outgoing right in the accent color, consecutive messages grouped with tight spacing, centered date separators, sent/delivered/read status on the last outgoing message, a typing indicator, and a composer pinned above the keyboard (inverted list anchored to the bottom, imePadding on Android)

cards.name: AI chat interface
cards.aka: assistant UI, chatbot, copilot panel, LLM chat
cards.desc: A chat built around a model: the answer streams in word by word, tool use and reasoning show as collapsible steps, and the send button turns into Stop while it works. Suggested prompts fill the empty screen and follow-ups appear after each answer.

cards.name: Error summary
cards.aka: error summary box, validation summary, "There is a problem"
cards.desc: When a form is submitted with mistakes, a box at the top lists every problem as a link that jumps to the field, and each field also shows its own message. Screen reader and keyboard users hear the full list first instead of hunting for red text.
cards.phrase: a GOV.UK-style error summary: on submit with errors, show a box at the top of the form with a thick red border, the heading "There is a problem", and a list of links (one per error, same wording as the field message) that move focus to the field; move focus to the summary on load (tabindex="-1", role="alert"), prefix the page <title> with "Error: ", and mark each invalid field with a red left bar, a red border and an "Error: Enter your date of birth" message above the input (aria-describedby)

cards.name: Check your answers
cards.aka: review page, summary page, confirm details, order review
cards.desc: Before submitting a long form, one page lists every answer in label and value pairs, grouped by section, each with a Change link that goes back to that question and then returns here. Then a clear final button.
cards.phrase: a check-your-answers page: heading "Check your answers before sending your application", answers grouped under section headings in a summary list (key in bold, value, right-aligned "Change" link with visually hidden text like "Change date of birth"), Change returns to that question and back to this page after, then a "Now send your application" section with a short declaration and a primary "Accept and send" button

cards.name: Task list page
cards.aka: task list, setup checklist, application hub, onboarding checklist
cards.desc: A hub page for a long job that lists its sections with a status beside each (Completed, In progress, Not yet started, Cannot start yet). People can do the sections in any order, leave and come back, and always see what is left.
cards.phrase: a task list hub page: title, "You have completed 2 of 5 sections" summary, tasks grouped under numbered headings, each row a link to that section with a status tag on the right (Completed in plain text, In progress and Not yet started as colored tags, Cannot start yet in gray and not linked), progress saved so people can leave and return, and a final "Check and send" task that unlocks when the rest are complete

cards.name: Account setup
cards.aka: profile creation, onboarding setup, personalization, welcome setup
cards.desc: The few screens right after sign-up where people add a name and photo, pick a username and answer one or two questions so the app can fit them. Each step is short, clearly optional parts can be skipped, and progress is shown.
cards.phrase: an account setup flow after sign-up: 2 to 3 short steps with a segmented progress bar and Skip on optional steps; step 1 profile with avatar upload (initials placeholder, camera badge), display name prefilled from the sign-in provider, and a username field that checks availability as you type (✓ available / taken with suggestions); step 2 a single question with selectable cards ("What will you use it for?") that tailors the first screen; Continue disabled until required fields are valid; everything editable later in settings

cards.name: Subscription management and cancel flow
cards.aka: cancel subscription, manage plan, billing settings, retention flow
cards.desc: A billing page where people can see their plan, next charge and invoices, and cancel in a couple of clicks from the same place they would look for it. A fair flow may offer a pause or a cheaper plan once, says exactly what happens and when, and never hides the cancel button or guilt-trips.
cards.phrase: a subscription management page and an honest cancel flow: billing settings show the plan, price, next renewal date, payment method and invoices, with "Cancel subscription" as a visible button; one confirmation step says what happens and when ("You keep Pro until Apr 3, then move to Free; nothing is deleted"), optionally offers a pause or downgrade once, asks for a reason as optional, and gives "Keep Pro" and "Cancel subscription" equal visual weight; no confirmshaming, no hidden links, no forced phone call, and a confirmation email afterwards

cards.name: Empty state
cards.aka: zero state, blank slate, first-use state
cards.desc: What a list or page shows before it has any content: a small illustration, one line saying what will live here, and the action that fills it. It turns a blank screen into the first step.
cards.phrase: designed empty states for every list and view: a small neutral illustration, a one-line title saying what goes here, one sentence of help, and the primary action that fills it (plus a secondary like Import); distinguish first-use empty, no-search-results and all-caught-up

cards.name: Skeleton loading
cards.aka: skeleton screen, placeholder shimmer, ghost UI
cards.desc: Gray shapes in the layout of the content that is coming, gently pulsing, shown while data loads. It feels faster than a spinner because the page already has its shape and nothing jumps when data arrives.
cards.phrase: skeleton screens while loading: gray placeholder blocks matching the real layout's sizes (so nothing shifts), a slow pulse or shimmer, real headers and navigation shown immediately, skeletons only after a ~300 ms delay to avoid flashing (SwiftUI .redacted(reason: .placeholder), shadcn Skeleton)

cards.name: Optimistic UI
cards.aka: optimistic update, instant feedback, latency hiding
cards.desc: The interface shows the result of your action immediately, as if the server already said yes, and quietly sends the request. If it fails, the change rolls back and a message offers a retry.
cards.phrase: optimistic updates: apply the change to the UI instantly, mark pending items subtly (lower opacity or a tiny clock), send the request in the background, and on failure roll back with a toast or inline "Couldn't save · Retry" (React useOptimistic or TanStack Query onMutate/onError rollback)

cards.name: Error state with retry
cards.aka: error page, failure state, inline error, error boundary
cards.desc: When something fails, say what happened in plain words, reassure about data, and offer the next step (usually Try again). Keep the failure scoped: the rest of the page and its navigation keep working.
cards.phrase: error states scoped to the region that failed (never a blank page): an icon, a plain-language title like "Couldn't load invoices", one sentence on why and whether data is safe, a Try again button that retries in place, a link to status or support, and a copyable error ID; inline field errors stay next to their field

cards.name: Offline state
cards.desc: When the network drops, the app says so with a quiet banner, keeps showing what it has cached, and queues changes to send later. Things that truly need a connection are disabled with a reason.
cards.phrase: offline handling: a non-blocking banner ("You're offline. Changes will sync when you reconnect."), cached content stays readable, edits queue locally and show a pending marker, online-only actions are disabled with a tooltip, and the banner turns into "Back online" then hides (NWPathMonitor on iOS, ConnectivityManager on Android, navigator.onLine plus a service worker on web)

cards.name: Undo instead of confirm
cards.aka: undo toast, snackbar with undo, soft delete
cards.desc: Do the action right away and offer Undo for a few seconds, instead of asking "Are you sure?" first. People stop reading confirm dialogs; an undo catches the real mistakes without slowing the common case.
cards.phrase: undo instead of confirmation dialogs: perform archive/delete immediately, show a snackbar or toast "Conversation archived · Undo" for 5–8 seconds, soft-delete on the server until it expires, and support ⌘Z / Ctrl+Z on desktop; keep a typed confirmation only for irreversible actions

cards.name: Badges and dots
cards.aka: notification badge, unread count, indicator dot
cards.desc: A small red count or dot on an icon or tab that says "something new here". Counts work for things people clear (messages); a plain dot works for "there is news" without pressure.
cards.phrase: badges for unread items: a red count badge on tab and app icons capped at "99+", a plain dot when the count doesn't matter, a blue unread dot on list rows, badges cleared as soon as the item is seen (SwiftUI .badge(), Material 3 BadgedBox, UNNotificationContent.badge); never badge for marketing

cards.name: Inline editing
cards.aka: click to edit, edit in place, editable cell
cards.desc: Text you can change right where it sits: click a title or a table cell, it becomes a field, Enter saves and Escape cancels. No separate edit page or modal.
cards.phrase: inline editing: hovering an editable value shows a subtle outline and pencil, click or Enter turns it into a field with the text selected, Enter or blur saves (optimistically), Escape cancels, invalid input shows an inline message without leaving edit mode; keyboard reachable with a visible focus ring

cards.name: Progressive disclosure
cards.aka: show more, advanced options, expandable section, disclosure
cards.desc: Show the few options most people need and tuck the rest behind an "Advanced" toggle or a "Show more" link. Beginners see a short form, experts find everything one click away.
cards.phrase: progressive disclosure: show only the 3–5 essential fields by default with sensible defaults, put the rest under a collapsed "Advanced options" disclosure (<details>/<summary> on web, DisclosureGroup in SwiftUI) that remembers its state, and never hide anything required to finish the task

cards.name: Follow platform conventions
cards.aka: native feel, platform idioms, HIG / Material compliance
cards.desc: Use each platform's own navigation, controls and gestures, so the app works the way people's other apps do. The same app looks different on iOS and Android, and that is correct.
cards.phrase: follow each platform's conventions instead of one custom look: on iOS a large-title nav bar, ‹ back with swipe-back, bottom tab bar and SF Symbols; on Android a top app bar with ← back, Material 3 navigation bar and FAB, and predictive back; on the web real links, browser back and standard keyboard shortcuts; use native controls (pickers, switches, sheets) wherever one exists

cards.name: Touch targets
cards.aka: hit area, tap target size, minimum target size
cards.desc: Anything tappable needs a hit area at least about the size of a fingertip, even when the icon inside is small, plus space between neighbors. The icon can be 20pt; the button around it cannot.
cards.phrase: touch targets of at least 44×44 pt on iOS and 48×48 dp on Android (44×44 CSS px on touch web, never under WCAG 2.2's 24×24 px), even for small icons, by padding the hit area rather than growing the icon; at least 8 pt/dp between adjacent targets

cards.name: Color contrast
cards.desc: Text and important icons need enough contrast against their background to be read in sunlight, on cheap screens and with low vision. The usual bar is WCAG AA: 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text and UI shapes.
cards.phrase: color contrast meeting WCAG 2.2 AA in both themes: at least 4.5:1 for body text and placeholders, 3:1 for text 24px+ (or 18.66px bold) and for icons, borders and focus rings; check muted grays and white-on-accent buttons with a contrast checker, and never use color alone to carry meaning

cards.name: Dark mode with semantic tokens
cards.aka: dark theme, color scheme, light/dark appearance
cards.desc: Colors are named by role (surface, text, accent) rather than by value, and each role has a light and a dark value. Dark mode then just swaps the set, instead of inverting colors or hand-picking each screen.
cards.phrase: light and dark themes from semantic color tokens (surface, surface-raised, text, text-muted, border, accent) with a value for each mode; follow the system setting (prefers-color-scheme / UITraitCollection / isSystemInDarkTheme) with a manual override; dark surfaces are dark gray (about #121212 to #1C1C1E, not pure black), elevation shown by lighter surfaces instead of shadows, accents desaturated slightly

cards.name: Responsive breakpoints
cards.aka: mobile-first, adaptive layout, fluid layout, breakpoints
cards.desc: One layout that reflows as the screen widens: a single column on phones, two on tablets, a sidebar plus several columns on desktop. Mobile-first means you design the narrow version first and add columns as space appears.
cards.phrase: mobile-first responsive layout: single column below 640px, two columns from 768px, sidebar plus three-column content from 1024px, max content width around 1200px; navigation moves from a bottom bar or menu to a sidebar; use container queries for components, and Material window size classes (compact / medium / expanded) or iOS size classes in native apps

cards.name: Design tokens
cards.aka: design variables, theme tokens, primitives and aliases
cards.desc: Every color, size, radius and font in the UI comes from a named variable instead of a raw value. Raw values live in a small palette; semantic names point at them; components use only the semantic names.
cards.phrase: use design tokens in three layers: primitives (blue-600 = #2563EB, space-4 = 16px, radius-md = 8px), semantic aliases (color.action.primary, color.text.muted, space.inset.md) and component tokens (button.bg); components reference only semantic tokens, never raw hex or px values; define them as CSS variables / a Tailwind theme / an asset catalog

cards.name: 8-point spacing grid
cards.desc: All padding, margins and gaps come from a short scale of multiples of 8 (with 4 for tight spots): 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48. Layouts look orderly because the same few distances repeat everywhere.
cards.phrase: an 8-point spacing system: every margin, padding and gap from the scale 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 64; 16 px screen edge padding on mobile, 24+ on desktop; related items closer together (8) than separate groups (24); component heights on the grid too (32/40/48)

cards.name: Type scale
cards.aka: typographic scale, text styles, type ramp
cards.desc: A small, fixed set of named text styles (display, title, headline, body, caption) with set sizes, weights and line heights. Screens pick from the set instead of choosing a font size each time.
cards.phrase: a type scale of 5–7 named styles used everywhere, e.g. Large Title 34, Title 22, Headline 17 semibold, Body 17, Callout 16, Footnote 13, Caption 12 (iOS Dynamic Type) or Material 3 display/headline/title/body/label; body at 16–17px with 1.4–1.5 line height, one font family, hierarchy from size and weight; support Dynamic Type / font scaling up to 200%

cards.name: Keyboard navigation and focus rings
cards.aka: focus states, tab order, focus-visible, keyboard accessibility
cards.desc: Everything you can click can also be reached with Tab and used with Enter or Space, in a sensible order, and the focused element shows a clear ring. Mouse users never see the ring; keyboard users always do.
cards.phrase: full keyboard support: logical tab order that follows the visual layout, a visible 2px focus ring with 2px offset at 3:1 contrast via :focus-visible, Enter/Space activate, Escape closes overlays and returns focus to the trigger, arrow keys inside menus and lists, a "Skip to content" link, and focus trapped inside open modals

cards.name: Screen reader labels
cards.aka: accessibility labels, alt text, ARIA, VoiceOver / TalkBack support
cards.desc: Every control gets a spoken name and role, so a blind user hears "Delete message, button" rather than "button" or "trash dot fill". Use real semantic elements (button, heading, list) and label icon-only controls.
cards.phrase: screen reader support: semantic elements first (button, a, h1–h3, ul, label), an accessible name on every icon-only control (aria-label / SwiftUI .accessibilityLabel / Compose contentDescription), meaningful alt text or alt="" for decoration, headings for rotor navigation, status changes announced via aria-live or UIAccessibility.post, and related elements grouped so they read as one

cards.name: Reduced motion
cards.aka: prefers-reduced-motion, motion sensitivity, Reduce Motion setting
cards.desc: When the user turns on Reduce Motion, big slides, zooms, parallax and auto-playing animation are replaced with quick cross-fades or nothing. Motion that can cause dizziness becomes optional; the app still shows state changes clearly.
cards.phrase: respect reduced motion: when prefers-reduced-motion is set (SwiftUI @Environment(\.accessibilityReduceMotion), Android ANIMATOR_DURATION_SCALE = 0), swap slide/zoom/parallax transitions for a 150–200 ms cross-fade, stop auto-playing and looping animation, and keep essential feedback like progress indicators

cards.name: Safe areas
cards.aka: safe area insets, notch and home indicator spacing, edge-to-edge insets
cards.desc: The parts of the screen not covered by the notch or Dynamic Island, rounded corners, the home indicator or system bars. Backgrounds can run edge to edge, but text and buttons stay inside the safe area.
cards.phrase: respect safe areas: backgrounds and media extend edge to edge, but text, buttons and tap targets stay inside the safe area insets (SwiftUI safe area / .ignoresSafeArea only for backgrounds, Android WindowInsets with enableEdgeToEdge, CSS env(safe-area-inset-top/bottom) with viewport-fit=cover); bottom buttons sit above the home indicator, never under it

cards.name: Thumb zone
cards.desc: On a phone held in one hand, the thumb reaches the bottom middle easily and the top corners hardly at all. Put frequent actions low (tab bars, primary buttons, bottom search) and rare or risky ones up top.
cards.phrase: design for one-handed use: primary actions, tab bar and search within the bottom third of the screen (bottom sheets and a bottom search bar rather than top-only controls), destructive or rare actions in the top corners, and nothing important only reachable in the top 25% of the screen on phones

cards.name: Density
cards.aka: compact vs. comfortable, display density, row height
cards.desc: How tightly information is packed. Compact fits more rows for experts scanning data; comfortable gives breathing room and bigger targets. Many tools let people choose.
cards.phrase: two density modes: comfortable by default (48–56px rows, 16px cell padding, 14–16px text) and compact for data-heavy views (32–36px rows, 8px padding, 13px text), switchable in a view menu and remembered per user; touch layouts never drop below 44pt rows

cards.name: Localization, RTL and text expansion
cards.desc: The UI survives translation: labels can grow 30 to 50 percent (German, Finnish) without truncating, Arabic and Hebrew mirror the whole layout right to left, and dates, numbers and currency follow the locale.
cards.phrase: localization-ready UI: no hard-coded strings, layouts that allow 40% longer text (buttons grow or wrap, never fixed widths), full RTL mirroring for Arabic and Hebrew using leading/trailing or CSS logical properties (margin-inline-start), directional icons flipped but not logos or media controls, and dates, numbers and currency via Intl / Locale formatters with ICU plurals

cards.name: Container queries
cards.desc: A component changes its layout based on how wide its own box is, not how wide the whole window is. The same card can sit in a wide main column and a narrow sidebar and look right in both.
cards.phrase: make components respond to their container, not the viewport: set container-type: inline-size on the wrapper, then @container (min-width: 400px) switches the card from stacked (image on top) to horizontal (image left, text, action right); size type and padding with container units (cqi); in Tailwind use @container on the parent and @md: variants on children; keep viewport media queries only for page-level layout

cards.name: Native popover, dialog and anchor positioning
cards.aka: popover API, <dialog>, CSS anchor positioning, top layer
cards.desc: Browsers now build in what used to need a JavaScript library: the popover attribute for menus and tooltips that close on outside click or Escape, <dialog> for modals with a real backdrop and focus handling, and CSS anchor positioning to attach a floating panel to its button.
cards.phrase: use the platform for overlays instead of a JS positioning library: <button popovertarget="menu"> with <div id="menu" popover> for menus and popovers (top layer, light dismiss and Escape for free), <dialog> opened with showModal() for modals (::backdrop, inert page, focus moved and restored), and CSS anchor positioning (anchor-name on the trigger, position-anchor and position-area: bottom span-right on the panel, position-try-fallbacks: flip-block) so it flips near edges; add Floating UI only as a fallback where anchor positioning is unsupported

cards.name: Fluid type with clamp()
cards.aka: fluid typography, responsive type, clamp() font size, Utopia scale
cards.desc: Font sizes that grow smoothly with the screen width between a minimum and a maximum, instead of jumping at breakpoints. A heading might be 32px on a phone, 64px on a wide screen, and anything in between.
cards.phrase: fluid typography with clamp(): headings like font-size: clamp(2rem, 1rem + 4vw, 4rem) so they scale smoothly from 32px at 400px wide to 64px at 1200px, body text clamp(1rem, 0.95rem + 0.25vw, 1.125rem); always mix a rem term into the preferred value so browser zoom and user font size still work; generate the scale with Utopia and apply the same approach to section spacing

cards.name: Skip link and visually hidden text
cards.aka: skip to content, skip navigation, sr-only, visually-hidden
cards.desc: A "Skip to main content" link that is hidden until the first press of Tab, so keyboard users can jump past the header and menu. Its partner is visually hidden text: words only screen readers announce, such as the full name of an icon button.
cards.phrase: add a skip link as the first focusable element: <a href="#main" class="sr-only focus:not-sr-only"> "Skip to main content" that appears top-left with a strong focus ring on the first Tab and moves focus to <main id="main" tabindex="-1">; use visually hidden text (Tailwind sr-only: clipped, 1px, not display:none) to give icon buttons and repeated "Read more" links full names, e.g. "Delete invoice INV-204"

cards.name: Apple Human Interface Guidelines
cards.desc: Apple's rules and components for iOS, iPadOS and macOS: SF Pro, system colors like systemBlue, inset grouped lists, segmented controls, switches and sheets, now with Liquid Glass. The easiest way to follow it is to use SwiftUI's built-in controls.
cards.phrase: follow the Apple Human Interface Guidelines using standard SwiftUI components (List with .insetGrouped style, Toggle, Picker with .segmented style, .borderedProminent buttons), SF Pro and SF Symbols, semantic system colors and Dynamic Type

cards.name: Material Design 3
cards.desc: Google's system: color roles generated from one seed color, pill buttons in filled, tonal, outlined and text styles, outlined text fields with floating labels, chips, cards, and a rounded-square FAB.
cards.phrase: use Material Design 3 components (Jetpack Compose androidx.compose.material3, or MUI / @material/web on the web) with a color scheme generated from one seed color, the M3 type scale, and a filled, tonal, outlined button hierarchy

cards.name: Microsoft Fluent 2
cards.aka: Fluent UI, Fluent UI React v9
cards.desc: Microsoft's system for Office, Teams and Windows: Segoe UI, a calm brand blue, 4px rounded controls, inputs with an accent underline on focus, message bars for inline status, and soft layered shadows.
cards.phrase: use Microsoft Fluent 2 components (@fluentui/react-components, Fluent UI React v9) inside a FluentProvider with webLightTheme / webDarkTheme, Segoe UI, Fluent System Icons, and MessageBar for inline status

cards.name: IBM Carbon
cards.desc: IBM's system for enterprise software: square corners, IBM Plex Sans, gray-filled inputs with a bottom border, wide buttons with the label on the left and the icon on the right, and a black UI shell header.
cards.phrase: use IBM Carbon components (@carbon/react) with the White or Gray 100 theme, IBM Plex Sans, the UI Shell header, square corners, the 2x grid, and inline notifications for status

cards.name: GitHub Primer
cards.desc: GitHub's system: dense and functional, with a green primary button, gray bordered default buttons, counters, colored labels, underline tab navigation and bordered boxes around lists. It reads as a developer tool.
cards.phrase: use GitHub Primer components (@primer/react) with Octicons (@primer/octicons-react) and Primer's light and dark color tokens, UnderlineNav for tabs, Label and CounterLabel, and a green primary Button only for the main action on each screen

cards.name: Shopify Polaris
cards.desc: Shopify's admin system: white cards on a light gray page, a near-black primary button, status badges, metric cards and index tables. Calm and built for scanning orders and products.
cards.phrase: use Shopify Polaris components (Polaris web components, or @shopify/polaris in React) with Page, Card, IndexTable and Badge, the default Polaris tokens, and Shopify admin layout conventions

cards.name: Radix UI and Radix Themes
cards.desc: Radix Primitives are unstyled, accessible building blocks (Dialog, Select, Popover) that many libraries, including shadcn/ui, are built on. Radix Themes adds a clean styled set with 12-step color scales and solid, soft, outline and ghost variants.
cards.phrase: use Radix Themes (@radix-ui/themes) with an indigo accent and slate gray, the solid / soft / outline / ghost variants and Radix Colors scales; build anything custom on Radix Primitives (radix-ui) so it stays accessible

cards.name: Tailwind UI / Tailwind Plus
cards.aka: Tailwind Plus, Catalyst, the Tailwind look
cards.desc: The official component collection from the Tailwind CSS team, renamed Tailwind Plus in 2025: indigo-600 buttons, ring-bordered inputs, subtle shadows, stat cards and app shells, as copy-paste Tailwind markup.
cards.phrase: use Tailwind Plus (Tailwind UI) patterns and the Catalyst React kit with Tailwind CSS: indigo-600 primary, the gray scale, inputs with ring-1 ring-gray-300 and focus:ring-indigo-600, shadow-sm cards, Inter, and Headless UI for menus and dialogs

cards.name: Ant Design
cards.desc: An enterprise system from Ant Group with a very large component set: #1677FF primary buttons, compact forms, data tables with tags and pagination, alerts, steps and breadcrumbs. Dense and made for admin dashboards.
cards.phrase: use Ant Design components (antd v5) with ConfigProvider theme tokens, Table with pagination and Tag, Form in vertical layout, Alert and Breadcrumb, and @ant-design/icons; keep the density of Ant Design Pro

cards.name: Column chart
cards.desc: Vertical bars rising from a zero baseline, one per category or time period. Length carries the value, which the eye reads very precisely.
cards.phrase: a column chart with one bar per period, starting at zero, bars a little wider than the gaps between them, light horizontal gridlines and no border around the plot

cards.name: Sorted bar chart
cards.desc: Horizontal bars sorted from largest to smallest, with labels to the left and values at the end of each bar. Sorting turns a pile of numbers into a ranking you read top to bottom.
cards.phrase: a horizontal bar chart sorted from largest to smallest, category labels left of the bars, the value printed at the end of each bar instead of an x-axis

cards.name: Grouped bar chart
cards.desc: Bars for two to four series placed next to each other inside each category. Good for comparing series within a group; harder to follow one series across groups.
cards.phrase: a grouped bar chart with the series side by side inside each category, at most four series, a consistent color per series and a legend placed above the plot

cards.name: Stacked bar chart
cards.desc: Each bar is split into segments that add up to a total. You can read the total and the bottom segment exactly; the middle segments float, so they are hard to compare.
cards.phrase: a stacked bar chart where the segments sum to each bar's total, the most important series at the bottom on the baseline, no more than four segments, and the total labeled above each bar

cards.name: Lollipop chart
cards.desc: A thin line ending in a dot instead of a solid bar. It keeps the bar chart's honesty with less ink, which helps when many bars are about the same length.
cards.phrase: a horizontal lollipop chart sorted by value: a thin stem from the zero baseline to a solid dot, labels on the left, values next to each dot

cards.name: Dot plot
cards.desc: Each category gets a row with one dot per series placed on a shared axis. Without bars, the axis doesn't need to start at zero, so small differences become visible.
cards.phrase: a Cleveland dot plot: one row per category, a dot for each series on a shared horizontal axis, faint dotted guide lines across each row, rows sorted by the latest value

cards.name: Dumbbell chart
cards.aka: barbell chart, gap chart, DNA chart
cards.desc: Two dots on one row joined by a thick line. The bar between them is the gap, so the chart shows both values and the size and direction of the change.
cards.phrase: a dumbbell chart: for each category, two colored dots (before and after) joined by a thick gray bar, rows sorted by the size of the gap, and a two-item legend above

cards.name: Slope chart
cards.desc: Two vertical axes, one for each time point, with a line connecting each category's two values. Steep lines jump out, and crossing lines show rank changes.
cards.phrase: a slope chart comparing two years: one line per category from the left axis to the right axis, labels with values at both ends, the steepest riser in color and the rest in gray

cards.name: Bullet chart
cards.desc: A compact bar showing the actual value, a short tick for the target, and shaded bands behind it for poor, fair and good. It packs a gauge into a single line.
cards.phrase: bullet charts, one per KPI: a dark bar for the actual value, a short vertical line for the target, and three shades of one hue behind it for poor, satisfactory and good ranges

cards.name: Radar chart
cards.aka: spider chart, star plot, web chart
cards.desc: Several axes radiate from a center and each series becomes a closed shape. It draws a memorable profile, but the area depends on the order of the axes, so comparisons are rough.
cards.phrase: a radar chart with six axes scored 0 to 1, two series drawn as translucent filled shapes with solid outlines, light concentric gridlines and axis labels outside the rim

cards.name: Pictogram chart
cards.aka: isotype chart, icon array, unit chart
cards.desc: Rows of repeated icons where each icon stands for a fixed amount. Counting little people is immediate and friendly, and it makes a number feel like a crowd.
cards.phrase: a pictogram chart where each icon stands for a fixed count, icons in tidy rows of the same size, partial icons cut off for remainders, and a key that says what one icon equals

cards.name: Line chart
cards.desc: Points joined by a line across time. The slope is the story: rising, falling, flat, or turning. The y-axis may start above zero because the eye reads position and slope, not length.
cards.phrase: a line chart with time on the x-axis, a 2px line per series, no markers on every point, light horizontal gridlines, and each line labeled at its right end instead of a legend

cards.name: Area chart
cards.desc: A line chart with the space below filled in. The fill adds weight and suggests volume, so it suits totals that build up, like users or revenue.
cards.phrase: an area chart of one series with a solid line on top of a soft translucent fill down to a zero baseline, light gridlines and the latest value labeled at the end

cards.name: Stacked area chart
cards.desc: Areas stacked on top of each other so the top edge is the total. Good for showing how a total is made up over time; only the bottom layer is easy to read exactly.
cards.phrase: a stacked area chart with the layers summing to the total, the most stable series at the bottom, thin white seams between layers, and labels placed inside the widest part of each layer

cards.name: Streamgraph
cards.desc: A stacked area chart centered on a wavy midline instead of a flat baseline, with smooth curves. It is organic and beautiful, and it shows rise and fall of themes more than exact values.
cards.phrase: a streamgraph: smooth stacked layers centered around a flowing midline, no y-axis, each layer in its own color with its label placed on the layer at its widest point

cards.name: Step chart
cards.desc: A line that moves in flat steps and vertical jumps instead of slopes. It shows values that change suddenly and then hold, like prices, rates and plan tiers.
cards.phrase: a step chart where the line stays flat until each change and then jumps vertically, with each step labeled with its new value and date

cards.name: Sparklines
cards.desc: Tiny line charts with no axes, set inline with text or in a table row. The shape of the trend sits next to the number it explains, and the last point is marked.
cards.phrase: sparklines in a table: one small line per row with no axes or gridlines, the last value marked with a dot and printed to the right, and the high point marked in gray

cards.name: Candlestick chart
cards.desc: Each period shows open, high, low and close: a thin wick spans the range and a thick body spans open to close, colored for up or down. The standard picture of a trading day.
cards.phrase: a candlestick chart: a thin wick from high to low and a body from open to close for each day, up days in green and down days in red, price axis on the right

cards.name: Horizon chart
cards.desc: A time series sliced into bands that are folded down and layered with darker shades, so a tall chart fits in a thin strip. Many series can be stacked for comparison.
cards.phrase: horizon charts, one thin row per series: values above the baseline in layered blues and below in layered reds, darker shades for higher bands, all rows sharing one time axis

cards.name: Bump chart
cards.desc: Lines that trace rank instead of value, with first place at the top. It shows who overtook whom without the clutter of the underlying numbers.
cards.phrase: a bump chart where y is rank with first place at the top, thick colored lines with a dot at each period, and names labeled at both ends

cards.name: Calendar heatmap
cards.desc: A grid with one small square per day, arranged by week and weekday, colored by how much happened. Weekly rhythms and long streaks show at once.
cards.phrase: a calendar heatmap: one square per day in columns by week and rows by weekday, five shades of one hue from light (none) to dark (most), month labels on top and a small legend

cards.name: Pie chart
cards.desc: A circle cut into slices whose angles add to 100%. Good for one big share against the rest; poor for comparing slices of similar size.
cards.phrase: a pie chart with at most five slices, starting at 12 o'clock and sorted clockwise from largest, labels with percentages placed next to each slice instead of a legend

cards.name: Donut chart
cards.desc: A pie with the middle removed, which leaves room for the total or headline number. People read the arc lengths about as well as pie angles.
cards.phrase: a donut chart with a thick ring, at most four segments, the total or key percentage in large type in the center hole, and short labels outside the ring

cards.name: 100% stacked bar
cards.desc: Every bar is the same height and split into shares, so you compare composition across categories or years. The two outer segments are easy to read; the middle ones less so.
cards.phrase: a 100% stacked bar chart where each bar sums to 100%, segments in a consistent order with the most important one on the baseline, percentages labeled inside large segments

cards.name: Treemap
cards.desc: A rectangle divided into smaller rectangles sized by value, with groups nested inside groups. It fits a whole hierarchy on one screen and shows the giants at once.
cards.phrase: a treemap with rectangles sized by value and grouped by parent category, each group in its own hue with children in the same hue, labels inside every rectangle large enough to hold one

cards.name: Sunburst chart
cards.desc: Rings of arcs where the inner ring is the top level and each outer ring splits its parent. It shows a hierarchy as a radial burst.
cards.phrase: a sunburst chart: the inner ring for top-level categories, the outer ring for their children in a lighter tint of the parent's color, and a total in the center

cards.name: Icicle chart
cards.aka: partition chart, flame graph (when used for profiling)
cards.desc: A hierarchy drawn as stacked rows of rectangles, each one split by its children below. It reads like a tree laid on its side and keeps labels horizontal.
cards.phrase: an icicle chart: the whole on the top row, each level below split proportionally by its children, rectangles colored by top-level parent and labeled where they fit

cards.name: Waffle chart
cards.desc: A 10 by 10 grid where each square is one percent, colored by category. Counting squares is easier than judging angles, and it feels concrete.
cards.phrase: a waffle chart of 100 small squares in a 10 by 10 grid, each square one percent, filled by category from the bottom left, with a legend that lists each share

cards.name: Marimekko chart
cards.aka: mosaic plot, Mekko chart, variable-width bar
cards.desc: A 100% stacked bar chart where bar widths also vary, so each tile's area is its share of the grand total. It shows two percentages at once: market size and share.
cards.phrase: a Marimekko chart where column width is each market's share of the total and the stacked segments are each company's share within that market, all tiles labeled with percentages

cards.name: Parliament chart
cards.desc: A half-circle of dots, one per seat, colored by party and ordered left to right. It mirrors a real chamber and makes a majority line easy to see.
cards.phrase: a parliament chart: one dot per seat arranged in concentric half-circle rows, grouped by party from left to right, with the seat total in the middle

cards.name: Histogram
cards.desc: Values grouped into equal bins, with a bar per bin showing how many fall inside. The bars touch because the bins are continuous. The bin width changes the story, so try a few.
cards.phrase: a histogram with equal-width bins and touching bars, a count axis starting at zero, and the bin edges labeled on the x-axis; mention the bin width in the subtitle

cards.name: Box plot
cards.desc: A box from the 25th to the 75th percentile with a line at the median, whiskers to the typical range, and dots for outliers. It summarizes a distribution in five numbers.
cards.phrase: box plots, one per group on a shared axis: a box for the middle 50%, a bold median line, whiskers to 1.5 times the IQR, and outliers as small open circles

cards.name: Violin plot
cards.desc: A smoothed density curve mirrored on both sides, so each group looks like a vase. It shows two humps and long tails that a box plot would hide.
cards.phrase: violin plots, one per group: a mirrored smoothed density shape filled with the group color, a short bold line at the median, and all violins on one shared value axis

cards.name: Strip plot
cards.desc: Every observation drawn as a dot along one axis, nudged sideways a little at random so dots don't hide each other. Nothing is summarized away.
cards.phrase: a strip plot with every observation as a small semi-transparent dot, jittered horizontally within each group, and a short line marking each group's median

cards.name: Beeswarm plot
cards.desc: Dots placed along an axis and pushed apart just enough not to overlap, so the cloud's outline traces the distribution. Each dot can be a person, country or company.
cards.phrase: a beeswarm plot: one dot per item along a single axis, dots packed without overlap so the swarm's silhouette shows the distribution, a few notable dots labeled

cards.name: Ridgeline plot
cards.desc: Several density curves stacked with slight overlap, like a mountain range seen from the side. Good for watching a distribution shift across months or groups.
cards.phrase: a ridgeline plot: one smoothed density curve per group stacked vertically with slight overlap, filled with a sequential palette from light to dark, labels on the left

cards.name: Density curve
cards.desc: A smooth curve instead of histogram bars, estimating how values are spread. Overlaying two or three curves shows how groups differ.
cards.phrase: overlaid density curves, one per group, each a solid line over a translucent fill of the same color, labeled at its peak instead of with a legend

cards.name: Cumulative distribution
cards.desc: A rising step line that shows what share of values fall below each point. You can read medians and percentiles straight off it, with no bins to choose.
cards.phrase: an empirical cumulative distribution plot: a step line per group from 0% to 100%, a percentage y-axis, and dashed guides marking the median and 90th percentile

cards.name: Scatter plot
cards.desc: One dot per item, placed by two numeric values. Clouds that slope up or down show correlation; dots far from the cloud are the interesting ones.
cards.phrase: a scatter plot with one semi-transparent dot per item, both axes labeled with units, a thin fitted trend line, and the three most extreme outliers labeled

cards.name: Bubble chart
cards.desc: A scatter plot where dot size encodes a third value and color can encode a fourth. Size reads loosely, so it works for "big ones over here" more than exact comparison.
cards.phrase: a bubble chart: x and y for two measures, bubble area proportional to a third value, color by group, white outlines so overlapping bubbles stay readable, and a size key

cards.name: Connected scatter plot
cards.desc: A scatter plot whose dots are joined in time order, so the line wanders through the space of two variables. Loops and reversals show how the relationship changed.
cards.phrase: a connected scatter plot: x and y for two measures, points joined in time order by a smooth line, the first and last points and key years labeled

cards.name: Heatmap
cards.desc: A grid of rows and columns where each cell's color shows a value. Patterns across two categories, like hour by weekday, pop out without reading a single number.
cards.phrase: a heatmap with rows and columns as two categories, each cell filled from a single-hue sequential scale, thin gaps between cells, and a color legend with labeled stops

cards.name: Hexbin plot
