cards.desc: A scatter plot with too many points, binned into hexagons colored by count. It turns an unreadable blob into a clear map of where the data is dense.
cards.phrase: a hexbin plot: points binned into small hexagons colored by count on a sequential scale, empty hexagons left blank, and a legend for the counts

cards.name: Parallel coordinates
cards.desc: Several vertical axes side by side, with each item drawn as a line crossing all of them. Bundles of lines reveal groups; crossing lines show trade-offs.
cards.phrase: a parallel coordinates plot with one vertical axis per attribute, one thin translucent line per item colored by group, and one selected item drawn thicker

cards.name: Scatterplot matrix
cards.desc: A grid of small scatter plots, one for every pair of variables, with the variable names on the diagonal. A quick first look at a new dataset.
cards.phrase: a scatterplot matrix: a small scatter plot for every pair of variables arranged in a grid, variable names on the diagonal, shared axes along each row and column

cards.name: Quadrant chart
cards.desc: A scatter plot split into four boxes by two reference lines, each box named. It turns two scores into four groups, which is why it is a strategy-deck favorite.
cards.phrase: a quadrant chart: a scatter plot divided by dashed lines at the midpoint of each axis, each quadrant labeled in its corner with a name, and the items labeled next to their dots

cards.name: Sankey diagram
cards.desc: Nodes joined by bands whose width is the amount flowing between them. It follows a quantity through stages and shows where it splits, merges and leaks away.
cards.phrase: a Sankey diagram with stages left to right, flow bands sized by volume and colored by their source, narrow vertical node bars, and labels with totals next to each node

cards.name: Chord diagram
cards.desc: Groups placed around a circle, with ribbons between them sized by how much flows each way. It shows a whole web of two-way relationships in a compact shape.
cards.phrase: a chord diagram: groups as colored arcs around a circle, translucent ribbons between them sized by flow and colored by the larger source, group names outside the circle

cards.name: Network graph
cards.desc: Dots for things and lines for the links between them, arranged by a physics simulation so connected nodes pull together. Clusters and hubs appear on their own.
cards.phrase: a force-directed network graph: nodes as circles sized by number of connections and colored by community, thin gray links, and only the biggest hubs labeled

cards.name: Arc diagram
cards.desc: Nodes laid along a line with links drawn as arcs above it. Ordering the nodes well makes clusters and long-distance links easy to see, and labels never collide.
cards.phrase: an arc diagram: nodes in a row along a horizontal baseline, links drawn as semicircular arcs above, arc thickness by link weight, and one selected node's arcs highlighted

cards.name: Tree diagram
cards.desc: A root at the top branching down into children with elbow connectors. It is the clearest way to show who reports to whom or what belongs inside what.
cards.phrase: a tree diagram from a root at the top to leaves at the bottom, right-angled elbow connectors, nodes colored by level, and every node labeled

cards.name: Gantt chart
cards.desc: One horizontal bar per task, placed on a calendar axis from start to finish. Overlaps and dependencies are visible, and a line marks today.
cards.phrase: a Gantt chart: one row per task with a rounded bar from start to end date on a weekly axis, bars colored by phase, and a vertical red line marking today

cards.name: Timeline
cards.desc: Events placed as markers along a single time axis, with labels alternating above and below to avoid crowding. It shows sequence and spacing at a glance.
cards.phrase: a horizontal timeline with a single axis, a dot for each event, labels alternating above and below the line with thin leader lines, and year ticks along the axis

cards.name: Funnel chart
cards.desc: Stages stacked top to bottom, each bar narrower than the last by the share that dropped out. The step-to-step conversion rate is the number people look for.
cards.phrase: a funnel chart: one centered bar per stage sized by count, stage names and counts on the left, and the conversion rate from the previous stage on the right

cards.name: Choropleth map
cards.desc: Regions filled with color by a value such as a rate or median. Use rates, not raw counts, or the map just shows where people live.
cards.phrase: a choropleth map with regions filled from a five-step sequential scale of one hue, values normalized per capita, thin white borders, and a legend with labeled class breaks

cards.name: Proportional symbol map
cards.desc: Circles placed on locations and sized by a count. Unlike a filled map, a small dense city gets a big circle and an empty region gets nothing.
cards.phrase: a proportional symbol map: translucent circles with area proportional to the count, placed on each city, biggest drawn first so small ones stay on top, and a size legend

cards.name: Dot density map
cards.desc: One small dot for every so many people or events, scattered inside each area. Color the dots by group to show how populations mix.
cards.phrase: a dot density map where each tiny dot equals a fixed number of people, dots colored by group, a pale base map with no borders, and a key stating what one dot equals

cards.name: Tile grid map
cards.desc: Every region gets the same small square or hexagon placed roughly where it sits. Size bias disappears, so tiny regions count as much as huge ones.
cards.phrase: a tile grid map with one equal-size square per region arranged to approximate geography, filled on a sequential scale, each tile labeled with its short code

cards.name: Cartogram
cards.desc: A map distorted so each region's size matches a value such as population. Circles pushed apart (Dorling) are the cleanest version.
cards.phrase: a Dorling cartogram: each region as a circle sized by population and nudged so circles do not overlap, keeping rough geographic positions, colored by category

cards.name: Flow map
cards.desc: Curved lines drawn from origins to destinations, with thickness for volume. Curves keep two-way flows from sitting on top of each other.
cards.phrase: a flow map: curved arcs from one hub to each destination, arc thickness proportional to volume, a muted base map, and the hub marked with a dark dot

cards.name: Spike map
cards.desc: Thin vertical spikes rising from each location, with height for the value. Spikes overlap far less than circles, so dense places stay readable.
cards.phrase: a spike map: thin translucent triangles rising from each location with height proportional to the value, over a pale base map

cards.name: Position on a common scale
cards.desc: Marks placed along one shared axis. It is the most accurate way people read numbers, which is why dot plots and scatter plots are so precise.
cards.phrase: encode the key measure as position along a shared axis, the most accurate channel, rather than as color or size

cards.name: Length
cards.desc: The length of a bar from a shared baseline. Nearly as accurate as position, provided the baseline is zero and every bar starts from it.
cards.phrase: show amounts as bar length from a shared zero baseline so lengths compare directly

cards.name: Angle and arc
cards.desc: The size of a slice or arc. People estimate angles roughly and tend to misjudge slices that aren't near a quarter or half.
cards.phrase: use angle (pie or donut slices) only for two or three shares with large differences; use bar length when values are close

cards.name: Area
cards.aka: size of a circle or square
cards.desc: How much space a mark covers. People underestimate area differences, so a value twice as big looks less than twice as big. Scale area, never radius, to the value.
cards.phrase: encode magnitude as circle area (radius proportional to the square root of the value) and include a size legend with three reference circles

cards.name: Color lightness
cards.desc: From pale to dark in one hue. People read it as "more" or "less" without a key, but can't tell exact values, so it suits heatmaps and maps.
cards.phrase: encode the value as lightness of a single hue, light for low and dark for high, with a legend showing the steps

cards.name: Color hue
cards.desc: Different hues for different groups. Hue is excellent for telling categories apart and poor for showing amounts, because red isn't "more" than blue.
cards.phrase: use hue only for categories, at most six distinct hues, with every other category in neutral gray

cards.name: Shape
cards.desc: Circles, triangles and squares for different groups. A good second channel that survives black and white printing and color blindness.
cards.phrase: use marker shape (circle, triangle, square) as a redundant second channel for groups so the chart still works in grayscale

cards.name: Line style
cards.desc: Solid, dashed and dotted lines that separate what happened from what is planned or estimated. Dashed reads as "not real yet" almost universally.
cards.phrase: draw measured data as solid lines and forecasts, targets or estimates as dashed lines in the same color

cards.name: Transparency
cards.desc: Semi-transparent marks that build up where they overlap. With thousands of points, dense areas grow darker, revealing structure a solid blob hides.
cards.phrase: draw points at about 20% opacity so overlapping points build up into darker areas where data is dense

cards.name: Zero baseline
cards.desc: Bar and area charts must start at zero because the eye compares lengths. Line and dot charts may zoom in, because they are read by position.
cards.phrase: start the value axis at zero for bars and areas, and draw the zero line slightly darker than the other gridlines

cards.name: Log scale
cards.desc: Each step up the axis multiplies by ten instead of adding. Steady growth rates become straight lines, and tiny and huge values fit on one chart.
cards.phrase: use a logarithmic y-axis with ticks at 1, 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 and the words "log scale" in the axis title, so constant growth rates appear as straight lines

cards.name: Indexed to 100
cards.desc: Every series divided by its own starting value and multiplied by 100, so all lines start together. It compares growth rather than size.
cards.phrase: index every series to 100 at the start date so lines begin at the same point, with a reference line at 100 and the y-axis labeled "index, Jan = 100"

cards.name: Change from a baseline
cards.desc: Bars that show growth or decline against the same period a year earlier, above and below a zero line. Positive and negative get different colors.
cards.phrase: plot year-over-year percent change as bars above and below a zero line, positive in blue and negative in red, with the zero line drawn in dark ink

cards.name: Per capita
cards.desc: Dividing counts by population, area or users so places of different size can be compared. Raw counts mostly show where people live.
cards.phrase: normalize counts by population and show rates per 100,000 people, stating the denominator in the subtitle

cards.name: Shared axis across panels
cards.aka: common scale, fixed y in facets
cards.desc: Small multiples that all use the same y-axis range, so a tall line really is bigger. Independent axes make every panel look equally dramatic.
cards.phrase: give every small-multiple panel the same y-axis range so heights compare across panels; only free the axes if each panel's shape matters more than its size

cards.name: Dual-axis chart
cards.desc: Two series with different units plotted against separate left and right axes. Any crossing or gap between the lines is an accident of how the two axes were scaled.
cards.phrase: Avoid a dual-axis chart with two unrelated y-scales; instead use two aligned panels sharing one x-axis, or index both series to a common start

cards.name: Truncated bar axis
cards.desc: Bars that start at a value above zero, so a 4% difference looks like a 300% one. The most common way charts mislead, by accident or on purpose.
cards.phrase: Avoid a bar chart whose axis starts above zero; start bars at zero, or use dots on a zoomed axis if small differences matter

cards.name: Inverted or unlabeled axis
cards.desc: A y-axis where up means less, or an axis with no labels at all. Readers assume up means more and will read the trend backwards.
cards.phrase: Avoid an inverted y-axis where higher values sit lower; keep larger values higher and label every axis

cards.name: Moving average
cards.desc: Each point replaced by the average of the last few, which irons out daily noise and weekday cycles while keeping the trend. Show the raw data faintly behind it.
cards.phrase: plot a 7-day moving average as a bold line over the raw daily values drawn as faint thin bars or a light line, and say "7-day average" in the label

cards.name: Running total
cards.desc: Each point is the sum of everything so far. It smooths noise and makes it easy to see whether you're on track to reach a year-end target.
cards.phrase: show a cumulative year-to-date line against a straight dashed line toward the annual target, labeling the gap at the latest point

cards.name: Median versus mean
cards.desc: With skewed data like incomes or house prices, the mean is dragged by a few giants. The median is the typical value. Say which one you show.
cards.phrase: summarize with the median rather than the mean because the data is skewed, mark both on the histogram, and state which one the headline uses

cards.name: Smoothed trend line
cards.aka: LOESS curve, regression line, line of best fit
cards.desc: A fitted line or gentle curve through a scatter plot that shows the overall direction. Always keep the points visible so readers can judge the fit.
cards.phrase: add a smoothed LOESS trend curve through the scatter in dark ink, keep the points visible behind it, and avoid extending the curve beyond the data

cards.name: Forecast with uncertainty band
cards.aka: fan chart, confidence band, prediction interval
cards.desc: A projected line continuing the data, wrapped in a shaded band that widens as the forecast goes further out. It shows the best guess and how sure it is.
cards.phrase: show the forecast as a dashed line continuing the actuals, inside a shaded band for the 80% interval that widens over time, and label the band

cards.name: Error bars
cards.desc: A line through each estimate showing its plausible range. Overlapping bars warn readers that an apparent difference may be noise.
cards.phrase: draw each estimate as a dot with a horizontal 95% confidence interval line, sorted by estimate, and note the interval in the subtitle

cards.name: Top N plus "Other"
cards.desc: Show the biggest few categories and fold the rest into one gray "Other" bar, kept at the bottom. Ten crowded slivers become a clear ranking.
cards.phrase: show the top five categories sorted by value and group the remainder into a single gray "Other" bar placed last, regardless of its size

cards.name: This year against last year
cards.desc: Each year drawn as its own line on a January-to-December axis, with past years in gray and the current year in color. Seasonal patterns line up, so the difference is the story.
cards.phrase: overlay each year as a separate line on a shared January to December axis, previous years in thin gray, the current year in bold color and labeled

cards.name: Categorical palette
cards.desc: Distinct hues of similar weight, one per group, with no implied order. Keep it to six or fewer, and keep each group's color the same on every chart.
cards.phrase: a categorical palette of up to six distinct hues with similar lightness, the same color for each group on every chart, and gray for anything else

cards.name: Sequential palette
cards.desc: One hue running from pale to dark, so darker means more. The default for heatmaps and filled maps.
cards.phrase: a single-hue sequential palette from very light for low values to dark for high values, in five to seven steps

cards.name: Diverging palette
cards.desc: Two hues meeting at a pale neutral in the middle. It shows above and below a meaningful midpoint: zero, average, target or 50%.
cards.phrase: a diverging palette from red through a pale neutral to blue, centered exactly on the meaningful midpoint, with equal steps on both sides

cards.name: Gray plus one accent
cards.desc: Everything in quiet gray except the one series that matters, in a strong color. The fastest way to tell readers where to look.
cards.phrase: draw every series in light gray except the one the story is about, which gets a single strong accent color and a direct label

cards.name: Stepped classes
cards.desc: A handful of color steps with clear breaks, instead of a smooth gradient. Readers can match a step to the legend, and you choose meaningful break points.
cards.phrase: bin values into five classes with round-number breaks and a stepped legend, rather than a continuous gradient

cards.name: Bivariate color
cards.desc: A 3 by 3 grid of blended colors, so each region shows two values at once. Powerful for "where are both high", but needs a clear square legend.
cards.phrase: a bivariate choropleth with a 3 by 3 blended palette and a square legend that labels both axes with arrows for "higher"

cards.name: Meaningful colors
cards.desc: Colors readers already know: red and blue for parties, green and red for good and bad, blue for water. Breaking a convention costs readers a second look.
cards.phrase: use conventional, meaningful colors (blue for gains and red for losses, party colors for parties) and repeat the meaning in labels or icons

cards.name: Cyclic palette
cards.desc: Hues that wrap around so the end matches the start, for values like hour of day, month or compass direction, where December sits next to January.
cards.phrase: a cyclic color palette for the hour of day so 11pm and midnight are similar colors, shown with a circular legend

cards.name: Viridis
cards.desc: Purple through teal to yellow, rising steadily in lightness. Readable for color-blind viewers and in grayscale, and the default in matplotlib since 2015.
cards.phrase: the viridis colormap (dark purple to yellow), perceptually uniform and color-blind safe

cards.name: Magma and inferno
cards.desc: Black through purple and orange to pale yellow, like something heating up. Same even lightness as viridis, with a hotter, more dramatic mood.
cards.phrase: the magma colormap from near-black through magenta and orange to pale yellow

cards.name: Cividis
cards.desc: Navy to yellow with almost no red or green, designed to look nearly the same to people with and without color vision deficiency.
cards.phrase: the cividis colormap (navy to yellow), designed to look the same with or without color vision deficiency

cards.name: ColorBrewer Blues
cards.desc: Seven tested steps of blue from Cynthia Brewer's ColorBrewer, the cartographer's standard. Each step stays distinct on screen and in print.
cards.phrase: the ColorBrewer "Blues" sequential palette in five to seven classes

cards.name: ColorBrewer RdBu
cards.desc: Red to blue through a near-white middle. The workhorse diverging palette for temperature anomalies, swings and survey scales.
cards.phrase: the ColorBrewer "RdBu" diverging palette with white at the midpoint

cards.name: Okabe-Ito
cards.desc: Eight categorical colors chosen so they stay distinct for every common type of color blindness. The safest choice for categories.
cards.phrase: the Okabe-Ito color-blind-safe categorical palette (orange, sky blue, bluish green, yellow, blue, vermillion, reddish purple)

cards.name: Tableau 10
cards.desc: Ten muted, balanced categorical colors that look professional and stay calm on large dashboards.
cards.phrase: the Tableau 10 categorical palette: muted, evenly weighted hues

cards.name: Grayscale with one spot color
cards.desc: Black, grays and a single accent ink, like a newspaper with one spot color. It survives photocopiers and forces you to rank what matters.
cards.phrase: only black, three grays and one accent color, so the chart still works when printed in black and white

cards.name: Dark-mode palette
cards.desc: Lighter, slightly less saturated versions of the same hues on a near-black ground, with gridlines barely above the background. Pure saturated colors glare on dark.
cards.phrase: a dark-mode version of the palette: the same hues lifted in lightness and slightly desaturated, on a near-black background with very faint gridlines

cards.name: Rainbow scale
cards.desc: A full rainbow for ordered data. Its lightness jumps around, so it invents sharp edges at yellow and cyan and hides real ones, and fails for color-blind readers.
cards.phrase: Avoid a rainbow or jet colormap for ordered values; use a perceptually uniform palette like viridis instead

cards.name: Red against green
cards.desc: Red and green as the only difference between good and bad. About 1 in 12 men can't reliably tell them apart.
cards.phrase: Avoid red versus green as the only cue; use a blue-orange pairing, or add icons, labels or patterns

cards.name: Too many colors
cards.desc: A different color for every one of twelve categories. Nobody can match twelve legend swatches, so the chart becomes a matching game.
cards.phrase: Avoid more than six category colors; highlight the few that matter and put the rest in gray

cards.name: KPI tiles
cards.desc: A row of cards across the top, each with one metric, its change against a comparison period, and a tiny trend line. The summary before the detail.
cards.phrase: a row of four KPI tiles across the top, each with a short label, the current value in large type, the change versus last period in green or red with an arrow, and a sparkline

cards.name: Inverted pyramid
cards.desc: The most important numbers at the top, trends and breakdowns in the middle, detailed tables at the bottom. People stop reading when they have their answer.
cards.phrase: lay the dashboard out as an inverted pyramid: KPI tiles on top, two or three trend and breakdown charts in the middle, and a detail table at the bottom

cards.name: Small multiples
cards.desc: The same small chart repeated for each group in a grid, with identical scales. The eye compares shapes across panels instead of untangling one crowded chart.
cards.phrase: small multiples: one small chart per group in a grid, identical axes and scales, the group name as each panel's title, and the other groups drawn faintly in gray behind each panel for context

cards.name: One hero chart
cards.aka: feature chart with supporting tiles, bento
cards.desc: One large chart takes most of the space and a few small tiles support it. Good when there's one main question and a couple of side ones.
cards.phrase: one large hero chart taking about two-thirds of the layout, with three small supporting tiles stacked beside it

cards.name: Filter bar
cards.desc: Dropdowns, date ranges and toggles along the top that apply to every chart below, with the current selection always visible.
cards.phrase: a filter bar across the top with a date range, region dropdown and segment toggle, applying to every chart, with active filters shown as removable chips

cards.name: Table with in-cell bars
cards.aka: data table with bars, heat table
cards.desc: A sortable table where numeric columns carry small bars or shading inside the cells. People who want exact numbers get them, and the bars still show the pattern.
cards.phrase: a table with right-aligned tabular numbers, a small horizontal bar inside each value cell scaled to the column maximum, and one column shaded as a heatmap

cards.name: Status board
cards.aka: RAG status, health board, service status
cards.desc: A list of items each with a colored status pill and a short reason, sorted so problems come first. The color is backed up by a word for color-blind readers.
cards.phrase: a status board listing each item with a pill reading "At risk", "Watch" or "On track" in red, amber or green, sorted worst first, with a one-line reason

cards.name: Annotated report page
cards.desc: A printed or PDF page that reads top to bottom: headline finding, one chart with notes, a paragraph of explanation, then supporting charts. No hover, so everything is labeled.
cards.phrase: a one-page static report: headline finding at the top, one fully annotated chart, a short paragraph of explanation, then two supporting charts, with all values labeled because there is no hover

cards.name: Tooltip
cards.aka: hover card, data label on hover
cards.desc: A small card that appears next to the point under the cursor, with the exact values and the name. It keeps the chart clean while still answering "which one is that?"
cards.phrase: tooltips on hover and tap showing the item name in bold and its values with units, positioned next to the point and never covering it

cards.name: Hover to highlight
cards.aka: focus on hover, dim the rest
cards.desc: Hovering one series brings it forward in color and fades everything else to gray. A crowded chart becomes readable one line at a time.
cards.phrase: on hover, highlight the series under the cursor in its color with a label, and fade all other series to light gray

cards.name: Crosshair readout
cards.desc: A vertical line follows the cursor across a time chart and lists every series' value at that moment. Synced across panels, it lines up related charts.
cards.phrase: a vertical crosshair that follows the cursor across the time axis, showing the date and each series' value at that point in a compact readout, synced across all charts

cards.name: Linked brushing
cards.desc: Drag a box over points in one chart, and the same items light up in every other chart. It connects views so you can ask "where are these on the other axis?"
cards.phrase: linked brushing: dragging a rectangle in the scatter plot selects those items, which stay colored in every other chart while unselected items fade to gray

cards.name: Drill-down
cards.desc: Click a bar to replace the chart with that bar's breakdown, and a breadcrumb trail leads back up. One chart covers a whole hierarchy.
cards.phrase: clicking a bar drills into its breakdown with an animated transition, and a breadcrumb above the chart ("All regions › Europe › France") leads back up

cards.name: Overview plus detail
cards.aka: focus + context, zoom and pan, range slider
cards.desc: A large chart of the selected window above a small strip of the whole timeline with a draggable window. You zoom without losing your place.
cards.phrase: a large detail chart above a small overview strip of the full time range, with a draggable, resizable window on the strip that sets the detail view's range

cards.name: Interactive legend
cards.aka: click to show or hide series
cards.desc: Legend items work as toggles: click one to hide or isolate that series. Hidden items stay in the legend, grayed out, so they can be brought back.
cards.phrase: make the legend interactive: clicking an item toggles that series, double-clicking isolates it, and hidden items stay in the legend in gray with a strike-through

cards.name: Animated transitions
cards.desc: When data or filters change, marks glide to their new positions instead of jumping. The eye can follow each item, so changes are understood, not just noticed.
cards.phrase: animate changes: when filters or sorting change, bars and points move smoothly to their new positions over about 400ms so each item can be followed

cards.name: Scrollytelling
cards.desc: The chart stays pinned while text steps scroll past; each step changes the chart, highlighting, zooming or adding data. Reading and seeing move together.
cards.phrase: scrollytelling: a sticky chart beside or behind scrolling text cards, each card triggering one change in the chart (highlight, zoom, add a series) with a smooth transition

cards.name: Animated time slider
cards.desc: A slider and play button move the chart through time, so bubbles drift and bars race. Watching the motion makes change memorable.
cards.phrase: a time slider with a play button that animates the chart through each year, the current year shown large and faint behind the data

cards.name: Headline title
cards.desc: A title that states the finding as a sentence, with a smaller subtitle saying what is plotted. Readers get the point before they read a single axis.
cards.phrase: a headline title that states the main finding as a short sentence, with a smaller subtitle naming the measure, units and time period

cards.name: Direct labels
cards.desc: Names placed right next to each line or bar in its own color, instead of in a legend. The reader never has to look away and match swatches.
cards.phrase: label each series directly at its end in the series color instead of using a legend

cards.name: Callout note
cards.desc: A short note set beside the chart with a thin line or arrow pointing to the exact spot it explains. One or two are plenty.
cards.phrase: add one or two short callout notes in small text with thin leader lines pointing to the exact data points they explain

cards.name: Reference line
cards.desc: A thin horizontal line for a target, average or threshold, labeled at its end. Bars above and below it read as hits and misses without any math.
cards.phrase: add a labeled dashed reference line for the target value across the plot, and color bars that miss the target differently

cards.name: Shaded period
cards.desc: A light vertical band behind the chart marking a period like a recession, a promotion or a strike, with a label at the top.
cards.phrase: shade the relevant period with a light gray vertical band behind the data, labeled at the top

cards.name: Event markers
cards.desc: Thin vertical lines with short labels marking launches, policy changes or outages, so readers can see what happened right before the line moved.
cards.phrase: mark key events with thin vertical lines and short labels at the top of the chart

cards.name: Units on the top tick
cards.desc: Put the units right on the highest axis label ("60k cups") instead of a rotated axis title. It saves space and nobody has to tilt their head.
cards.phrase: put the units on the top y-axis label (for example "60k cups") instead of a rotated axis title

cards.name: Source and notes line
cards.desc: A small line under the chart naming the data source, any adjustments and who made it. It makes the chart trustworthy and traceable when it travels.
cards.phrase: a small footer under the chart with "Source:" and the data source, a short note on any adjustments, and the date of the data

cards.name: Plain-language uncertainty
cards.desc: Saying how sure you are in words next to the number: "likely between 41% and 47%". Bands and error bars help analysts; words help everyone else.
cards.phrase: state uncertainty in plain words next to the key number (for example "likely between 41% and 47%") in addition to any band or error bar

cards.name: Martini glass
cards.desc: A narrow guided stem where you walk the reader through the key points in order, opening into a wide bowl where they can explore freely.
cards.phrase: structure it as a martini glass: three or four guided steps that make the main point in order, then an open, explorable chart with filters at the end

cards.name: Build it up step by step
cards.desc: Start with an empty axis, add one series, then the comparison, then the surprise. Each step gets its own sentence. It works on slides and in scrollytelling.
cards.phrase: reveal the chart in three steps: first the axes and one series with the setup sentence, then the comparison series, then the highlight and annotation that delivers the finding

cards.name: Before and after
cards.desc: Two states of the same chart side by side or behind a slider, so the change itself is the subject. Same scales on both sides, or the comparison lies.
cards.phrase: show before and after side by side with identical scales and layout, labeled "Before" and "After", with the key difference annotated

cards.name: Zoom from context to detail
cards.desc: Show the whole picture first, then zoom into the part that matters with a visible connection between the two, so the reader knows where they are.
cards.phrase: show the full context chart first, then a zoomed inset of the important range, joined to it by guide lines so the reader sees where the detail comes from

cards.name: One big number
cards.desc: A single striking figure in very large type, a short line saying what it means, and a small chart for context. Sometimes the best chart is a number.
cards.phrase: lead with one big number in very large type, a one-line explanation beneath it, and a small supporting chart for context

cards.name: Make the number concrete
cards.desc: Translate an abstract quantity into something familiar: football fields, a city's population, a daily habit. It turns a number into a picture people can feel.
cards.phrase: translate the key number into a familiar comparison (for example "enough to fill 40 Olympic pools") and show it as a simple row of icons

cards.name: How to read this chart
cards.desc: A small worked example next to an unfamiliar chart: one mark explained with arrows ("each dot is a city; bigger means more people"). Essential for anything new.
cards.phrase: add a small "How to read this" key that explains one example mark with arrows and plain words

cards.name: You are here
cards.desc: Let readers put themselves on the chart, with their age, salary or town highlighted among everyone else. Personal relevance is the strongest hook in data stories.
cards.phrase: let the reader enter their own value and highlight their position in the distribution with a "You" label, everyone else in gray

cards.name: 3D effects
cards.desc: Tilted pies and extruded bars. Perspective makes the front slices look bigger and hides values behind each other, and adds nothing true.
cards.phrase: Avoid 3D effects, perspective or extrusion of any kind; keep every chart flat and 2D

cards.name: Pie with many slices
cards.desc: Eight, ten, fifteen slices. Nobody can compare thin wedges or match them to a legend, and the small ones all look the same.
cards.phrase: Avoid pie charts with more than five slices; use a sorted bar chart instead

cards.name: Spaghetti chart
cards.desc: Ten or more colored lines tangled on one chart with a long legend. Every line hides another.
cards.phrase: Avoid line charts with more than five colored lines; highlight the important few and gray the rest, or split into small multiples

cards.name: Chartjunk
cards.desc: Gradients, drop shadows, heavy borders, clip-art and dense gridlines that compete with the data. Every mark should earn its place.
cards.phrase: Avoid chartjunk: gradients, shadows, heavy borders, background images and dense gridlines; keep only the data, labels and faint gridlines

cards.name: Rotated labels
cards.desc: Category names tilted 45 or 90 degrees to cram them under columns. Readers twist their heads and still misread them.
cards.phrase: Avoid rotated or diagonal axis labels; switch to horizontal bars so labels read normally

cards.name: Legend far from the data
cards.desc: A legend in a corner with six swatches that readers must match to lines across the chart, back and forth, for every series.
cards.phrase: Avoid a separate legend far from the data; label series directly next to the lines or bars

cards.name: Tufte minimalism
cards.desc: Remove everything that isn't data. No gridlines, axis lines only as long as the data range, serif labels, and the data drawn in thin dark ink.
cards.phrase: Tufte-style minimalism: maximize the data-ink ratio, no gridlines or chart border, range-frame axes that span only the data, small serif labels, thin dark lines and direct labels

cards.name: Weekly news magazine
cards.desc: A small red tag at the top left, a bold short title and a one-line subtitle, horizontal gridlines only, the y-axis labels on the right and a flat palette of blues.
cards.phrase: news-magazine chart style: a small red rectangle above a bold sans-serif title and a short subtitle, white background, light horizontal gridlines only, y-axis labels on the right, flat dark-blue and light-blue lines, source line at bottom left

cards.name: Financial paper
cards.desc: A warm salmon-pink background, a serif headline, slim lines in deep blue, claret and teal, and fine horizontal gridlines. Restrained and very recognizable.
cards.phrase: financial-newspaper chart style: warm salmon-pink background, a serif headline, slim lines in deep blue, claret and teal, fine horizontal gridlines, labels in a clean sans-serif

cards.name: Newspaper graphics desk
cards.desc: Mostly gray data with one series in color, a few short annotations set right on the chart in small type, generous white space and no legend.
cards.phrase: newspaper graphics style: white background, data mostly in light gray with one series in a strong color, short annotations in small text placed directly on the chart, very light gridlines and no legend

cards.name: Data-science blog
cards.desc: A light gray background with heavy gridlines, thick bright lines in blue, red and gold, a bold title and no axis lines. Friendly and data-forward.
cards.phrase: data-blog chart style: light gray background, prominent white gridlines, thick bright lines in blue, red-orange and gold, a bold left-aligned title and subtitle, no axis spines

cards.name: Bold black business
cards.desc: A black background, a huge bold white headline, and data in saturated electric colors. Loud and confident, built to stop a scroll.
cards.phrase: bold dark editorial style: black background, very large bold white sans-serif headline, saturated electric blue, magenta and orange data, thin dark-gray gridlines

cards.name: Research explorer
cards.desc: Clean line charts with countries labeled at the line ends, dotted gridlines, a clear title and subtitle, and a source and license line underneath. Built for reuse.
cards.phrase: research-explorer chart style: white background, title and explanatory subtitle at the top left, muted multi-color lines labeled at their ends, dotted light gridlines, and a source and license line at the bottom

cards.name: Hand-drawn comic
cards.desc: Wobbly hand-drawn lines, handwriting labels and arrows with jokes. It signals "rough and informal", which is perfect for sketches and talks.
cards.phrase: hand-drawn comic style: wobbly black ink lines, handwritten labels, no gridlines, a few arrows with casual annotations, on a white background

cards.name: Swiss modernist
cards.desc: A strict grid, Helvetica-like type in a few weights, black and one red, flush-left text and big numbers. Clean, objective and architectural.
cards.phrase: Swiss modernist style: strict grid, a neo-grotesque sans-serif in two weights, black on white with one red accent, flush-left text, large numerals and no decoration

cards.name: Terminal chart
cards.desc: Bars and sparklines drawn with block characters in a monospaced font, glowing on a dark terminal. Charts that live in logs, CLIs and READMEs.
cards.phrase: a terminal-style text chart: horizontal bars drawn with block characters (█▉▊▋▌) in a monospaced font, values printed after each bar, green on a near-black background

cards.name: Playfair's engraved charts
cards.desc: The first line, bar and pie charts, hand-engraved and hand-colored: two time series with the area between them shaded to show the balance of trade, fine grid and copperplate lettering.
cards.phrase: in the style of an 18th-century engraved statistical plate: cream paper, fine sepia grid, two hand-drawn time series with the gap between them washed in pale yellow and pink, copperplate script labels

cards.name: Nightingale's rose
cards.desc: Twelve wedges, one per month, with area showing deaths by cause: preventable disease in blue dwarfing wounds in red. A chart that changed hospital policy.
cards.phrase: a Nightingale-style polar area diagram: twelve monthly wedges radiating from the center with area proportional to value, layered pale blue, red and black, on cream paper with fine serif labels

cards.name: Minard's flow map
cards.aka: Napoleon's march, flow map with time
cards.desc: A thick tan band that shrinks as the army advances on Moscow, a thin black band for the retreat, and a temperature line below. Six variables in one drawing.
cards.phrase: a Minard-style flow map: a band whose width is the quantity, tan for the outward journey and black for the return, drawn over a sparse map with a linked temperature line underneath

cards.name: Snow's cholera map
cards.aka: Broad Street pump map, dot map of cases
cards.desc: A street map with a small black bar for every death, stacked at each address, clustering around one water pump. The map that founded epidemiology.
cards.phrase: a John Snow-style dot map: a fine black street plan with each case drawn as a small black tick stacked at its address, clustering around a marked source, on aged paper

cards.name: Du Bois data portraits
cards.aka: W.E.B. Du Bois, 1900 Paris Exposition plates
cards.desc: Hand-drawn gouache plates in flat crimson, gold, green, black and tan on buff paper, with hand-lettered capitals and bold, inventive forms like spiraling bars.
cards.phrase: in the style of W.E.B. Du Bois's 1900 data portraits: flat gouache colors (crimson, gold, emerald green, black, tan) on buff paper, hand-lettered all-caps titles, bold simple forms with thin black outlines

cards.name: Isotype
cards.desc: Rows of identical, flat, boxy pictograms where each icon is a fixed count, in a few solid colors. Designed so anyone could read statistics, regardless of language.
cards.phrase: Isotype style: rows of identical flat pictograms, each standing for a fixed quantity, in two or three solid colors (black, red, blue) on off-white, with plain sans-serif labels

cards.name: Bertin's visual variables
cards.desc: Black-and-white matrices of marks varying in size, value, grain, orientation and shape. The grammar that later became Tableau and ggplot.
cards.phrase: in the manner of Jacques Bertin: black ink on white, a reorderable matrix whose cells vary only in mark size and value, with a strict grid and small sans-serif labels

cards.name: Gapminder bubbles
cards.desc: Countries as translucent bubbles sized by population and colored by region, income on a log x-axis, life expectancy on y, and the year as a huge pale number behind.
cards.phrase: a Gapminder-style bubble chart: income on a log x-axis, life expectancy on the y-axis, bubbles sized by population and colored by world region (cyan, pink, lime, yellow) with dark outlines, and the year as a huge pale numeral in the background

cards.name: Pulsar plot
cards.desc: Dozens of stacked white line traces on black, each hiding the one behind it, rising into peaks in the center. A radio astronomy plot that became an album cover.
cards.phrase: a pulsar-style ridgeline: many thin white line traces stacked closely on a black background, each filled black so it hides the lines behind, with sharp peaks clustered in the center

cards.name: Data humanism
cards.desc: Small hand-drawn glyphs where every petal, color and stroke encodes a detail of one person's data, with a rich legend. Slow, personal, imperfect on purpose.
cards.phrase: data humanism style: each record drawn as a small hand-made glyph whose petals, colors and marks encode its attributes, soft watercolor tones and fine ink lines on white, with an illustrated legend

cards.name: Generative text drawings
cards.desc: Branching lines where every sentence of a book becomes a stroke, colored by theme and bending at each paragraph. Literature turned into structure.
cards.phrase: a generative drawing of a text: each sentence a straight segment whose length is its word count, turning right at every sentence break, colored by theme, on white with no axes

cards.name: Delicate radial data art
cards.desc: Fine strokes, small dots and soft pastel accents arranged radially or in flowing rows, with tiny italic labels. Feels like a scientific illustration or jewelry.
cards.phrase: delicate data art: hair-thin lines and small circles in a radial arrangement, a soft palette of dusty pink, sage and ochre on off-white, tiny italic labels and generous empty space

cards.name: Luminous radial
cards.aka: Nadieh Bremer style, glowing data art
cards.desc: Vivid gradients and glowing arcs on a dark ground, built from code in radial compositions. Precise like a chart, rich like a print.
cards.phrase: luminous radial data art: arcs and circles arranged around a center, vivid magenta, orange and teal gradients with a soft glow on a deep navy background, minimal thin labels

cards.name: Emotional arcs
cards.desc: Each life drawn as an arc that should run its full length but stops short where it ended, the missing years shown as a faint ghost. Data that asks you to feel the loss.
cards.phrase: emotional arc visualization: each person drawn as an arc in bright orange that stops where their life ended, continuing as a faint gray ghost for the years they lost, on a dark charcoal background

cards.name: Illustrated charts
cards.desc: Charts painted or drawn by hand, where bars become objects and people, with handwritten labels and warm, uneven color. Approachable and human.
cards.phrase: an illustrated chart that looks hand-painted: bars drawn as real objects with uneven watercolor fills, handwritten labels and values, warm muted colors on a cream background

cards.name: Climate stripes
cards.desc: One vertical stripe per year, colored blue for cool and red for warm, with no axes, numbers or words. Reduces a century to a single, unforgettable image.
cards.phrase: climate-stripes style: one thin vertical stripe per year, colored on a red-blue diverging scale centered on the long-term average, with no axes, labels or gridlines

cards.name: Generative data art
cards.aka: data sculpture, flow fields, AI data paintings
cards.desc: Thousands of particles or strokes driven by the data, flowing like smoke or paint in luminous color. It trades precision for awe and is meant to be felt, not read.
cards.phrase: generative data art: thousands of thin flowing strokes following a flow field driven by the data, luminous color gradient from deep blue through violet to warm orange, dark background, no axes

cards.name: Sports analytics chart
cards.desc: A court, pitch or field drawn faintly, with hexagons sized by attempts and colored by efficiency. Sport fans read it instantly because the space is familiar.
cards.phrase: a sports-analytics shot chart: a faint half-court outline, hexagons sized by number of attempts and colored from cool blue (below average) to hot red (above average), with a compact legend

cards.name: System context diagram
cards.aka: C4 level 1, context diagram, big picture
cards.desc: Your software system as one box in the middle, with the people who use it and the other systems it talks to around it. No technology, no internals: just who and what it depends on, and why.
cards.phrase: a C4 system context diagram: one box for our system in the center, people as person shapes, external systems as grey boxes around it; every box shows name, [type] and a one-line purpose, every arrow a verb label, and no internals

cards.name: Container diagram
cards.desc: Zooms into one system and shows its containers: the separately running or deployed things such as web apps, APIs, databases, queues and mobile apps. Each box names its technology, and each arrow names the protocol.
cards.phrase: a C4 container diagram for one system inside a labeled boundary: each container as a box with name, [Container: technology] and its job, databases as cylinders, external systems grey outside the boundary; label every arrow with intent and protocol, e.g. reads accounts [JSON/HTTPS]

cards.name: Component diagram
cards.desc: Zooms into one container and shows the major components inside it: controllers, services, repositories, facades, the groupings of code behind one interface. Arrows show which component calls which, and what sits outside the container.
cards.phrase: a C4 component diagram zoomed into one container: its boundary as a labeled dashed box, 3 to 7 components inside as boxes with name and [Component], neighbouring containers and systems grey outside, arrows labeled with what is called

cards.name: Code diagram
cards.aka: C4 level 4, class diagram, code view
cards.desc: Zooms into one component and shows the code that implements it, usually as a UML class diagram of its main classes and interfaces. It is the most detailed C4 level and the one most often skipped.
cards.phrase: a C4 code-level view of one component as a UML class diagram: only the 3 to 6 classes and interfaces that matter, public methods only, dependency arrows dashed, implementation arrows with hollow heads, nothing from other components

cards.name: System landscape diagram
cards.desc: A context diagram for a whole organization: every software system and the people who use them, with no single system in focus. It shows how the estate hangs together and which systems are the hubs.
cards.phrase: a C4 system landscape: all software systems of the organization as boxes inside an enterprise boundary, grouped by business domain, people outside on the left; arrows only for the main relationships, each with a short verb label

cards.name: Dynamic diagram
cards.aka: C4 dynamic view, runtime view, collaboration view
cards.desc: Uses the same boxes as a container or component diagram, but shows one scenario at runtime: numbered arrows give the order of the calls for a single use case like signing in. It is the C4 cousin of a communication diagram.
cards.phrase: a C4 dynamic diagram for one scenario: only the containers or components involved, arrows numbered 1, 2, 3 in call order with a short label each, and the scenario name as the title; no more than 8 steps

cards.name: Deployment diagram
cards.desc: Shows where containers run in one environment: nested deployment nodes such as a region, a cluster, a VM or a browser, with container instances placed inside them. Each environment, like staging or production, gets its own diagram.
cards.phrase: a C4 deployment diagram for production: deployment nodes as nested solid boxes labeled with name and [technology], e.g. region > cluster > service; container instances inside with an instance count; arrows labeled with protocol

cards.name: C4 notation conventions
cards.desc: C4 is notation independent, but it asks for a few habits: every box carries a name, an element type, the technology and a short description; every arrow is one-way and labeled with intent and protocol; and every diagram has a title and a key.
cards.phrase: C4 notation conventions: each box shows its name in bold, [element type: technology] beneath, then a one-sentence description; arrows one-way with a verb phrase and [protocol]; a title stating scope and level, and a key for shapes, colors and line styles

cards.name: Box-and-arrow sketch
cards.aka: whiteboard diagram, napkin sketch, architecture sketch
cards.desc: Boxes for things, arrows for how they connect, drawn fast with no formal notation. It is how most architecture conversations start, on a whiteboard or in Excalidraw.
cards.phrase: a quick box-and-arrow sketch: one box per running thing with a plain name, arrows in the direction data flows, a short label on every arrow, left to right, under 8 boxes, and one handwritten note on the part under discussion

cards.name: Layer diagram
cards.aka: layer cake, stack diagram, layered architecture diagram
cards.desc: Horizontal bands stacked on top of each other, each a layer of the system, with the rule that a layer only calls the one below it. A vertical bar on the side often holds cross-cutting concerns like auth and logging.
cards.phrase: a layer diagram: full-width horizontal bands from top (presentation) to bottom (infrastructure), each labeled with its name and two example contents, one arrow on the side saying calls go down only, and cross-cutting concerns as a vertical bar on the right

cards.name: UML class diagram
cards.aka: class diagram, domain model diagram, object model
cards.desc: Classes as three-part boxes holding the name, attributes and operations, joined by typed relationships: association with multiplicities, composition with a filled diamond, and inheritance with a hollow triangle. It shows the static shape of a model.
cards.phrase: a UML class diagram: three-compartment boxes (name, key attributes, key operations), associations with multiplicities at both ends, composition with a filled diamond on the owner, inheritance with a hollow triangle on the parent, abstract names in italics, under 8 classes

cards.name: Entity relationship diagram
cards.aka: ERD, ER diagram, crow's foot diagram, data model
cards.desc: Tables or entities as boxes listing their columns and keys, joined by lines whose ends show cardinality in crow's foot notation: a bar for one, a circle for zero, a three-pronged foot for many. It shows how data relates and what must exist for what.
cards.phrase: an entity relationship diagram in crow's foot notation: one box per table with its name in caps, columns listed with PK and FK marked, relationship lines with correct cardinality at both ends, a verb on each line, one subject area of at most 8 tables

cards.name: Dependency graph
cards.aka: module graph, package dependency diagram, import graph
cards.desc: Modules, packages or services as nodes and dependencies as arrows from the user to the thing it uses. Laid out in layers, it shows what everything rests on and makes cycles and surprising imports jump out.
cards.phrase: a dependency graph laid out top to bottom: each module as a small rounded node, arrows from the depending module to the one it imports, stable shared modules at the bottom, any cycle drawn in red and called out

cards.name: Network topology diagram
cards.aka: network diagram, topology map, infrastructure network diagram
cards.desc: Devices and network segments: the internet edge, firewalls, routers and switches, subnets or VLANs with their address ranges, and the hosts in each. It shows what can physically or logically reach what.
cards.phrase: a network topology diagram: internet on the left, firewall next, each subnet or VLAN as a labeled zone with its CIDR range, a switch per zone and hosts hanging off it with their last octet; plain lines without arrowheads for links

cards.name: Threat model data flow diagram
cards.aka: threat model DFD, trust boundary diagram, STRIDE diagram
cards.desc: A data flow diagram drawn for security: external entities as rectangles, processes as circles, data stores as open-ended boxes, and dashed trust boundaries wherever data crosses from less trusted to more trusted. Every flow that crosses a boundary is a place to ask what could go wrong.
cards.phrase: a threat model data flow diagram: external entities as rectangles, processes as circles, data stores as two parallel lines, labeled flow arrows, trust boundaries as red dashed lines, and a numbered marker on each flow that crosses a boundary for the threat discussion

cards.name: Cloud architecture diagram
cards.aka: AWS architecture diagram, Azure diagram, reference architecture
cards.desc: Managed services placed inside the provider's nesting of account, region, VPC, availability zone and subnet. It shows redundancy, network placement and which managed services the system leans on.
cards.phrase: a cloud architecture diagram: nested labeled boundaries for region, VPC and availability zones, managed services as labeled boxes in the right subnet, the request path from users to data drawn first and solid, replication and background flows dashed

cards.name: Sequence diagram
cards.aka: UML sequence diagram, interaction diagram, swimlane of calls
cards.desc: Participants sit in a row across the top, each with a dashed lifeline running down. Messages are horizontal arrows between lifelines, ordered top to bottom in time, with replies drawn dashed. It shows one scenario, such as a single request, from start to finish.
cards.phrase: a sequence diagram of one scenario: participants left to right in the order they are first called, the caller or user first, dashed lifelines, solid arrows for calls labeled with the operation, dashed arrows for replies labeled with the result, time running down

cards.name: Activation bars
cards.aka: execution specification, focus of control, activation box
cards.desc: Thin rectangles on a lifeline that show when a participant is busy handling a call, from the message that starts the work to the reply. A call to itself stacks a second, offset bar on top, so nesting stays visible.
cards.phrase: a sequence diagram with activation bars: a bar on each lifeline from the incoming call to its reply, self-calls as a looped arrow with a second bar offset to the right, and no bar on a participant that is idle

cards.name: Combined fragments
cards.aka: alt, opt, loop, par, interaction operators, sequence frames
cards.desc: Labeled frames drawn across lifelines that add control flow to a sequence: alt for if/else with a guard per section, opt for an optional part, loop for repetition and par for things that run at the same time. Dashed lines split the sections of an alt or par.
cards.phrase: a sequence diagram with combined fragments: alt frames for branches with a [guard] on each section separated by a dashed line, opt for optional steps, loop with its condition, par for parallel work; at most one level of nesting

cards.name: Sync, async and reply arrows
cards.aka: message types, synchronous call, asynchronous message, return message
cards.desc: Sequence diagrams use three arrow styles. A solid line with a filled head is a synchronous call where the caller waits; a solid line with an open head is an asynchronous message where the caller carries on; a dashed line is the reply.
cards.phrase: a sequence diagram that distinguishes message types: solid line with filled arrowhead for a blocking call, solid line with open arrowhead for an async message or event, dashed line for a reply, and a small key explaining the three

cards.name: Notes, actors and grouping boxes
cards.aka: sequence notes, participant boxes, actor shapes
cards.desc: Three small additions that make a sequence easier to read: stick-figure actors for humans, notes attached to one lifeline or spanning several, and colored boxes that group participants that belong together, such as everything inside the backend.
cards.phrase: a sequence diagram with a stick-figure actor for the human, a shaded labeled box grouping the backend participants, and notes over the lifelines for rules or timings that the message labels cannot carry

cards.name: Communication diagram
cards.desc: The same information as a sequence diagram, arranged as a graph: objects are boxes placed freely, links are plain lines between them, and each message is a small arrow beside a link with a sequence number like 1, 1.1, 1.2. Time is in the numbers, not the layout.
cards.phrase: a UML communication diagram: objects as boxes with underlined :Type names, plain lines for links, each message as a small arrow next to its link labeled with a nested sequence number and operation, e.g. 1.2: charge(), no more than 10 messages

cards.name: Happy path beside failure path
cards.aka: failure sequence, unhappy path, error flow
cards.desc: Two short sequences of the same interaction drawn side by side: what happens when everything works, and what happens when one step times out or fails. The failure side shows the timeout, the retry and how the system recovers or gives up.
cards.phrase: a pair of sequence diagrams side by side for the same interaction: left the happy path in green, right the failure path in red showing the timeout, the retry with the same idempotency key and the final outcome, with matching participants and order

cards.name: State machine diagram
cards.aka: state diagram, state transition diagram, finite state machine, FSM
cards.desc: The states one thing can be in, drawn as rounded boxes, and the transitions between them as arrows labeled event [guard] / action. A filled dot marks the start and a bullseye the end. Anything not drawn is not allowed.
cards.phrase: a state machine diagram: states as rounded boxes named as adjectives or past participles, a filled dot for the initial state, a bullseye for final states, each transition arrow labeled event [guard] / action, and no transitions that the code does not allow

cards.name: Hierarchical statechart
cards.aka: Harel statechart, nested state machine, composite states, orthogonal regions
cards.desc: A state machine with depth and concurrency: states nest inside a parent state, so one arrow from the parent covers all its children, and a parent can split into regions that run at the same time. It keeps big machines from exploding into hundreds of arrows.
cards.phrase: a hierarchical statechart: a composite state as a large rounded box with its name at top left, child states inside with their own initial dot, orthogonal regions separated by a dashed line, and transitions from the composite border that apply to every child

cards.name: Timing diagram
cards.aka: UML timing diagram, waveform diagram, signal timing chart
cards.desc: Each participant gets a horizontal row, and a stepped line shows which state it is in along a shared time axis. Arrows between rows show the messages that cause the changes, and brackets mark duration constraints.
cards.phrase: a timing diagram: one row per participant with its name on the left and its states listed as levels, a stepped line showing the state over a shared time axis in milliseconds at the bottom, arrows between rows for causing messages, and a {≤ n ms} bracket for constraints

cards.name: Timeline
cards.desc: Events placed in order along one time axis, each with a timestamp and a short label. Shading a span shows how long something lasted, such as the customer impact during an incident.
cards.phrase: a horizontal timeline: one axis left to right with events as dots placed to scale, each with a timestamp and a short label alternating above and below, the impact window shaded, and the key gap called out

cards.name: Gantt chart
cards.desc: Tasks as rows and time as columns, with a bar per task from its start to its end. Arrows link tasks that depend on each other, diamonds mark milestones, and a line marks today.
cards.phrase: a Gantt chart: tasks as rows listed in start order, weeks as columns, one bar per task, dependency arrows from the end of one bar to the start of the next, milestones as diamonds, and a dashed today line

cards.name: Lifecycle loop
cards.aka: cycle diagram, loop diagram, continuous cycle
cards.desc: A handful of stages placed around a ring with arrows from each to the next, ending back at the start. It says that the process repeats and that the last stage feeds the first.
cards.phrase: a lifecycle loop: 4 to 6 stages as labeled pills spaced evenly around a ring, curved arrows clockwise from each stage to the next, the arrow back to the first stage highlighted and labeled with what feeds back

cards.name: Flowchart
cards.aka: process flow, flow diagram, process map
cards.desc: Boxes for steps, diamonds for yes or no decisions, and arrows for the order they happen in. Rounded pills mark where the process starts and ends, so a reader can trace every path from one to the other.
cards.phrase: a flowchart read top to bottom or left to right, with rounded pills for start and end, rectangles for steps written as verb phrases, diamonds for yes or no questions with both exits labeled, and no more than about 12 shapes

cards.name: Decision tree
cards.aka: decision diagram, question tree, classification tree
cards.desc: A tree that starts with one question and splits on each answer until every branch ends in an outcome. Read from the root down, each path is one rule, so the whole tree is a complete set of if-then rules you can check by eye.
cards.phrase: a decision tree drawn top down, with each question in a box, each branch labeled with its answer, and every leaf a colored outcome pill; keep it to three levels and make sure every path ends in a leaf

cards.name: Swimlane diagram
cards.aka: cross-functional flowchart, Rummler-Brache diagram, lane diagram
cards.desc: A flowchart split into horizontal or vertical lanes, one per role, team or system. Each step sits in the lane of whoever does it, so every arrow that crosses a lane line is a handoff, and handoffs are where work waits and gets lost.
cards.phrase: a swimlane diagram with one horizontal lane per role, lane names in a header strip on the left, steps as boxes in the lane of whoever does them, decisions as diamonds, time flowing left to right, and every lane-crossing arrow treated as a handoff

cards.name: UML activity diagram
cards.desc: UML's flowchart. A filled dot starts the flow, rounded actions follow, and a thick bar forks the flow into steps that run in parallel and joins them again. A bullseye ends it.
cards.phrase: a UML activity diagram flowing left to right, starting at a filled dot and ending at a bullseye, with rounded action boxes, a thick fork bar where steps run in parallel and a matching join bar where they all must finish

cards.name: BPMN process diagram
cards.aka: BPMN 2.0, business process model and notation, process model
cards.desc: A standard notation for business processes. Circles are events (thin to start, thick to end), rounded boxes are tasks, and diamonds are gateways: an X picks one path, a plus runs all paths. Pools hold one organization and lanes split it by role.
cards.phrase: a BPMN 2.0 process inside one pool with a lane per role, a thin-circle start event, rounded tasks named verb plus noun, an exclusive gateway (diamond with X) with labeled outgoing flows, and a thick-circle end event on every path

cards.name: Data flow diagram
cards.aka: DFD, data flow, Gane-Sarson diagram, Yourdon-DeMarco diagram
cards.desc: Shows where data comes from, which processes transform it, where it is stored and where it goes. External entities are squares, processes are circles, data stores are open-ended boxes, and every arrow is named after the data it carries. It shows no timing or order.
cards.phrase: a data flow diagram with external entities as squares, numbered processes as circles, data stores as open-ended rectangles with an id, and every arrow labeled with the data it carries as a noun; no control flow, timing or decisions

cards.name: Customer journey map
cards.aka: user journey map, experience map, journey map
cards.desc: A row of stages a customer goes through, with what they do, think and feel at each one. An emotion curve runs underneath, and the low points are where the team should look first.
cards.phrase: a customer journey map with 4 to 6 stage columns left to right, rows for what the customer does and their touchpoint, and an emotion curve underneath with a dashed neutral line; mark low points as pain points with a one-line note

cards.name: Service blueprint
cards.desc: A journey map that also shows the organization behind it. Rows run from customer actions, through frontstage staff and screens, to backstage work and support systems, split by the line of interaction, the line of visibility and the line of internal interaction.
cards.phrase: a service blueprint with columns for each step left to right and rows for customer actions, frontstage, backstage and support systems, separated by labeled lines of interaction, visibility and internal interaction, with vertical arrows where a row triggers the one below

cards.name: Value stream map
cards.aka: VSM, material and information flow diagram
cards.desc: A lean diagram of every step a piece of work goes through from request to delivery, with the time each step actually takes and how long work sits waiting between steps. A timeline ladder along the bottom adds them up, and the wait usually dwarfs the work.
cards.phrase: a value stream map with process boxes left to right, a data box under each with process time, inventory triangles between steps, and a timeline ladder along the bottom showing wait time on the high steps and work time on the low steps, totaled at the end

cards.name: User story map
cards.aka: story map, story mapping, backbone and walking skeleton
cards.desc: User activities run left to right across the top as a backbone, in the order a user does them. The stories that make up each activity hang underneath, most important first, and horizontal lines slice them into releases.
cards.phrase: a user story map with user activities as a backbone across the top in journey order, user tasks under each, story cards hanging beneath in priority order, and dashed horizontal release lines labeled MVP and Release 2 that cut across every column

cards.name: Pipeline diagram
cards.aka: CI/CD pipeline, deployment pipeline, data pipeline, stage diagram
cards.desc: A row of stages that every change or every batch of data passes through in order, with the jobs inside each stage and their status. A failed job stops everything to its right.
cards.phrase: a pipeline diagram with stages as chevrons left to right, the jobs of each stage stacked beneath with a pass or fail mark, gates and manual approvals drawn as their own step, and stages after a failure shown dashed as blocked

cards.name: EventStorming board
cards.aka: event storming, big picture EventStorming, process modelling EventStorming
cards.desc: A wall of sticky notes that tells a business process as a timeline of domain events, written in the past tense on orange notes. Blue commands trigger them, pale yellow aggregates handle the commands, lilac policies react to events, and pink notes mark hot spots.
cards.phrase: an EventStorming board read left to right as a timeline: orange past-tense domain events, blue commands before the events they cause, pale yellow aggregates under each command and event pair, lilac policies that react to an event, and pink hot spots for open questions

cards.name: Mind map
cards.aka: mindmap, idea map, radial map, spider diagram
cards.desc: One central topic with branches radiating out, each branch a subtopic and each twig a detail. The layout is free and organic, and the position of a word tells you what it belongs to, so you can capture ideas as fast as people say them.
cards.phrase: a mind map with the central topic in the middle, 4 to 6 main branches radiating out as thick curved limbs in one color each, single words or short phrases on the lines, thinner twigs for details, and no more than about 30 words

cards.name: Concept map
cards.aka: concept diagram, knowledge map, semantic network
cards.desc: Concepts in boxes or ovals joined by arrows, and every arrow carries a linking phrase, so each concept, phrase and concept reads as a sentence. Cross-links between distant parts of the map show the relationships a mind map cannot.
cards.phrase: a concept map with each concept as a short noun in a rounded box, arrows labeled with a verb phrase so every link reads as a sentence from one concept to the next, a few cross-links between distant concepts, and no unlabeled arrows

cards.name: Tree diagram
cards.aka: hierarchy diagram, org chart, organizational chart, tree chart
cards.desc: A hierarchy drawn as a tree: one root at the top, each node connected to its parent by an elbow line, and siblings side by side on the same level. Org charts are the best-known kind, and the same shape works for site maps, file systems and taxonomies.
cards.phrase: a tree diagram drawn top down with the root at the top, one box per node with its name and role, siblings aligned on one level, parents joined to children by right-angle elbow connectors, and the same box size on each level

cards.name: Issue tree
cards.aka: logic tree, MECE tree, hypothesis tree, driver tree
cards.desc: A question on the left broken into its parts on the right, level by level. At each split the branches should be mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive (MECE): no overlaps and no gaps, so every possible answer falls under exactly one branch.
cards.phrase: an issue tree read left to right, with the key question at the root on the left, each level splitting into two to four branches that are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, elbow connectors, and the leaves phrased as questions or hypotheses you can test

cards.name: Fishbone diagram
cards.aka: Ishikawa diagram, cause-and-effect diagram, herringbone diagram
cards.desc: The problem sits at the head of a fish on the right, and a spine runs to it. Ribs off the spine are categories of cause, such as people, process and tools, and each rib collects the specific causes a team names for it.
cards.phrase: a fishbone diagram with the problem as the head on the right, a horizontal spine, three to six slanted ribs labeled with cause categories above and below, and short specific causes as horizontal twigs off each rib

cards.name: Affinity map
cards.aka: affinity diagram, KJ method, sticky-note clustering
cards.desc: Lots of single observations, one per sticky note, sorted into clusters by similarity, then each cluster given a name. The themes come up from the notes instead of being decided first.
cards.phrase: an affinity map with one observation per sticky note in the person's own words, notes grouped into loose clusters with a dashed boundary and a short theme name on top, three to six clusters, and a count of notes per theme

cards.name: 2×2 matrix
cards.aka: two-by-two, quadrant chart, four-box, impact effort matrix
cards.desc: Two axes, each split into low and high, make four quadrants, and items are placed by where they score on both. Each quadrant gets a name that says what to do with things that land in it.
cards.phrase: a 2×2 matrix with clearly named axes and low and high at each end, a named action for each quadrant in its corner, items placed as labeled dots, and the quadrant you want people to act on lightly shaded

cards.name: Venn diagram
cards.aka: set diagram, overlap diagram, Euler diagram (when not all overlaps exist)
cards.desc: Overlapping circles, one per set or quality, where each overlap holds what belongs to both. The center of a three-circle Venn is usually the point of the slide: the things that meet every condition.
cards.phrase: a Venn diagram with two or three translucent overlapping circles of equal size in distinct colors, each set named in its own region outside the overlaps, overlaps labeled only where they mean something, and the center region called out

cards.name: Spectrum
cards.aka: axis placement, continuum, scale, slider diagram
cards.desc: One line between two named extremes, with items placed along it. It shows that a choice is a matter of degree, and it makes people commit to where each thing sits relative to the others.
cards.phrase: a spectrum drawn as one horizontal line with the two extremes named at each end, items placed along it as labeled dots with leader lines, and a dashed arrow for any item you propose to move

cards.name: Pyramid
cards.aka: hierarchy of levels, triangle diagram, layered pyramid
cards.desc: A triangle cut into horizontal bands, where the width of each band says how much or how many, and the order says what rests on what. The bottom is the broad foundation and the top is the narrow peak.
cards.phrase: a pyramid of three to five horizontal bands, widest at the bottom, each band named inside, with the width meaning quantity and each level resting on the one below, plus one side note explaining what changes from bottom to top

cards.name: Onion diagram
cards.aka: concentric layers, concentric circles, layer diagram, stakeholder onion
cards.desc: Nested rings around a core, where each ring wraps the one inside it. It shows what is central and protected and what sits further out, and in software it usually means dependencies point inward only.
cards.phrase: an onion diagram of three to five concentric rings with the core in the center, each ring named at its top, the rings shading darker toward the core, and one arrow and note stating what moving inward means

cards.name: Cycle diagram
cards.desc: Steps arranged in a circle with arrows from each to the next and from the last back to the first. It says the process never really ends: the output of the last step feeds the first step of the next round.
cards.phrase: a cycle diagram of three to six steps evenly spaced around a circle, read clockwise from the top, each step a short verb in a box, curved arrows between neighbours with the last arrow returning to the first, and the loop's name in the center

cards.name: Iceberg diagram
cards.aka: iceberg model, systems thinking iceberg, above and below the waterline
cards.desc: A small tip above the waterline and a much larger mass below. The tip is what people see, such as events or symptoms, and the layers underneath are the patterns, structures and beliefs that produce them.
cards.phrase: an iceberg diagram with a wavy waterline, a small tip above it naming what is visible, and a larger mass below divided into two or three labeled layers getting deeper and less visible, with a note on the layer you will act on

cards.name: Wardley map
cards.desc: A map of the components behind a user need. The vertical axis is the value chain, from visible to the user at the top to invisible at the bottom, and the horizontal axis is evolution from genesis through custom-built and product to commodity. Arrows show where components are moving.
cards.phrase: a Wardley map with the user need as the anchor at the top, components as dots on a value chain going down from visible to invisible, the x axis divided into genesis, custom, product and commodity, dependency lines between components, and dashed red arrows for expected evolution

cards.name: One reading direction
cards.aka: flow direction, left to right, top to bottom, rank direction
cards.desc: The main flow runs one way across the whole diagram, usually left to right or top to bottom, so it reads like a sentence. Side branches and error paths leave the main line at right angles and never double back against it.
cards.phrase: one reading direction, left to right for the main flow; each step sits to the right of the one before it, branches and error paths drop downward, and no arrow on the main path points back to the left

cards.name: Grouping with boundaries and proximity
cards.aka: boundaries, containers, clusters, common region, swim groups
cards.desc: Things that belong together sit close together, and a labeled boundary draws the line around them: a team, a deployment unit, a network zone. The reader sees the groups before reading a single box.
cards.phrase: group related elements inside labeled dashed boundaries (team, deployment unit or network zone), keep members of a group close together with wider gaps between groups, and say in the boundary label what the grouping means

cards.name: Label every arrow
cards.aka: labeled relationships, edge labels, connector labels
cards.desc: Every line says what moves along it or what the relationship is, as a short verb or protocol: "reads via SQL", "publishes OrderPlaced", "HTTPS/JSON". The reader never has to guess why two boxes are connected.
cards.phrase: label every arrow with a short verb phrase or protocol saying what travels along it (for example "HTTPS/JSON", "reads via SQL", "publishes OrderPlaced"); the arrowhead points in the direction the request or data moves

cards.name: Legend and key
cards.desc: A small box in a corner that explains every shape, color and line style that carries meaning. With a key, the diagram stands on its own when someone screenshots it into a slide or a chat.
