cards.phrase: add a small legend in the bottom-right corner that explains every color, line style and shape used (for example blue = our services, dashed box = external, dashed line = async event), with no more than five entries

cards.name: Color that means something
cards.aka: semantic color, color encoding, status colors
cards.desc: Color encodes one thing, such as status, owner or new versus existing, and everything else stays neutral. Two or three colors with a stated meaning do more than a full palette.
cards.phrase: use color for one meaning only and say it in the legend (for example green = healthy, amber = degraded, red = down); everything else stays neutral gray, use at most three colors, and repeat the meaning with a label or icon

cards.name: Highlight one path, gray the rest
cards.aka: focus and context, emphasis, de-emphasis, spotlight
cards.desc: The part of the diagram the explanation is about is drawn in strong color and heavier lines, and everything around it is faded to light gray. The context stays visible so the reader knows where they are, but the eye goes straight to the path.
cards.phrase: draw the whole system in light gray, then highlight only the path being explained in one strong color with thicker lines, so the context is visible but the eye lands on that path first

cards.name: Align to a grid
cards.aka: snap to grid, alignment, consistent spacing, orthogonal layout
cards.desc: Boxes sit on shared rows and columns with equal gaps, matching sizes for things of the same kind, and connectors run straight or at right angles. An aligned diagram looks deliberate, and misalignment becomes a signal you can use.
cards.phrase: place every box on a shared grid of rows and columns with equal spacing, use the same width and height for elements of the same kind, and route connectors straight or with right-angle bends only

cards.name: Numbered steps
cards.aka: numbered flow, step markers, sequence numbers
cards.desc: Small numbered markers on the arrows or boxes give the order of events, and a short key or caption explains each number. The picture shows where things happen and the numbers show when.
cards.phrase: mark each step with a filled numbered circle (1, 2, 3...) placed on the arrow where it happens, in the order events occur, with a short numbered key under the diagram explaining each step in a few words

cards.name: Progressive build-up
cards.aka: build, reveal, step-by-step diagram, animation frames
cards.desc: The same diagram shown several times, each version adding one new element in a highlight color while earlier parts turn gray. It works on slides, in docs as a short series, and in talks where you click through.
cards.phrase: show the diagram as a sequence of frames, each adding exactly one new element or arrow in the highlight color while earlier elements turn gray; every element keeps the same position in every frame

cards.name: Zoom levels
cards.aka: views at different altitudes, levels of detail, drill-down, overview then detail
cards.desc: A set of diagrams at different altitudes, where one box in the high-level view is opened up into its own diagram at the next level. Each view keeps one level of abstraction and points to the one above and below.
cards.phrase: split the explanation into views at different zoom levels: a high-level view with the system as one box, then a view that opens that box to show its parts inside a matching labeled boundary; keep one level of abstraction per view and the same names across views

cards.name: Callouts and annotations
cards.aka: annotations, margin notes, leader lines, marginalia
cards.desc: Short notes placed right next to the part of the diagram they explain, joined to it by a leader line or arrow. They carry the why ("cold after every deploy", "900 ms here") that a box and arrow cannot say on their own.
cards.phrase: add at most three short callouts, each placed beside the element it explains and joined to it with a thin leader line, written in a contrasting color and a handwritten or italic style so they read as commentary on top of the diagram

cards.name: Small multiples and before/after
cards.aka: side by side, comparison panels, before and after, trellis
cards.desc: The same diagram drawn two or more times at the same scale and layout, each panel showing one state, time or option. Because everything else is identical, the eye finds the difference instantly.
cards.phrase: draw two panels side by side, labeled before and after, at the same scale with every unchanged element in exactly the same position; draw what changed in a highlight color and keep everything else neutral

cards.name: Exploded view
cards.aka: cutaway, layer view, pulled-apart stack, isometric layers
cards.desc: The parts of a stack or assembly are pulled apart along one axis, with dashed guide lines showing where they fit back together and labels beside each layer. A cutaway does the same by removing the outer layer to show what is inside.
cards.phrase: an exploded view: the layers drawn as flat stacked plates pulled apart along one vertical axis, in their real order, with dashed guide lines joining their corners and a label with a leader line beside each layer

cards.name: Analogy diagram
cards.aka: metaphor diagram, mapping diagram, like-a picture
cards.desc: A familiar thing (a post office, a restaurant kitchen, a library) drawn next to the technical system, with each part mapped to its counterpart. The reader borrows a model they already have and then sees where it stops holding.
cards.phrase: an analogy diagram: a top row with a familiar real-world scene and a bottom row with the technical system in the same layout, each pair joined by a dashed vertical line, plus a one-line note on where the analogy breaks

cards.name: Explorable explanation
cards.aka: interactive diagram, reactive document, live figure
cards.desc: A diagram on a web page with controls the reader can drag or toggle, such as a slider for load or a switch for a failure, and the picture updates as they do. The reader builds intuition by trying values instead of reading about them.
cards.phrase: an interactive explanation: one diagram or chart with a single labeled control (slider or toggle) that changes one input, the picture and a numeric readout update live as it moves, and a sensible default value plus a static fallback image

cards.name: Spaghetti diagram
cards.desc: Every box is connected to many others with crossing lines, so no path can be followed and no structure is visible. It usually comes from drawing every dependency that exists instead of the ones that answer the question.
cards.phrase: Avoid a spaghetti diagram where every element connects to many others with crossing lines, so no single path can be followed from start to end and no grouping is visible

cards.name: Unlabeled arrows
cards.desc: Lines join boxes with no label, so the reader has to guess whether each one is a call, a dependency, a data flow or a deployment. Different readers guess differently and walk away with different pictures.
cards.phrase: Avoid arrows without labels, where a reader has to guess whether each line means calls, depends on, sends data to or deploys to, and which way it points

cards.name: Mixed levels of abstraction
cards.aka: mixed altitude, zoom-level soup, apples and screws
cards.desc: One diagram puts a whole business system, a Java class, an EC2 instance and a database table side by side as if they were peers. The reader cannot tell what is inside what or which level the diagram is about.
cards.phrase: Avoid mixed levels of abstraction, with whole systems, code classes, servers and database tables drawn side by side as peers in one view, so nobody can tell what sits inside what

cards.name: Rainbow colors with no meaning
cards.aka: decorative color, color for its own sake
cards.desc: Every box gets a different color because the tool offers them, so color carries no information but readers still look for a pattern in it. Important elements no longer stand out because everything does.
cards.phrase: Avoid rainbow colors with no meaning, where every box gets a different color and there is no legend saying what the colors stand for, so readers hunt for a pattern that is not there

cards.name: Wall of text in boxes
cards.aka: paragraphs in shapes, documentation in a box
cards.desc: Boxes stuffed with sentences or bullet lists describing what each component does, shrunk to a tiny font to fit. The shapes and arrows disappear behind the text, and the diagram becomes a hard-to-read document.
cards.phrase: Avoid a wall of text in boxes, with sentences or bullet lists crammed into shapes in a tiny font so the structure disappears behind the words

cards.name: Icon soup
cards.aka: logo salad, clip-art architecture, icon-only diagram
cards.desc: A diagram made mostly of product icons and logos with few or no text labels. Readers have to recognize dozens of tiny symbols, three different cylinders look alike, and nobody can tell which box is your service.
cards.phrase: Avoid icon soup: product icons and logos with no text labels, so readers have to recognize small symbols to know what each element is or which one is your own service

cards.name: Arrows that mean different things
cards.aka: overloaded arrows, inconsistent notation, one line many meanings
cards.desc: The same solid arrow is used for a runtime call, a build dependency, a data flow and a deployment, sometimes pointing the way data moves and sometimes the way control goes. Even with labels, the reader has to reread each line to know what kind of thing it is.
cards.phrase: Avoid arrows that mean different things, where the same line style is used for calls, dependencies, data flows and deployments, and arrow direction is not consistent

cards.name: Stale diagram that drifted from reality
cards.aka: outdated diagram, diagram rot, the wiki picture
cards.desc: A diagram that was right when drawn and has not been touched since: it shows a database that was retired and misses the service everyone now depends on. Readers trust it, so it misleads more than having no diagram at all.
cards.phrase: Avoid a stale diagram with no date, owner or source file, that still shows retired components and misses ones added since it was drawn, so readers trust a picture of a system that no longer exists

cards.name: Decorative 3D, shadows and gradients
cards.aka: chartjunk, isometric for looks, glossy boxes
cards.desc: Boxes extruded into 3D blocks, drop shadows, gradients and bevels that carry no information. The depth suggests layering or size that is not there, labels get squeezed onto slanted faces, and it prints and themes badly.
cards.phrase: Avoid decorative 3D, drop shadows, gradients and bevels on boxes and arrows that add no information, suggest depth or layering that is not there and print badly

cards.name: Mermaid
cards.desc: A Markdown-like text syntax for flowcharts, sequence, state, class, ER and Gantt diagrams, rendered in the browser by a JavaScript library. GitHub, GitLab, Notion, Obsidian and most docs site generators render a ```mermaid fence directly, so the diagram lives in the README.
cards.phrase: Mermaid source in a ```mermaid fenced block (GitHub renders it inline), using the right diagram keyword (flowchart LR, sequenceDiagram, stateDiagram-v2, erDiagram); short node ids, labels in double quotes whenever they contain spaces, parentheses or colons, and no HTML or custom CSS in labels

cards.name: PlantUML
cards.desc: A long-established text language for UML and related diagrams (sequence, component, class, activity, state, deployment) between @startuml and @enduml. It renders through a Java tool or a PlantUML server, and the C4-PlantUML library adds C4 shapes.
cards.phrase: PlantUML between @startuml and @enduml; declare every actor, component and database with an alias before using it, write arrows as a --> b : label, set left to right direction for flows, and use the C4-PlantUML include for architecture views

cards.name: D2
cards.desc: A modern text language for diagrams from Terrastruct: nodes and containers as nested blocks, connections as a -> b: label, and shapes like cylinder, person and queue. A single CLI renders SVG or PNG with a choice of layout engines.
cards.phrase: D2 source with direction: right, boundaries as nested container blocks, shape: cylinder for datastores, every connection written as a -> b: label, and short keys with readable labels; reference nested nodes by their full path like cloud.api

cards.name: Graphviz DOT
cards.desc: The original graph description language: you list nodes and edges, and a layout engine (dot, neato, fdp) decides where everything goes. Many tools emit DOT, so it is often the output format for generated diagrams.
cards.phrase: Graphviz DOT as a digraph with rankdir=LR, node defaults set once (shape=box, style=rounded), shape=cylinder for datastores, a label on every edge, and subgraph cluster_ blocks with a label for each boundary

cards.name: Structurizr DSL
cards.desc: A text language for the C4 model by Simon Brown: you describe the model once (people, systems, containers and their relationships) and then define views at each zoom level. Every view is drawn from the same model, so names and relationships stay consistent.
cards.phrase: Structurizr DSL: one workspace with a model of people, software systems and containers (each with a technology string) and a description on every relationship, then systemContext and container views using include * and autolayout lr

cards.name: Excalidraw
cards.desc: An open-source virtual whiteboard that draws everything with a rough, hand-drawn line and a handwritten font. Files are JSON, and exported PNG and SVG can embed the scene so the image opens again for editing.
cards.phrase: an Excalidraw-style sketch: rough hand-drawn boxes and arrows, a handwritten font, a dozen elements at most with short labels, one accent color for the important part; if a file is wanted, valid .excalidraw JSON with rectangle, text and arrow elements bound to each other

cards.name: ASCII and box-drawing diagrams
cards.aka: ASCII art, text diagrams, Unicode box drawing, comment diagrams
cards.desc: A diagram typed as plain text with box-drawing characters or plain ASCII, living in a code comment, a commit message or a plain-text README. It shows up wherever the code is read: the editor, the terminal, a diff.
cards.phrase: a plain-text diagram for a code comment using Unicode box-drawing characters (┌ ─ ┐ │ └ ┘ ┬) with ▶ and ▼ for arrowheads, aligned for a monospace font, under 80 columns wide, with short protocol labels beside the lines

cards.name: draw.io
cards.desc: A free canvas editor with a big shape library (cloud icons, UML, network, BPMN) where you place and connect everything by hand. Files are mxGraph XML, and a .drawio.svg or .drawio.png is both the picture and the editable source.
cards.phrase: a draw.io diagram as uncompressed mxGraph XML (mxfile, diagram, mxGraphModel, root), each shape an mxCell with vertex="1", a style and mxGeometry, each arrow an mxCell with edge="1" and source and target ids, and labels in the value attribute

cards.name: Diagram source in the repo
cards.aka: docs as code, diagrams as code, versioned diagrams
cards.desc: The diagram's text source sits in the same repository as the code it describes, next to the docs that use it, and CI renders it to SVG. Changing the system and changing its picture happen in the same pull request.
cards.phrase: keep the diagram source as a text file in the repo next to the docs that use it (for example docs/diagrams/checkout.mmd), render it to SVG in CI, and never commit an exported image without its source

cards.name: Alt text and a text description
cards.aka: accessible diagrams, long description, accTitle and accDescr
cards.desc: Every diagram image gets alt text that says in a sentence or two what it shows, and complex diagrams also get a longer text description nearby listing the parts and how they connect. Screen reader users, search and anyone whose image fails to load get the same information.
cards.phrase: give each diagram alt text of one or two sentences stating what it shows and its main relationship, plus a longer text description listing the elements and connections for complex diagrams (in Mermaid, use accTitle and accDescr)

cards.name: Works in dark mode, print and grayscale
cards.desc: The diagram stays readable on a dark background, on a black and white printout and for color blind readers. Meaning is carried by labels, line styles and shapes as well as color, and the background is transparent or follows the theme.
cards.phrase: make it readable in light mode, dark mode and grayscale print: no hard-coded white background, text and lines with enough contrast on both, and every color difference repeated with a label, line style or shape

cards.name: Title, caption and date
cards.aka: figure caption, diagram metadata, as-of date
cards.desc: A title that states the question the diagram answers, and a caption with its scope, the date or version it reflects and where its source lives. A reader can tell at a glance whether it is the right diagram and whether it is current.
cards.phrase: give the diagram a title phrased as the question it answers (for example "How a checkout gets paid") and a one-line caption with its scope, the date or version it reflects and the path to its source file

cards.name: Generated from code or infrastructure
cards.aka: auto-generated diagrams, living diagrams, reverse-engineered diagrams
cards.desc: A tool draws the diagram from the real thing: Terraform state, Kubernetes manifests, the import graph of the codebase or the database schema. It cannot drift, because it is regenerated on every build.
cards.phrase: generate the diagram from the source of truth (Terraform, Kubernetes manifests, the import graph or the database schema) in CI, filtered to the elements that answer the question, and flag the pull request when the committed diagram is out of date

cards.name: Review diagram changes in pull requests
cards.aka: diagram review, rendered diffs, visual diff
cards.desc: Diagram changes go through the same pull request review as code, with the rendered before and after in front of the reviewer. A text format makes the diff readable, and a rendered preview lets people comment on the picture itself.
cards.phrase: treat diagram changes like code: update the diagram source in the same pull request as the change it reflects, include a rendered before-and-after image in the PR description, and give the diagrams a code owner

cards.name: Monolith
cards.desc: The whole application is one codebase, one build and one process: UI, business logic and data access ship together and share one database. You scale it by running more identical copies behind a load balancer.
cards.phrase: a single deployable monolith with one database, run as several stateless copies behind a load balancer; keep sessions and files out of local memory and disk so any copy can serve any request

cards.name: Modular monolith
cards.desc: One deployable split inside into modules along business lines. Each module owns its tables and exposes a small public interface; other modules may only call that interface. You keep one build, one deploy and real transactions, with boundaries you can later cut along.
cards.phrase: a modular monolith: one deployable split into modules by business capability, each owning its own schema and exposing a small public interface; no cross-module table access or imports of internals, enforced by an architecture test in CI

cards.name: Microservices
cards.desc: The system is split into small services, each owned by one team, deployed on its own and owning its own data. Services talk over the network through APIs or events, and no service reads another's database.
cards.phrase: microservices split by business capability, one team per service, each with its own datastore and CI/CD pipeline; synchronous calls only at the edge, events between services, and no shared database or shared domain library

cards.name: Service-oriented architecture
cards.aka: SOA, ESB architecture, enterprise service bus
cards.desc: Large enterprise services (CRM, ERP, billing) plug into a central enterprise service bus. The bus routes messages, transforms formats and often runs orchestration logic, usually over SOAP/WSDL contracts.
cards.phrase: a service-oriented integration layer where systems talk through a central bus with canonical message formats; keep the bus to routing and format translation and keep business rules in the services

cards.name: Serverless functions
cards.aka: FaaS, functions as a service, Lambda architecture (informal)
cards.desc: Code runs as short-lived functions that the cloud starts in response to events: an HTTP request, a queue message, a file upload or a schedule. The platform scales each function from zero to many instances and you pay per invocation.
cards.phrase: serverless functions triggered by HTTP, queue and schedule events, one function per use case, stateless with state in a managed database; set timeouts and concurrency limits per function and send failed events to a dead-letter queue

cards.name: Right-sized services
cards.desc: A handful of larger services, each matching one team and one big business area, instead of dozens of tiny ones. Inside, each service is a modular monolith. You split again only where a part has a clear need of its own.
cards.phrase: a small number of right-sized services (3 to 6), one per team and business area, each a modular monolith inside with its own database; split further only for a measured scaling, security or release-cadence need

cards.name: Cell-based architecture
cards.aka: cellular architecture, bulkheaded cells, shuffle sharding (related)
cards.desc: The whole stack is deployed many times as independent cells, each serving a slice of customers with its own app servers and database. A thin router sends each tenant to its cell, so a bad deploy or overload hurts one cell and not everyone.
cards.phrase: a cell-based architecture: identical full-stack cells (app, cache, database) each serving a fixed set of tenants, a thin stateless router mapping tenant to cell, deploys rolled out cell by cell, and no calls between cells

cards.name: Space-based architecture
cards.aka: tuple space, in-memory data grid architecture
cards.desc: Processing units each hold the hot data in a replicated in-memory grid, so requests never wait on the database. Changes replicate between units, and a data pump writes them to the database asynchronously in the background.
cards.phrase: space-based processing: stateless processing units that read and write a replicated in-memory data grid, with an asynchronous data pump persisting changes to the database and a reader that reloads the grid on cold start

cards.name: Client-server and n-tier
cards.desc: The system is split into physical tiers: a presentation tier (browser or desktop client), an application tier holding the business logic, and a data tier. Each tier only talks to the one next to it, and each can be scaled and secured separately.
cards.phrase: a 3-tier layout: a thin client, a stateless application tier that holds all business rules, and a database reachable only from the application tier, each tier in its own network zone

cards.name: Peer-to-peer
cards.desc: Every node is both client and server. Peers find each other through a distributed hash table or a tracker, then exchange data directly, so capacity grows as more peers join and there is no central server to fail.
cards.phrase: a peer-to-peer design where each node runs the same code, discovers peers through a Kademlia-style DHT with bootstrap nodes, exchanges content-addressed chunks directly and verifies every chunk by hash

cards.name: Micro-frontends
cards.desc: The web UI is split into pieces that different teams build and deploy on their own, then composed in the browser or at the server by a thin shell. Each piece usually pairs with its own team's backend.
cards.phrase: micro-frontends composed by a thin app shell that owns routing, auth and the design system; each team ships its fragment and its backend independently, fragments talk only through URL and custom DOM events, and shared libraries are pinned as singletons

cards.name: Self-contained systems
cards.desc: Each system is a full vertical: its own web UI, logic and database, owned by one team. Systems integrate mainly through links and UI includes in the browser, and replicate data between them asynchronously, so one can be down while the others keep working.
cards.phrase: self-contained systems: each business area is a separate web app with its own UI, logic and database, integrated through hyperlinks and server-side includes, sharing data only through async feeds, never by synchronous calls on the request path

cards.name: Local-first
cards.desc: Each device keeps a full local copy of the user's data and the app reads and writes it directly, so it is instant and works offline. A sync layer exchanges changes in the background, and CRDTs or server reconciliation merge concurrent edits without conflicts.
cards.phrase: local-first: the UI reads and writes a local SQLite/IndexedDB store, mutations are queued and synced in the background through a sync server, and concurrent edits merge with CRDTs (Yjs or Automerge) so the app works fully offline

cards.name: Edge-first
cards.aka: edge computing, compute at the CDN edge
cards.desc: Request handling runs in many small points of presence close to users, on the CDN itself. Reads come from edge caches or replicated key-value stores, and only writes or misses travel back to a central origin database.
cards.phrase: an edge-first setup: request handlers run on edge workers near users, serving reads from edge KV or cache with short TTLs, and forwarding writes to a single-region origin database with read-your-writes handled by a session token

cards.name: Layered architecture
cards.desc: Code is stacked in horizontal layers: presentation (controllers), business logic (services) and data access (repositories). Each layer calls only the layer directly below it.
cards.phrase: a strict layered structure (controller, service, repository): controllers only parse and validate input, services hold the business rules and transactions, repositories hold all queries, and no layer skips the one below it

cards.name: Hexagonal architecture
cards.desc: The application core defines ports: interfaces for what it offers (driving side) and what it needs (driven side). Adapters on the outside plug into those ports: HTTP and CLI call in, while database and payment adapters implement the outgoing ports.
cards.phrase: hexagonal (ports and adapters): the core defines inbound use-case ports and outbound ports such as OrderRepository and PaymentGateway; HTTP, CLI and tests are driving adapters, Postgres and Stripe are driven adapters, and the core imports no framework or SDK

cards.name: Clean architecture
cards.aka: Uncle Bob clean architecture, the dependency rule
cards.desc: Code sits in concentric rings: entities in the center, then use cases, then interface adapters (controllers, presenters, gateways), then frameworks and drivers on the outside. Source dependencies only point inward; outer rings implement interfaces that inner rings declare.
cards.phrase: clean architecture with four rings (entities, use cases, interface adapters, frameworks); dependencies point only inward, each use case is one class with an input and output DTO, and frameworks and the ORM live only in the outer ring

cards.name: Onion architecture
cards.desc: Layers wrap the domain model like an onion: domain model, then domain services, then application services, with UI, infrastructure and tests on the outside. Inner layers declare interfaces such as repositories, and the infrastructure layer implements them.
cards.phrase: onion architecture: the domain model in the center with no dependencies, repository interfaces declared in the domain services layer, application services orchestrating use cases, and infrastructure implementing those interfaces from the outer ring via dependency injection

cards.name: Vertical slice architecture
cards.desc: Code is organized around requests or features instead of technical layers. Each slice holds everything one use case needs, from endpoint to query, and slices share as little as possible, so each one can choose the simplest approach that fits.
cards.phrase: vertical slices: one folder per use case (e.g. PlaceOrder/) holding its endpoint, request/response types, handler, validation and data access; slices never call each other, and shared code moves into the domain only after the second real use

cards.name: Package by feature
cards.aka: package by component, screaming architecture (vs package by layer)
cards.desc: Top-level folders are named after business features (orders, users, billing) and each holds its own controller, service and data code. In package by layer, the top folders are controllers/, services/ and repos/ and one feature is scattered across all of them.
cards.phrase: package by feature: top-level folders per business feature (orders/, billing/), each holding its own routes, service and data access, with one index file as the public API; other features import only from that index

cards.name: Bounded contexts
cards.desc: A large domain is split into bounded contexts, each with its own model and language, and owned by one team. The same word (Customer) means different things in Sales and Billing. A context map names how contexts relate: upstream/downstream, anti-corruption layer, open host service, shared kernel.
cards.phrase: split the domain into bounded contexts, each with its own model and ubiquitous language and one owning team; draw a context map and put an anti-corruption layer wherever a context consumes another context's or a legacy system's model

cards.name: Aggregates, entities and value objects
cards.desc: An aggregate is a cluster of objects changed together under one root that enforces the invariants. Entities have identity, value objects are immutable and compared by value (Money, Email). Outside code holds only the root, saves one aggregate per transaction, and refers to other aggregates by id.
cards.phrase: rich aggregates: each aggregate root guards its invariants in methods (no public setters), uses immutable value objects for money, quantities and ids, references other aggregates by id only, is saved one per transaction and records domain events

cards.name: Functional core, imperative shell
cards.desc: Decisions live in pure functions that take plain data and return plain data or a list of actions, with no I/O and no clock. A thin shell around them loads data, calls the core, then performs the resulting writes, emails and calls.
cards.phrase: functional core, imperative shell: business decisions as pure functions over plain data that return a list of effects; a thin shell loads inputs, calls the core and executes the effects, and only the shell touches the database, network or clock

cards.name: Microkernel
cards.desc: A small host core provides the lifecycle, a registry and a stable extension API. Features ship as plugins that register against named extension points, and the core discovers and loads them at startup or at runtime.
cards.phrase: a microkernel: a minimal core with a plugin registry and versioned extension points (typed hooks), plugins declared by manifest and loaded in isolation, so a failing plugin is disabled without taking down the host

cards.name: Pipes and filters
cards.desc: Processing is a chain of independent filters, each taking a stream of records in and putting a stream out, joined by pipes. Filters do one thing, know nothing about their neighbours, and can be reordered, reused or run in parallel.
cards.phrase: a pipes-and-filters pipeline of small single-purpose stages with one shared record type, connected by bounded queues or streams with backpressure; each stage is pure where possible and testable on its own

cards.name: MVC
cards.desc: The controller takes user input and updates the model. The model holds data and rules, and the view renders the model for the user. On the server (Rails, Django) the controller also picks which view to render per request.
cards.phrase: MVC with thin controllers that only map requests to model calls and pick a view, models that hold the business rules, and views with no logic beyond formatting

cards.name: MVVM
cards.desc: The view model exposes observable state and commands shaped for one screen. The view binds to it declaratively and re-renders on change, and the view model calls into the model and services. The view model has no reference to the view, so it is testable without UI.
cards.phrase: MVVM: one view model per screen exposing immutable observable UI state and command methods, no references to view or platform types, and all data access through injected repositories so the view model is unit-tested without UI

cards.name: Unidirectional data flow
cards.aka: Elm architecture, TEA, Redux, Flux, MVI
cards.desc: State lives in one store. The view renders from state and can only dispatch messages; a pure update function takes the old state and a message and returns new state, plus effects to run. Data moves in one loop, so every change is traceable.
cards.phrase: unidirectional data flow: a single immutable state tree, views that only render state and dispatch typed actions, a pure reducer (state, action) => state, and side effects isolated in middleware or effect handlers

cards.name: Actor model
cards.desc: An actor is a unit of private state with a mailbox. It processes one message at a time, so it needs no locks, and talks to other actors only by sending messages. Supervisors watch child actors and restart them when they crash.
cards.phrase: the actor model: one actor per entity (e.g. per device or chat room) owning its state, processing its mailbox one message at a time, communicating only by async messages, under supervisors that restart crashed children (let it crash)

cards.name: Entity component system
cards.desc: Entities are just ids. Components are plain data (Position, Velocity, Health) stored in tight arrays per type. Systems are functions that run every tick over all entities that have a given set of components.
cards.phrase: an entity component system: entities as plain ids, components as plain data in contiguous arrays per type, and systems as functions that query for a set of components and run in a fixed order each tick

cards.name: Message queue
cards.desc: A producer puts a message on a queue and exactly one consumer takes it. The broker keeps the message until the consumer acks it, then deletes it. If the consumer dies before acking, the message becomes visible again after a timeout.
cards.phrase: a point-to-point message queue between the producer and the worker: each message is handled by one consumer, acked only after the work commits, with a visibility timeout longer than the slowest expected handler

cards.name: Publish/subscribe
cards.desc: A publisher sends a message to a topic and every subscriber gets its own copy. Each subscription usually has its own queue, so a slow or broken subscriber does not hold up the others. The publisher does not know who is listening.
cards.phrase: publish/subscribe for order events: one topic per event type, one durable queue per subscribing service, so each subscriber gets its own copy and fails or lags independently

cards.name: Event streaming log
cards.aka: Kafka-style log, append-only log, event stream
cards.desc: Messages are appended to a partitioned log and kept for a retention period instead of being deleted on read. Each record has an offset in its partition. Each consumer group tracks its own committed offset, so many groups read the same data at their own pace and can rewind to replay.
cards.phrase: a Kafka-style partitioned log for domain events, 7-day retention, consumer groups that commit offsets only after processing, and the ability to reset a group's offset to replay

cards.name: Competing consumers
cards.desc: Several identical consumers read from the same queue, and each message goes to whichever one is free. You add consumers to raise throughput and lose nothing when one dies, because its unacked messages go back to the others.
cards.phrase: competing consumers on the jobs queue: N stateless workers pulling with a prefetch of 10, autoscaled on queue depth and oldest-message age, with handlers that tolerate parallel and duplicate delivery

cards.name: Partition keys and ordering
cards.aka: message key, ordering key, message group
cards.desc: The producer gives each message a key, and the broker hashes the key to pick a partition. All messages with the same key land in the same partition and are read in order by one consumer. Different keys run in parallel with no ordering between them.
cards.phrase: partition events by entity id (order_id as the message key) so all events for one order are processed in order by one consumer, with no ordering assumed across different orders

cards.name: Delivery guarantees
cards.desc: Where you ack decides what a crash does. Ack before the work and a crash loses the message (at-most-once). Ack after and a crash redelivers it (at-least-once). Effectively-once is at-least-once plus a consumer that ignores duplicates; end-to-end exactly-once across systems does not exist.
cards.phrase: at-least-once delivery everywhere (ack only after the handler's transaction commits) plus deduplication by message id in the consumer, giving effectively-once processing

cards.name: Idempotent consumer
cards.desc: A consumer written so that handling the same message twice leaves the same result as handling it once. You get there with conditional updates, upserts, natural keys, or by passing the message id as an idempotency key to anything downstream that has side effects.
cards.phrase: idempotent message handlers: state changes as conditional updates or upserts keyed on business ids, and the message id passed as the idempotency key to every external call with side effects

cards.name: Dead letter queue
cards.aka: DLQ, dead letter channel, parking lot
cards.desc: After a message fails a set number of times, the broker or consumer moves it to a separate queue instead of retrying forever. Someone gets alerted, inspects it, fixes the cause and redrives it back to the main queue.
cards.phrase: a dead letter queue per consumer queue: after 5 failed attempts with backoff the message moves to the DLQ with the error attached, an alert fires when DLQ depth is above 0, and there is a one-command redrive

cards.name: Poison message handling
cards.desc: A poison message is one that will never succeed, such as bad JSON or a reference to a deleted record. Retrying it forever crash-loops the consumer and, on an ordered log, blocks everything behind it. Detect it (parse errors, delivery count) and park it right away with the reason.
cards.phrase: poison message handling: schema or parse failures are parked to the DLQ immediately with the error and raw payload, other failures after a max delivery count of 5, so one bad message never blocks the partition

cards.name: Backpressure
cards.desc: When the consumer is slower than the producer, something has to give. Backpressure means the slow side pushes back: a bounded buffer that blocks or rejects when full, a 429 to callers, or pull-based consumption where the consumer asks only for what it can handle.
cards.phrase: explicit backpressure: bounded in-memory queues (max 1,000 items) that block producers when full, pull-based consumers with a fixed prefetch, and HTTP 429 with Retry-After at the edge when the backlog is over its limit

cards.name: Request-reply over messaging
cards.aka: async RPC, correlation identifier, return address
cards.desc: The requester sends a message with a correlation id and a replyTo address, then listens on its own reply queue. The responder does the work and sends the result to replyTo with the same correlation id, so the requester can match the reply to the pending request.
cards.phrase: request-reply over the broker: each request carries a correlation id and a replyTo queue, the requester keeps a map of pending ids with a 5 s timeout, and replies with unknown or expired ids are logged and dropped

cards.name: Background job queue
cards.aka: task queue, job runner, worker queue
cards.desc: The web request writes a job (name plus arguments) to a queue and returns right away. Separate worker processes pick jobs up, run them, and retry with backoff on failure. Most libraries add priorities, rate limits, uniqueness and a dashboard.
cards.phrase: a background job queue (BullMQ on Redis) for slow work: the request enqueues a job with ids only, never full objects, and returns 202; workers retry 5 times with exponential backoff, and every job is safe to run twice

cards.name: Scheduled and delayed jobs
cards.desc: Delayed jobs run once at a future time; scheduled jobs run on a cron pattern. Doing this through the job system (not a cron entry on one box) gives you retries, one run per tick across many workers, and visibility. Give each delayed job a deterministic id so it can be cancelled or replaced.
cards.phrase: scheduled and delayed work through the job queue: delayed jobs with a deterministic job id so they can be cancelled, cron schedules in UTC that run once per tick across all workers, and a stated policy for missed runs

cards.name: Event-driven architecture
cards.desc: Services react to events instead of calling each other. In the broker topology each service listens for events and publishes its own, with no one in charge. In the mediator topology a central component receives the event and directs the steps in order.
cards.phrase: event-driven integration between services using the broker topology for simple fan-out reactions and a mediator (orchestrator) only where a process has ordered steps and error handling

cards.name: Event notification
cards.desc: The event says only that something happened and carries an id. A consumer that needs details calls back to the source to fetch them. Events stay small and the source stays the only owner of the data.
cards.phrase: thin event notifications: events carry the event type, entity id, version and timestamp only, and consumers fetch current state from the owning service's API when they need it

cards.name: Event-carried state transfer
cards.desc: The event carries the full new state of the entity, or at least everything consumers need. Consumers keep their own local copy up to date and never call back. They keep working when the source is down.
cards.phrase: event-carried state transfer for customer data: CustomerUpdated events carry the full current customer snapshot, published to a compacted topic keyed by customer id, and each consumer keeps its own read-only copy

cards.name: Domain events vs integration events
cards.aka: internal events, public events, published language
cards.desc: Domain events are raised inside one bounded context, in-process, in the model's own language, and can change freely. Integration events are the small, versioned, public contract another context subscribes to. A translator maps from the first to the second, often through the outbox.
cards.phrase: separate domain events (in-process, internal to the module, free to change) from integration events (versioned public contracts with a documented schema); only integration events leave the bounded context, via the outbox

cards.name: Event sourcing
cards.desc: You store the sequence of events that happened to an entity instead of its current state. Current state is a fold over the events, often sped up by snapshots. You get a full audit trail and can rebuild any view, and writes use optimistic concurrency on the stream version.
cards.phrase: event sourcing for the Account aggregate only: an append-only event stream per account with optimistic concurrency on the expected version, state rebuilt by folding events, snapshots every 100 events, and read models built by projections

cards.name: CQRS
cards.desc: Writes and reads go through separate models. Commands validate and change state in a write model shaped for consistency. Queries read from read models shaped for each screen, updated from the write side's events, often in a different store.
cards.phrase: CQRS for the orders area: commands go through the domain model to the write database, queries read denormalized read models updated from events, and the UI handles read-your-own-writes by returning the new version from commands

cards.name: Projections and read models
cards.desc: A projection subscribes to events and builds a table shaped for one query. It saves its position in the stream in the same transaction as its writes, so it resumes exactly where it stopped. Because it is derived, you can drop it and rebuild it from the start.
cards.phrase: projections that build one read table per query from the event stream, store their checkpoint in the same transaction as the read-model write, are idempotent per event, and can be rebuilt from position 0 into a new table then swapped

cards.name: Saga (choreography)
cards.desc: A multi-step business process across services where each service listens for the previous step's event, does its local transaction and publishes the next event. No one coordinates. On failure, services listen for failure events and run their own compensations.
cards.phrase: a choreographed saga for checkout: each service reacts to the previous event, commits locally, and emits the next event or a failure event that triggers compensation upstream; a correlation id on every event and a dashboard of in-flight sagas

cards.name: Saga (orchestration)
cards.desc: A saga orchestrator holds the process state and sends commands to each service in turn, waiting for each reply. On failure it decides which compensations to run. The process is explicit, in one place, and persisted so it survives restarts.
cards.phrase: an orchestrated saga for checkout: a persisted orchestrator that sends reserve, charge and ship commands one at a time, waits for replies with per-step timeouts, and runs compensations in reverse order on failure

cards.name: Compensating transactions
cards.desc: Across services you cannot roll back, so each step that changes state has an undo action that runs if a later step fails. Compensations run in reverse order and are business actions (refund, release, cancel), and they must be idempotent and retried until they succeed.
cards.phrase: a compensating action for every state-changing saga step (release stock, refund payment, cancel booking), run in reverse order on failure, idempotent and retried until success, with irreversible steps such as notifications placed last

cards.name: Durable execution
cards.aka: workflow engine, durable functions, workflows as code
cards.desc: You write a long-running process as ordinary code, and the engine records the result of each step. If the worker crashes, another one replays the code from the recorded history and continues where it left off. Sleeps of days, retries and timeouts are built in.
cards.phrase: durable execution (Temporal) for the onboarding flow: deterministic workflow code that calls activities for all I/O, each activity with a timeout and retry policy, durable timers for waits, and workflow versioning for changes to running instances

cards.name: Transactional outbox
cards.desc: Instead of writing to the database and publishing to the broker (two writes that can half-fail), the service writes the event to an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change. A relay reads the outbox, by polling or from the WAL, and publishes to the broker.
cards.phrase: a transactional outbox: the event row is inserted in the same database transaction as the state change, and a relay publishes outbox rows in order (polling every 500 ms or via Debezium) and marks them sent, at-least-once

cards.name: Inbox pattern
cards.desc: The consumer records each message id in an inbox table with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as its business change. A redelivered message hits the constraint, so the consumer skips it and acks. This turns at-least-once delivery into effectively-once processing.
cards.phrase: an inbox table (message_id primary key, received_at) written in the same transaction as the handler's changes; a unique violation means a duplicate, so skip and ack; prune rows older than 14 days

cards.name: Change data capture
cards.desc: A connector reads the database's replication log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog) and turns every committed insert, update and delete into an event on a stream. Downstream systems such as search, caches and the warehouse stay in sync without the app publishing anything.
cards.phrase: log-based change data capture with Debezium from the Postgres WAL into Kafka, one topic per table, publishing the outbox table rather than raw business tables to other teams, with alerts on replication slot lag

cards.name: Event schema registry and versioning
cards.desc: Event schemas live in a registry that checks each new version for compatibility before producers can use it. Messages carry a schema id instead of the full schema. Old events still in the log are upgraded to the current shape when read (upcasting), and breaking changes get a new event type or topic.
cards.phrase: versioned event schemas in Protobuf with a schema registry enforcing backward compatibility in CI (add optional fields only, never rename or reuse field numbers), breaking changes as a new event type, and upcasters for old stored events

cards.name: Database per service
cards.desc: Each service owns its tables and is the only thing that reads or writes them. Other services get the data through its API or by consuming its events, never by querying its database. Separate schemas on one server count, as long as the access rules hold.
cards.phrase: database per service: each service owns its tables and is the only writer and reader; other services use its API or its events, never its database, enforced with separate database users or schemas

cards.name: Shared database
cards.desc: All modules (or several apps) use one database. Inside a monolith this is the normal and sensible choice: you get joins, foreign keys and real transactions for free. The risk is coupling through tables, where any code can read any table and one schema change breaks distant parts of the app.
cards.phrase: one shared Postgres database for the monolith, with a schema per module (orders, billing, catalog); modules write only their own schema and read others only through module APIs or published views

cards.name: Polyglot persistence
cards.desc: Use different storage engines for different kinds of data in the same system: a relational database for transactions, a key-value store for sessions, a search engine for text, object storage for files. Each store holds the data it is best at, and one of them stays the source of truth.
cards.phrase: Postgres as the source of truth for transactional data; add Redis for sessions and rate limits, OpenSearch for full-text search and S3 for files only where a concrete query needs it, each fed from Postgres

cards.name: Read replicas
cards.desc: One primary takes all writes and streams its changes to one or more replicas, which serve reads. Replication is usually asynchronous, so a replica can be milliseconds to seconds behind the primary.
cards.phrase: one primary for writes and async read replicas for read-only queries; route reads that follow a write in the same session to the primary, and alert when replica lag exceeds 5 s

cards.name: Sharding
cards.desc: Split one dataset across several database nodes by a shard key, so each node holds and serves only part of it. Hash sharding spreads keys evenly but makes range scans hit every shard; range sharding keeps neighbours together but can create hot shards.
cards.phrase: shard by tenant_id using hash sharding (Citus or Vitess) so every query for one tenant hits one shard; no cross-shard transactions, and fan-out queries only for admin reporting

cards.name: Table partitioning
cards.desc: One logical table is stored as many smaller tables split by a key, usually time or tenant, inside a single database. Queries that filter on the key only touch the matching partitions, and old data is removed by dropping a partition instead of a huge DELETE.
cards.phrase: Postgres range partitioning by month on created_at for the events table, partitions created ahead by pg_partman, retention by dropping partitions older than 12 months

cards.name: Multi-tenancy models
cards.desc: Silo gives each tenant its own database. Pool puts every tenant in the same tables with a tenant_id column, ideally enforced by row-level security. Bridge sits between them: one database, a schema per tenant.
cards.phrase: pool multi-tenancy: every tenant table has tenant_id NOT NULL, Postgres row-level security policies filter on current_setting('app.tenant_id') set per transaction, and indexes lead with tenant_id

cards.name: Materialized views
cards.desc: A query whose result is stored as a table and refreshed on a schedule or on change. Reads become a cheap lookup instead of a heavy aggregate, at the price of the data being as old as the last refresh.
cards.phrase: a Postgres materialized view for the daily sales aggregates with a unique index, refreshed CONCURRENTLY every 5 minutes by a scheduled job, and the page shows the last refresh time

cards.name: Search index from the primary store
cards.aka: derived search index, CDC to search
cards.desc: Full-text and faceted search run on a dedicated engine, but the data is written to the primary database first. Changes flow to the index through change data capture or an outbox, and the index can always be rebuilt from the primary.
cards.phrase: Postgres stays the source of truth; changes stream to OpenSearch via Debezium CDC into an idempotent indexer that upserts by id, with a zero-downtime reindex through an index alias

cards.name: Object storage with metadata in a database
cards.desc: Files go to object storage and the database keeps a row with the key, size, type, owner and status. The client uploads straight to the bucket with a short-lived presigned URL, so large files never pass through your servers.
cards.phrase: files in S3 with metadata in Postgres: the API creates a pending row and returns a presigned PUT URL (5 min expiry, content-type and max size fixed), an S3 event marks the row ready, and a daily job deletes orphans

cards.name: Time-series store
cards.desc: A store built for timestamped measurements: fast appends, compression, time-bucketed queries, rollups and automatic retention. Raw points are kept briefly and downsampled into coarser buckets kept longer.
cards.phrase: TimescaleDB hypertable for sensor readings partitioned by time, continuous aggregates at 1 minute and 1 hour, raw data retained 30 days, 1-minute rollups 1 year, compression after 7 days

cards.name: Vector store for retrieval
cards.desc: Text is split into chunks, each chunk is turned into an embedding vector, and the vectors are stored with an approximate nearest-neighbour index. At query time the question is embedded too and the closest chunks are fetched and passed to the model.
cards.phrase: pgvector in the main Postgres: chunks of about 500 tokens with doc_id and an embedding column, an HNSW index with cosine distance, hybrid retrieval with full-text search, top 5 chunks filtered by tenant

cards.name: OLTP and OLAP split
cards.desc: The app database (OLTP) handles small transactional reads and writes. Data is copied to a columnar warehouse (OLAP) where analysts run big scans, and transformations are written as SQL models inside the warehouse (ELT, typically with dbt).
cards.phrase: keep analytics off the app database: load Postgres into the warehouse hourly with Airbyte, model it in dbt (staging, then marts) with tests on keys, and point dashboards only at marts

cards.name: Data lakehouse
cards.desc: Data sits in object storage as open table formats (Iceberg, Delta Lake) that add transactions, schemas and time travel on top of Parquet files. It is refined in layers: bronze holds raw copies, silver cleaned and joined data, gold business-ready tables, and many engines can query the same tables.
cards.phrase: a lakehouse on S3 with Apache Iceberg tables in a REST catalog: bronze as raw append-only ingests, silver deduplicated and typed, gold aggregated per use case; Spark for transforms, Trino for queries

cards.name: Repository
cards.desc: A collection-like interface for loading and saving one aggregate, such as get(id) and save(order). Domain code depends on the interface, and the database details live in one implementation behind it.
cards.phrase: a repository per aggregate (OrderRepository with get, save and a few named queries), domain code depends on the interface, one Postgres implementation and an in-memory fake for tests; no generic Repository<T>

cards.name: Unit of work
cards.desc: An object that tracks every entity loaded and changed during one business operation and writes all the changes in a single transaction at the end. ORMs like Hibernate, EF Core and SQLAlchemy have one built in.
cards.phrase: one unit of work per request or command: load entities, change them in memory, then commit once in a single transaction that also writes outbox rows; no commits inside domain methods

cards.name: Active record
cards.desc: Each object wraps one table row and carries its own persistence methods: find, save, destroy. Fields map one-to-one to columns, and validations and associations live on the model class.
cards.phrase: active record models (Rails style) with validations and associations on the model, eager loading with includes to avoid N+1, and logic that spans several models moved into service objects

cards.name: ORM vs query builder vs raw SQL
cards.aka: data mapper, SQL builder, hand-written SQL
cards.desc: A data mapper ORM maps objects to tables and tracks changes for you. A query builder writes SQL in typed code and returns plain rows. Raw SQL gives full control and you map rows by hand.
cards.phrase: use Kysely as a typed query builder for most data access, raw parameterized SQL for reports, no ORM change tracking; every query visible in code and covered by an integration test against real Postgres

cards.name: DTOs and mapping at boundaries
cards.aka: data transfer objects, view models, anti-corruption mapping
cards.desc: Each layer has its own shapes: request and response DTOs at the API, domain objects in the middle, rows at the database. Explicit mapping functions translate at each boundary, so a column rename does not change your public API.
cards.phrase: separate request DTOs (validated with zod), domain types and database rows, with explicit mapping functions at each boundary; never return ORM entities or rows directly from the API

cards.name: Optimistic concurrency
cards.aka: optimistic locking, version column, ETag, compare-and-set
cards.desc: Each row has a version number. An update only succeeds if the version is still the one you read, and bumps it; zero rows updated means someone else changed it first. Over HTTP the version travels as an ETag with If-Match.
cards.phrase: optimistic concurrency with an integer version column: UPDATE ... WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2, zero rows returns 409 Conflict; the API exposes it as an ETag and requires If-Match on PUT and PATCH

cards.name: Pessimistic locking
cards.aka: SELECT FOR UPDATE, row locks, advisory locks
cards.desc: Lock the row before changing it so other transactions wait until you commit. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks rows; SKIP LOCKED lets workers grab different rows of a job table; advisory locks guard things that are not rows, like "only one importer runs".
cards.phrase: pessimistic locking with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside short transactions, locks taken in a consistent order to avoid deadlocks, lock_timeout of 2 s, and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for the job queue

cards.name: Soft delete
cards.desc: Rows are marked deleted with a timestamp instead of being removed, so they can be restored and audited. Every normal query then has to filter them out, and unique constraints only apply to live rows.
cards.phrase: soft delete with a nullable deleted_at timestamptz, a default scope or view that hides deleted rows, partial unique indexes WHERE deleted_at IS NULL, and a job that hard-deletes after 30 days

cards.name: Audit log and history tables
cards.aka: temporal tables, system-versioned tables, change history
cards.desc: Keep a record of who changed what and when. Temporal (system-versioned) tables keep every old version of a row automatically and let you query the table as of a past time; an application audit log writes an explicit entry with actor, action and before and after values in the same transaction.
cards.phrase: an append-only audit_log table (actor, action, entity, before and after as jsonb, request id, timestamp) written in the same transaction as the change, with no updates or deletes allowed on it

cards.name: Expand and contract migrations
cards.desc: Change a schema in small steps where old and new code both keep working. Add the new column, write to both and backfill, switch reads to the new column, then drop the old one in a later deploy.
cards.phrase: expand and contract for schema changes: add nullable columns, dual-write and backfill in batches, switch reads, drop the old column in a later release; no locking ALTERs on large tables and indexes built CONCURRENTLY

cards.name: Cache-aside
cards.desc: The app checks the cache first. On a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache with a TTL, and returns it. Writes go to the database and delete the cached key.
cards.phrase: cache-aside in Redis for product reads: get, on miss load from Postgres and set with a 5 min TTL; writes update Postgres then delete the key; cache errors fall through to the database

cards.name: Write-through and write-behind caching
cards.desc: Write-through writes to the cache and the database in the same request, so the cache is always warm and current. Write-behind writes to the cache and acknowledges at once, then flushes to the database later in batches.
cards.phrase: write-behind for view counters: INCR in Redis on each hit, a worker flushes deltas to Postgres every 10 s in one batched upsert; losing up to 10 s of counts on a crash is acceptable

cards.name: Cache invalidation and stampede protection
cards.desc: When a hot key expires, hundreds of requests can miss at once and all hit the database. Add random jitter to TTLs so keys do not expire together, and coalesce concurrent misses so only one request recomputes while the rest wait for its result.
cards.phrase: stampede protection: TTL 300 s with ±10% jitter, per-key request coalescing (singleflight) so one miss recomputes, serve stale for up to 60 s while refreshing, invalidate by deleting keys on write

cards.name: Consistency models
cards.desc: Strong consistency means every read sees the latest write. Eventual means replicas converge later. Between them, read-your-writes guarantees you see your own changes, and monotonic reads guarantee you never see data go backwards in time.
cards.phrase: read-your-writes for the user's own data: after a write, return the commit LSN in a cookie and serve that user's reads from the primary or from a replica that has replayed past it; everything else may read eventually consistent replicas

cards.name: Idempotency keys for writes
cards.desc: The client sends a unique key with each write. The server stores the key with the result in the same transaction, and a retry with the same key gets the stored result instead of doing the work twice.
cards.phrase: idempotency keys on all POSTs: Idempotency-Key header required, stored with a request hash and the response in the same transaction under a unique constraint, replay on repeat, 409 if in flight, 422 if the body differs, keys expire after 24 h

cards.name: UUIDv7 and ULID keys
cards.aka: time-ordered IDs, vs auto-increment, vs UUIDv4
cards.desc: UUIDv7 and ULID put a millisecond timestamp in the first 48 bits followed by random bits. They can be generated anywhere without a round trip like random UUIDs, yet sort by creation time like auto-increment, so B-tree inserts stay at the end of the index.
cards.phrase: UUIDv7 primary keys generated in the app (or Postgres 18 uuidv7()), stored as the native uuid type, never random UUIDv4 for clustered or indexed keys

cards.name: REST resource API
cards.desc: Model the domain as resources with stable URLs and act on them with HTTP methods: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH updates, DELETE removes. Status codes, caching headers and content types do the work that custom envelopes would otherwise do.
cards.phrase: a resource-oriented REST API: plural nouns (/orders, /orders/{id}), standard methods and status codes (201 + Location on create, 204 on delete, 404/409/422 for errors), PATCH with JSON Merge Patch, and Idempotency-Key on POST

cards.name: GraphQL
cards.desc: Clients send a query that names exactly the fields they want, and one endpoint resolves it against a typed schema. With federation, each team owns a subgraph and a router stitches them into one supergraph and plans the calls.
cards.phrase: a GraphQL API with a schema-first SDL, DataLoader batching per request, query depth and cost limits, persisted queries in production, and errors in the errors array with stable extension codes

cards.name: gRPC
cards.desc: Services are defined in .proto files and code generators produce typed client stubs and server interfaces. Calls go over HTTP/2 with compact protobuf messages, and support unary calls plus client, server and bidirectional streaming.
cards.phrase: gRPC between internal services: .proto contracts in a shared repo linted and breaking-change checked with Buf, deadlines set on every call, status codes mapped deliberately (UNAVAILABLE retryable, INVALID_ARGUMENT not)

cards.name: Typed RPC
cards.desc: The client calls server procedures as if they were local functions, and the type checker sees both sides. tRPC shares TypeScript types directly with no codegen. Connect generates clients from protobuf and speaks gRPC, gRPC-Web and plain JSON over HTTP.
cards.phrase: typed RPC with tRPC: one router per feature, Zod input validation on every procedure, queries vs mutations kept distinct, and the AppRouter type imported by the client so a server change breaks the client build

cards.name: JSON-RPC
cards.desc: A tiny protocol: send an object with method, params and id, get back a result or an error with the same id. It is transport-agnostic, so it runs over HTTP, WebSockets or stdio. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) uses it for tool calls between AI clients and servers.
cards.phrase: JSON-RPC 2.0: namespaced methods (tools/call, orders/get), every request carries an id, standard error codes (-32600, -32601, -32602) plus app codes from -32000, and batch requests supported

cards.name: Webhooks
cards.desc: When something happens, the provider POSTs an event to a URL the consumer registered. The body is signed with a shared secret so the receiver can verify it, and failed deliveries are retried with backoff for hours or days.
cards.phrase: webhooks per the Standard Webhooks spec: HMAC-SHA256 signature over id + timestamp + body, 5-minute timestamp tolerance, retries with exponential backoff for up to 3 days, and receivers that return 2xx fast, enqueue, and dedupe by event id

cards.name: WebSockets
cards.desc: An HTTP request upgrades into a long-lived, two-way connection where either side can send frames at any time. Each server node holds its own sockets, so broadcasting to users on other nodes goes through a shared pub/sub.
cards.phrase: WebSockets with auth on the upgrade request, ping/pong heartbeats every 30 s, client reconnect with jittered backoff and resume from last seen sequence number, and fan-out across nodes via Redis pub/sub

cards.name: Server-sent events
cards.desc: The client opens one ordinary HTTP request and the server keeps it open, writing text events down it as they happen. Browsers reconnect on their own and send Last-Event-ID so the server can resume.
cards.phrase: server-sent events: text/event-stream with an id on every event, resume from Last-Event-ID, a comment heartbeat every 15 s to keep proxies from closing the stream, and proxy buffering turned off for that route

cards.name: Long polling
cards.desc: The client makes a request and the server holds it open until there is news or a timeout passes, then responds. The client immediately asks again, passing the last position it saw.
cards.phrase: long polling with a 25 s server hold (below every proxy timeout), a since cursor on each request, 200 with events or 204 on timeout, and immediate re-poll on the client

cards.name: Async request-reply
cards.desc: For work that takes longer than a request should, the API validates the input, queues the job and returns 202 Accepted with a Location pointing to a status resource. The client polls that URL (or gets a webhook) until the job finishes and links to the result.
cards.phrase: async request-reply: POST returns 202 Accepted with Location: /jobs/{id} and Retry-After; the job resource reports queued, running, succeeded or failed with progress, and on success links to the result; jobs are kept 7 days

cards.name: Contract-first API
cards.desc: Write the API description (OpenAPI for HTTP, AsyncAPI for events) before the code, review it like code, and generate server stubs, typed clients, docs and mocks from it. CI diffs each change against the last released spec and fails on breaking changes.
cards.phrase: contract-first with OpenAPI 3.1 in the repo: lint with Spectral, generate typed clients and server request validation from it, run oasdiff in CI to block breaking changes, and validate real responses against the spec in tests

cards.name: API versioning
cards.aka: URL versioning, header versioning, API evolution
cards.desc: Three common ways to change an API without stranding clients: put a major version in the path, pin each client to a dated version in a header and translate old shapes at the edge, or never break anything and only add. Most mature APIs combine additive evolution with rare major versions.
cards.phrase: API versioning by additive evolution first (new optional fields and endpoints only, never rename, retype or remove), a major version in the URL (/v2) only for real breaks, and Deprecation + Sunset headers with usage tracking before removing anything

cards.name: Cursor pagination
cards.desc: Offset pagination asks the database to count past every skipped row, so deep pages get slow, and rows inserted meanwhile shift pages and cause duplicates or gaps. Cursor pagination returns an opaque token that encodes the last row's sort key, and the next query seeks straight past it.
cards.phrase: cursor pagination: opaque base64 cursor encoding (created_at, id), WHERE (created_at, id) < cursor ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC, limit default 50 max 200, response returns next_cursor and has_more, backed by a composite index

cards.name: Rate limiting and quotas
cards.desc: Each caller gets a budget, usually a token bucket that refills at a steady rate and allows short bursts. Calls over budget get 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After, and response headers tell clients how much is left. Quotas are the slower, longer budgets (per day or per plan).
cards.phrase: rate limiting per API key with a token bucket (100 req/s, burst 200) in Redis at the gateway, 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit headers when exceeded, separate stricter limits on login and expensive endpoints, and clients that honor Retry-After

cards.name: Problem details errors
cards.desc: A standard JSON shape for HTTP errors: a type URI that identifies the error kind, a human title, the status, a detail for this occurrence and an instance pointing at the request. You can add your own fields such as a trace id or per-field validation errors.
cards.phrase: errors as RFC 9457 problem details (application/problem+json) with a stable type URI per error kind, a field-level errors array for 422 validation failures, a traceId extension, and no stack traces or SQL in detail

cards.name: Consumer-driven contract tests
cards.desc: Each consumer writes tests against a mock provider, and those tests record the exact requests and responses it relies on into a contract file. The provider replays every consumer's contracts against its real code in CI, and a broker answers whether a given version is safe to deploy.
cards.phrase: consumer-driven contract tests with Pact: consumers publish pacts from unit tests to a Pact Broker tagged by branch and environment, providers verify them in CI, and every deploy is gated by can-i-deploy

cards.name: API gateway
cards.desc: One entry point in front of many services that handles the cross-cutting work: TLS, authentication, rate limits, routing, request size limits and logging. Services behind it can stay simpler and are not exposed directly.
cards.phrase: an API gateway that terminates TLS, validates JWTs, applies per-key rate limits, routes by path to services, and adds a request id; no business logic or response reshaping in the gateway

cards.name: Backend for frontend
cards.desc: Each client type gets its own thin backend, owned by the team that builds that client. It aggregates and reshapes calls to downstream services into exactly what its screens need, and can hold sessions so tokens never reach the browser.
cards.phrase: a backend for frontend per client (web, mobile), owned by that client team, that aggregates downstream calls, shapes responses per screen, keeps OAuth tokens server-side behind an httpOnly session cookie, and holds no domain rules

cards.name: Service mesh
cards.desc: Every service instance gets a proxy (a sidecar, or a per-node proxy in newer ambient modes) that handles its network traffic. A control plane pushes config to all proxies, giving you mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic splitting and uniform metrics without changing app code.
cards.phrase: a service mesh (Linkerd or Istio ambient) providing automatic mTLS between services, per-route timeouts and retry budgets set in mesh config rather than app code, and golden-signal metrics per route

cards.name: Sidecar
cards.desc: A helper process deployed next to the main app, sharing its lifecycle, network namespace and often a volume. It adds a capability such as log shipping, TLS, config reloads or secrets fetching, so the app does not have to implement it.
cards.phrase: a sidecar container (Kubernetes native sidecar) next to the app that ships logs from the shared volume and fetches secrets into it, with its own CPU and memory limits, started before and stopped after the app

cards.name: Ambassador
cards.desc: A local proxy that the app calls on localhost instead of calling a remote service directly. The ambassador handles the messy client-side work: connection pooling, retries, circuit breaking, TLS, and routing to the right shard or region.
cards.phrase: an ambassador proxy on localhost that the app calls for the payments provider, owning TLS, connection pooling, 2 s timeouts, retries with jittered backoff on 503 only, and a circuit breaker; the app itself does no retries

cards.name: Anti-corruption layer
cards.desc: A layer at the boundary with another system that translates its model into yours and back. Your domain code only ever sees your own types, so the other system's naming, quirks and changes are contained in one place.
cards.phrase: an anti-corruption layer between our domain and the legacy ERP: one module that maps ERP records to our domain types (and back), validates them, and is the only code that imports ERP client types

cards.name: Strangler fig migration
cards.desc: Put a routing layer in front of the old system, then rebuild one slice at a time and switch its routes to the new code. The legacy system shrinks until nothing routes to it and it can be switched off.
cards.phrase: a strangler fig migration: a proxy in front of the monolith routes migrated paths to the new service and everything else to the monolith, with each slice switchable per route via config and shadow traffic compared before cutover

cards.name: Facade over legacy
cards.desc: A clean, small API placed in front of one or more awkward legacy systems. Callers use the facade's simple operations, and the facade does the multi-step calls, protocol conversion and data cleanup behind it.
cards.phrase: a facade service exposing a small REST API (GET /customers/{id}) over the mainframe, CRM and billing database, with its own response model, per-backend timeouts, and short-lived caching of slow lookups

cards.name: Adapter at the boundary
cards.desc: Wrap each external SDK or API behind an interface your code owns, and put all the mapping in one adapter class. The rest of the code talks to your interface, so swapping vendors or faking it in tests touches one file.
cards.phrase: an adapter per external service: an interface in our domain terms (Payments.charge), one adapter class that alone imports the vendor SDK and maps its types and errors to ours, and an in-memory fake for tests

cards.name: Reverse proxy and load balancer
cards.aka: L4 vs L7 load balancing, ingress
cards.desc: A reverse proxy accepts client connections and forwards them to a pool of backends. An L4 balancer works on TCP or UDP connections and only sees IPs and ports. An L7 balancer terminates HTTP, so it can route by host, path or header, retry, and balance per request.
cards.phrase: an L7 load balancer (Envoy or ALB) that terminates TLS, routes by host and path, balances per request with least-request, health-checks backends with outlier ejection, and drains connections on deploy

cards.name: Service discovery
cards.desc: Instances register their address with a registry when they start and are removed when health checks fail. Callers look up a logical name (orders) and get healthy addresses, either directly (client-side) or through a load balancer or DNS (server-side).
cards.phrase: service discovery through Kubernetes Services and DNS names (orders.default.svc), readiness probes that gate registration, and callers that never hard-code instance IPs

cards.name: Edge functions and CDN
cards.aka: edge compute, CDN in front of APIs
cards.desc: A CDN with points of presence near users sits in front of your API. It caches cacheable responses and runs small functions at the edge for auth checks, redirects, geo routing, A/B assignment or header rewrites, so only misses and dynamic calls reach the origin.
cards.phrase: a CDN in front of the API caching public GET responses with Cache-Control s-maxage and stale-while-revalidate, never caching responses that vary by user, and an edge function that verifies the JWT and rejects bad requests before the origin

cards.name: File and batch integration
cards.aka: batch ETL, file drop, SFTP exchange
cards.desc: One system exports a file (CSV, Parquet, JSON lines) on a schedule to shared storage, and another picks it up and loads it. Done well, each file has a manifest or done marker, a schema, and loads are idempotent so reruns are safe.
cards.phrase: batch file integration: nightly Parquet export to S3 under dated prefixes with a _SUCCESS manifest holding row count and schema version, an idempotent loader that upserts by key, and an alert if the file is late or counts do not match

cards.name: API composition
