cards.name: Search placeholder
cards.desc: Tell people what they can search for, using real examples of the things in your product ("Search files, people and comments"). It's a small spot that quietly teaches scope.
cards.phrase: write the search placeholder to say exactly what it searches ("Search files, people and comments")

cards.name: Tooltip
cards.desc: A short supplement, never the only home for something people must know. One sentence, no period if it's a fragment. It explains what a control does or defines a term; if it needs a heading, a list or a link, it wants to be a popover or a help article.
cards.phrase: write tooltips as one short line that adds information the label can't hold, never repeating the label and never hiding essential info

cards.name: First use
cards.desc: The screen before the person has made anything. Says what will live here and why it's worth having, then offers one clear way to start, ideally the smallest possible first step. This is onboarding in disguise, so it carries more weight than it looks.
cards.phrase: write a first-use empty state: one line on what will appear here and why it's useful, and one button for the smallest first step

cards.name: No results
cards.desc: Repeat what they searched for, so they can spot a typo, and offer a way forward: a broader search, a spelling suggestion, or a way to create the thing they were looking for. Never blame the query.
cards.phrase: write a no-results state that repeats the search term, suggests a fix (spelling, broader terms, clearing filters) and offers to create the thing if that makes sense

cards.name: Filtered to nothing
cards.desc: The data exists but the person's own filters hide all of it. Say so, name the filters, and offer to clear them in one press. Otherwise people think their stuff is gone.
cards.phrase: write a filtered-empty state that says the filters hide everything, names the active filters, and offers a one-press "Clear filters"

cards.name: All done
cards.aka: inbox zero, caught up, cleared state
cards.desc: The person emptied it on purpose. Mark the moment lightly, tell them what happens next (new items will show up here), and don't push a new task at them. A little warmth fits here because nothing is wrong.
cards.phrase: write an "all caught up" state that lightly acknowledges the person cleared it and says when new items will appear, without pushing another task

cards.name: No access
cards.desc: The thing exists but this person can't see it. Say that plainly, say who can grant access (by name, if you know it), and give them a way to ask. Don't pretend it doesn't exist if they followed a link to it.
cards.phrase: write a no-access state that says the person doesn't have access, names who can grant it, and offers a "Request access" action

cards.name: Not enough data yet
cards.desc: For analytics, recommendations or streaks that need time before they mean anything. Say what's being collected, how long until there's something to see, and show a preview of what it will look like.
cards.phrase: write a "not enough data yet" state that says what's being collected and when there will be something to see

cards.name: Couldn't load
cards.desc: The area is empty because something broke, not because there's nothing there. Say that it didn't load (so people don't think their data is gone), give the likely reason if you know it, and offer Try again.
cards.phrase: write a load-failure state that makes clear the data exists but didn't load, gives the reason if known, and offers "Try again"

cards.name: Loading message
cards.desc: Say what's happening in a present-tense verb phrase ("Uploading 3 photos"), and add the time if it's more than a few seconds. Rotating jokes wear thin by the third visit; honest progress never does.
cards.phrase: write loading text as a present-tense verb phrase saying what's happening, plus a time estimate when it takes more than a few seconds

cards.name: Progress with steps
cards.desc: For long, multi-part work, name the current step and show how far along it is. Steps in plain words ("Checking files", "Copying 1,204 of 3,500") help people decide whether to wait or come back.
cards.phrase: for long tasks, show the current step in plain words with a count ("Copying 1,204 of 3,500 files") alongside the progress bar

cards.name: Long wait, we'll tell you
cards.desc: If it takes minutes or more, release the person: say it'll keep going without them and how they'll find out it's done. Then actually send that email or notification.
cards.phrase: for waits longer than a minute, tell the person they can leave and exactly how they'll be told when it's done

cards.name: Save status
cards.desc: A quiet line near the title that tells people their work is safe: "Saving…", then "Saved", then "Saved 2 minutes ago". When it can't save, this is the one place it must get loud, and say what's at risk.
cards.phrase: write a quiet save-status line ("Saving…", "Saved", "Saved 2 minutes ago") that turns into a clear warning only when work is at risk

cards.name: Skeleton screens
cards.desc: When content loads in under a few seconds, show its shape instead of words. The copy decision here is to write nothing, and to keep any static labels (titles, tab names) real so the page orients people while the data arrives.
cards.phrase: for short loads, show skeleton placeholders with real headings and no loading text

cards.name: Success toast
cards.desc: Past tense, the object, and nothing else: "Invoice sent", "3 files moved to Archive". It mirrors the button that triggered it, so "Send invoice" becomes "Invoice sent". No exclamation mark for routine actions.
cards.phrase: write success toasts in the past tense, naming the object, mirroring the button that triggered them ("Invoice sent"), with no exclamation marks

cards.name: Undo instead of confirm
cards.desc: For actions that are reversible, do the thing and offer Undo, rather than asking "Are you sure?" first. It's faster for the 99 percent who meant it and safer for the 1 percent who didn't, because people read toasts more than they read dialogs.
cards.phrase: for reversible actions, skip the confirmation dialog: perform the action and show a toast with Undo

cards.name: Done page
cards.desc: After a bigger task (an order, an application, a booking) confirm it happened, give the reference number, say what happens next and when, and offer the one next thing they're most likely to want.
cards.phrase: write a confirmation page: say it worked, give the reference number, say what happens next and when, and offer one likely next action

cards.name: Milestone moment
cards.desc: For the rare real achievement: a first publish, a 30-day streak, a finished course. Name the specific thing they did, keep it short, and give the moment a next step that builds on it. If everything celebrates, nothing does.
cards.phrase: for a real milestone, write a short celebration that names the specific achievement and suggests a next step; use it rarely

cards.name: What, why, what now
cards.desc: The shape under every good error. What happened, in the person's terms. Why, if knowing it changes what they do. What they can do now, as a button where possible. Apologize only when it's really your fault, and then once.
cards.phrase: write every error as what happened, why (if it helps), and what to do now, in plain words, with an action button where possible

cards.name: Our fault
cards.desc: When it's on your side, say so plainly, reassure about what's safe, and say what you're doing or when to try again. "We" owns it. A short apology fits here. No error codes in the headline; put a reference number at the bottom for support.
cards.phrase: for server-side errors, say it's on our end, reassure what's safe, say when to retry, and put any error code small at the end for support

cards.name: Offline
cards.desc: Say what still works and what doesn't, rather than just "No internet". Tell people whether their actions will queue and sync later. And tell them when they're back, briefly.
cards.phrase: write offline messages that say what still works, whether changes will sync later, and briefly confirm when the connection is back

cards.name: 404 page
cards.desc: Says the page isn't here and the likely reason (moved, deleted, or a typo in the link), then gives two useful ways forward: search, and the most likely destination. A light touch of personality is fine here, since nothing important was lost.
cards.phrase: write a 404 page: say the page isn't here and why that might be, a light touch of personality, and two useful ways forward

cards.name: Payment declined
cards.desc: Stressful and sometimes embarrassing, so be calm and private. Say the payment didn't go through, give the reason the bank gave if it's useful, say what's not affected yet, and make updating the card one step. Never imply the person did something wrong.
cards.phrase: write payment-failure copy that's calm and private: what didn't go through, what's not affected yet, the deadline, and a one-step way to update the card

cards.name: Limits and too many tries
cards.desc: Say what the limit protects, when they can try again (a time, not "later"), and a way around it if there is one. Lockouts on sign-in especially need a way out today ("Reset your password").
cards.phrase: for limits and lockouts, say why the limit exists, exactly when they can try again, and any way around it now

cards.name: Edit conflict
cards.aka: version conflict, someone else changed this
cards.desc: Two people changed the same thing. Name who and when, say what's preserved, and give clear choices about whose version wins. Never silently discard either version.
cards.phrase: write edit-conflict copy that names who changed it and when, reassures that both versions are kept, and offers clear choices

cards.name: Partial failure
cards.desc: When some things worked and some didn't, lead with the count of each, list the ones that failed and why, and offer to retry only those. "Upload failed" when 47 of 50 succeeded is both wrong and alarming.
cards.phrase: for partial failures, lead with how many succeeded and failed, name the failed items and the reason, and offer to retry only those

cards.name: System banner
cards.desc: Site-wide news: planned maintenance, an ongoing incident, a policy change. State what's affected and when in the first few words, link to details, and make it dismissible unless it's an active outage.
cards.phrase: write a system banner that says what's affected and when in the first few words, with a link to details

cards.name: Approaching a limit
cards.desc: Warn early enough to act, with the actual numbers and what happens at the limit. Then offer both paths: free up space, or get more. A warning that only offers an upgrade reads as a sales pitch.
cards.phrase: write a usage warning with the actual numbers, what happens at the limit, and two ways out (free up space, or upgrade)

cards.name: Unsaved changes
cards.desc: When someone is about to lose work, say exactly what will be lost and give a way to keep it in the same dialog. "Save and leave" removes the need for two steps.
cards.phrase: write an unsaved-changes warning that names what will be lost and offers "Save and leave", "Leave without saving" and staying

cards.name: Change is coming
cards.desc: Announce removals and big changes early: what's changing, the date, what people need to do (if anything), and what happens if they don't. Repeat it as the date gets close.
cards.phrase: write a change notice that says exactly what's changing, the date, what the person needs to do, and what happens if they do nothing

cards.name: Welcome screen
cards.desc: One sentence on what the product does for this person, then the first step. If you know why they signed up (an invite, a template, an ad), say it back to them. Skip the feature tour; the first result teaches more than any slide.
cards.phrase: write a welcome screen with one sentence on what the product does for this person and a single first step; skip excitement and feature lists

cards.name: Sign-up form
cards.desc: Ask for as little as possible, say why you need anything unusual, and put the value and the cost (free? card needed?) next to the button. The button names the outcome: "Create account", or better, "Start planning".
cards.phrase: write a sign-up form with the fewest possible fields, a short reason for anything unusual, the cost stated by the button, and an outcome-named button

cards.name: Setup questions
cards.desc: Only ask what you'll use right away, and say how you'll use it ("We'll suggest recipes that fit"). Make every question skippable and every answer changeable later, and tell people so.
cards.phrase: write setup questions that each say how the answer helps the person, are skippable, and note they can be changed later

cards.name: Getting-started checklist
cards.desc: Three to five tasks, each a verb phrase that leads straight to the action, ordered by value. Show progress and let people dismiss it. The first item should already be done ("Create your account") to give a small head start.
cards.phrase: write a getting-started checklist of 3 to 5 verb-led tasks ordered by value, with the first already done and a way to dismiss it

cards.name: Sample content
cards.desc: Pre-fill an empty product with an example so people can see it working before they put in effort. Label it clearly as an example and make it one click to remove, so nobody mistakes it for real data.
cards.phrase: write labels for sample content that make it unmistakably an example and offer a one-click way to remove it

cards.name: Permission priming
cards.desc: Before the system's own permission prompt, explain in your words what you'll do with access and what they get, at the moment they need it. Offer "Not now" so a refusal doesn't burn the one-time system prompt.
cards.phrase: write a pre-permission screen shown in context that explains what access is used for and what the person gets, with a "Not now" option

cards.name: Coach mark
cards.aka: onboarding tip, hotspot, tooltip tour step
cards.desc: Points at one control and says what it does and why you'd want it, in under 20 words. A title is optional; a "Got it" is not. Show it when the control is relevant, not on the first screen load.
cards.phrase: write a coach mark that points at one control and says what it does and why it helps in under 20 words, with "Got it"

cards.name: Product tour
cards.desc: If you must have one, keep it to three steps that each teach something people can't easily discover, with a step count and a visible way to skip. Better: replace it with contextual tips that appear when each feature is relevant.
cards.phrase: write a product tour of at most three steps, each teaching one non-obvious thing, with a step counter and a visible "Skip tour"

cards.name: Progressive disclosure
cards.desc: Show the essentials, and tuck the rest behind a link or expander whose label says exactly what's inside ("Advanced sharing settings", "How we calculate this"). People who need it find it; everyone else isn't slowed down.
cards.phrase: put secondary information behind expanders whose labels say exactly what's inside ("How we calculate your pace")

cards.name: What's new
cards.desc: Lead with what the person can now do, in their words, then show where to find it. One feature per announcement. Show it to the people it's relevant to, at a moment they're not mid-task.
cards.phrase: write a feature announcement that leads with what the person can now do, where to find it, and one action to try it

cards.name: Contextual nudge
cards.desc: A quiet hint that shows up because of what the person just did: they've moved the same file three times, so suggest a rule. Explain the shortcut and make it easy to ignore forever.
cards.phrase: write a contextual nudge triggered by what the person just did, suggesting a shortcut, with a way to dismiss it for good

cards.name: Help links
cards.desc: Link to help with the question it answers ("How do refunds work?"), not "Help" or "Learn more". It tells people whether the article is worth opening, and makes the link useful to screen-reader users.
cards.phrase: write help links as the question the article answers ("How do shared links expire?")

cards.name: Confirmation dialog
cards.desc: Use only for actions that are hard to undo. The title names the action and object as a question, the body says the consequence (who's affected, what's lost), and the button repeats the verb. If you can offer Undo instead, do that.
cards.phrase: write a confirmation dialog only for hard-to-undo actions: the title names the action and object, the body states the consequence, the button repeats the verb

cards.name: Type to confirm
cards.desc: For the most destructive actions (deleting a workspace, a repository, all data), ask people to type the name. Spell out exactly what will be destroyed, with numbers, and keep the button disabled until the name matches.
cards.phrase: for irreversible, high-impact deletes, spell out exactly what will be destroyed with numbers and ask the person to type the name to confirm

cards.name: Permission purpose string
cards.aka: iOS usage description, Info.plist purpose string
cards.desc: The line you supply that appears inside the system's own permission prompt. It must say what you use access for, specifically, in a full sentence. Platforms reject vague ones, and people refuse them.
cards.phrase: write the system permission purpose string as one full sentence saying specifically what the access is used for

cards.name: Consent and cookies
cards.desc: Make accepting and declining equally easy and equally visible, describe each choice by what it does, and never pre-tick boxes. "Reject all" next to "Accept all", in the same style.
cards.phrase: write consent copy where accept and decline are equally easy and visible, each purpose is described plainly, and nothing is pre-checked

cards.name: Privacy note at collection
cards.desc: A one-line explanation right where you collect something sensitive: what it's for, who sees it, how long you keep it. It earns more trust than any privacy policy, because people actually read it.
cards.phrase: next to any sensitive field, write a one-line privacy note saying what it's used for and who sees it

cards.name: Plan comparison
cards.desc: Name plans by who they're for, put the full price and billing period together, and list differences, not everything. The button says what happens ("Start 14-day trial", "Switch to Team"), and the one recommended plan is marked with a reason.
cards.phrase: write plan cards named by who they're for, with full price and billing period together, only the differences listed, and an action-named button

cards.name: Upgrade at the limit
cards.desc: When someone hits a paid feature, say what they tried to do, what the plan that includes it costs, and let them finish what they were doing if at all possible. Lead with their task, not the plan name.
cards.phrase: write an upgrade prompt that names what the person tried to do, the plan and price that includes it, and how they can continue without upgrading

cards.name: Trial ending
cards.desc: Warn a few days before the charge, with the date, the amount and how to cancel, in plain view. People who feel tricked by a trial don't come back; people reminded honestly often stay.
cards.phrase: write a trial-ending reminder that states the charge date, exact amount and how to cancel in its first lines

cards.name: Receipt
cards.desc: What was paid, for what, when, with which card, and how to get a PDF or a refund. Put the amount in the subject line. This is a document people forward to accountants, so it's all facts.
cards.phrase: write a receipt with the amount in the subject line and the item, date, payment method, PDF link and refund route in the body

cards.name: Cancellation flow
cards.desc: Let people cancel in as few steps as they took to sign up. Say what happens to their data and when access ends, offer one alternative (pause, downgrade) once, and confirm in plain words. No guilt.
cards.phrase: write a cancellation flow that says when access ends and what happens to the person's data, offers one alternative once, and confirms without guilt

cards.name: Price change notice
cards.desc: Say the old price, the new price, the date, and the reason in one honest sentence. Tell people what they can do (switch plans, cancel) and give them time to do it. Don't bury the number.
cards.phrase: write a price-change notice with the old and new price, effective date, a one-line honest reason, and the options the person has

cards.name: Push notification
cards.desc: A title that makes sense on a lock screen with no context, and a body that adds the one detail that matters. Personal, timely, specific. If it isn't something the person would want to be interrupted for, it shouldn't be a push.
cards.phrase: write a push notification whose title makes sense alone on a lock screen and whose body adds the one detail that matters, under 100 characters

cards.name: Transactional email
cards.desc: The subject line carries the news ("Your order ships tomorrow"), the first line repeats it with the key detail, and there's one main button. Write it to be skimmed on a phone in a crowded inbox.
cards.phrase: write a transactional email with the news in the subject line, the key detail in the first sentence, and one main button

cards.name: Verification and magic links
cards.desc: Put the code in the subject or first line, say how long it lasts, and say what to do if they didn't ask for it. People are juggling tabs; make it findable and safe.
cards.phrase: write a verification message with the code in the first line, how long it's valid, and what to do if the person didn't request it

cards.name: Password reset
cards.desc: On the form, say the email is on its way without confirming whether an account exists (that would leak who's signed up). In the email, one button, an expiry, and a line for people who didn't ask.
cards.phrase: write password-reset copy that doesn't reveal whether an account exists, gives the link's expiry, and reassures people who didn't request it

cards.name: Digest
cards.desc: Leads with the number and the most important item, groups the rest, and links each line to the thing itself. Lets people change the frequency from the email. Skips sending when there's nothing to say.
cards.phrase: write a digest email that leads with what needs the person, groups the rest, links each item, and includes a frequency setting

cards.name: Text message
cards.desc: Name the sender first (texts arrive from numbers people don't recognize), then the one fact, then any action, in 160 characters or fewer. Include how to stop them where the law requires it.
cards.phrase: write an SMS that names the sender first, gives one fact and one action, fits in 160 characters, and includes opt-out where required

cards.name: Prompt starters
cards.desc: Three or four examples of real things this assistant does well in this product, written as the person would type them. They teach scope better than any description and remove the blank-page problem.
cards.phrase: write 3 or 4 prompt starters that show specific things the assistant does well in this product, phrased the way a person would type them

cards.name: Working state
cards.desc: Say what the assistant is doing in concrete steps ("Reading 12 files", "Checking your calendar"), not that it's "thinking". For long tasks, let people stop it and say what will be kept if they do.
cards.phrase: write an assistant working state that names the concrete step in progress and offers a Stop control

cards.name: AI disclosure
cards.desc: Label what the AI wrote or changed, close to the content, in neutral words ("Drafted with AI. Check before sending."). Say what to check, if something specific is likely to be wrong. Avoid both hype and blanket disclaimers.
cards.phrase: label AI-generated content close to it in neutral words and say what the person should check before using it

cards.name: Sources and citations
cards.desc: When an answer comes from the person's own data or the web, mark the claims and link each to its source. Name the sources in their words (file names, page titles). Say plainly when there was no source.
cards.phrase: when answering from documents, mark each claim with a numbered citation that links to the source by its recognizable name, and say when no source was found

cards.name: Can't do that
cards.aka: capability limit, refusal, out of scope
cards.desc: Say plainly what the assistant can't do here, in one line, then what it can do that's closest. No apology spiral, no pretending to try. If a human or another tool can help, point there.
cards.phrase: when the assistant can't do something, say so in one line and offer the closest thing it can do, without apologizing at length

cards.name: Agent action confirmation
cards.aka: human in the loop, approve action
cards.desc: Before an assistant does something with consequences (sends, deletes, pays, posts), show exactly what it will do, to whom, with what content, and ask for approval with a verb button. Afterwards, say what it did and offer undo.
cards.phrase: before an AI agent takes a consequential action, show exactly what it will do, to whom and with what content, and ask for approval with a specific verb button

cards.name: Feedback ask
cards.desc: Quiet and optional: two icons with clear accessible names, and after a thumbs-down, a few specific reasons to pick from plus a free-text box. Say what the feedback is used for.
cards.phrase: write an optional feedback ask with clear labels and, after negative feedback, a few specific reasons to choose from and a note on how feedback is used

cards.name: Oops and whoops
cards.desc: "Oops!" makes a failure sound trivial, which is fine for a missing emoji and grating for a lost order. Most errors are serious to someone. Say what happened instead.
cards.phrase: avoid "Oops", "Uh-oh" and other cutesy openers in errors; say what happened instead

cards.name: Something went wrong
cards.desc: The catch-all tells people nothing they didn't know. Even when you can't say why, say what failed and what's safe. Engineers can usually supply more detail than the default string; ask them.
cards.phrase: avoid generic errors like "Something went wrong"; always say what failed, what's safe and what to try

cards.name: Confirmshaming
cards.desc: Wording the "no" option to make people feel bad ("No thanks, I don't like saving money"). It works once and costs trust forever, and regulators now name it as a dark pattern. Write the decline as neutral as the accept.
cards.phrase: never use confirmshaming; write the decline option as neutrally as the accept ("No thanks")

cards.name: Click here
cards.desc: "Click here" assumes a mouse, says nothing about the destination, and is useless in a screen reader's list of links. Put the link on the words that say where it goes.
cards.phrase: never write "click here" or "here" as link text; link the words that describe the destination

cards.name: Are you sure?
cards.desc: "Are you sure?" questions the person's competence and doesn't say what's at stake. Name the action and the consequence instead, or skip the dialog and offer Undo.
cards.phrase: never write "Are you sure?"; name the action and its consequence, or offer Undo instead of asking

cards.name: Blaming words
cards.desc: "Invalid", "illegal", "you failed to" and "wrong" put the fault on the person. Describe the fix instead. The facts are the same; the feeling is very different.
cards.phrase: avoid blaming words like "invalid", "illegal", "failed to" and "wrong"; describe what to do instead

cards.name: System words
cards.desc: Words from the codebase leak into interfaces: "null", "sync token", "entity", "request failed with status 403". Translate each one to what the person sees and can do. Keep codes, but small and at the end, for support.
cards.phrase: never show internal or technical terms (null, 403, sync token, payload); translate them into what the person sees and can do

cards.name: False urgency
cards.desc: Countdown timers that reset, "Only 2 left!" that's always 2, "Offer ends tonight" every night. People notice, and some regulators now treat it as deception. Use real deadlines, stated plainly.
cards.phrase: never use false urgency or scarcity; state real deadlines plainly

cards.name: Please and thank-you overload
cards.desc: "Please" on every instruction and "Sorry" on every error turn into noise, and they make instructions longer. Save "please" for when you're asking a real favor, and "sorry" for real failures you caused.
cards.phrase: don't overuse "please" or "sorry"; keep them for real favors and real failures

cards.name: Jokes at bad moments
cards.desc: Humor is a tool for low-stakes moments: a 404, an empty search, a loading screen on day one. In payment failures, data loss, security warnings or anything health-related, it reads as not caring. When unsure, be plain.
cards.phrase: use humor only in low-stakes moments; keep errors involving money, data, security or health plain and calm

cards.name: Content-first design
cards.desc: Write the real copy before (or while) designing the screen, so the layout fits the words rather than the other way round. Lorem ipsum hides the hard questions: what's this called, what if it fails, what if the name is 40 characters long.
cards.phrase: start from the content: list what this screen has to say and in what order before suggesting any layout

cards.name: String table
cards.aka: copy deck, strings file, content spreadsheet
cards.desc: Every string in a feature in one table: key, text, where it appears, character limit, and notes for translators. It's how copy travels from design to code without getting retyped wrong, and it shows gaps at a glance.
cards.phrase: return the copy as a string table with columns for key, string, where it appears, character count and notes for translators

cards.name: Word list
cards.desc: The decided terms for your product: which word for each concept, the words you don't use, capitalization and spelling. Short and kept up to date, it does more for consistency than any long style guide.
cards.phrase: use this word list exactly; never substitute the "don't use" terms (paste your list here)

cards.name: Voice chart
cards.desc: A small grid that defines the product's voice with three or four traits, each with "this, not that" and an example. It turns "friendly but professional" into something a writer, or a model, can actually follow.
cards.phrase: follow this voice chart: for each trait, write like the "we are" column and never like the "we're not" column (paste your chart)

cards.name: Highlighter test
cards.desc: Highlight the words in a draft that the person needs to act. Anything not highlighted is a candidate to cut. A quick way to see how much of a message is throat-clearing.
cards.phrase: apply a highlighter test: keep only the words the reader needs to act, and explain what you cut

cards.name: Text expansion check
cards.desc: Test every string at 130 to 140 percent of its English length, and with the longest real values (a 40-character name, a 7-digit number). Pseudo-localized text like "[Ŝéñð îñṽîţéš ~~~]" shows truncation and hard-coded strings before translators do.
cards.phrase: check each string at 140% length and with the longest realistic values, and flag any that would truncate

cards.name: Comprehension test
cards.aka: copy testing, five-second test, cloze test
cards.desc: Show the screen to someone who hasn't seen it and ask what it means and what they'd do next. If they can't say, the copy isn't done. For a quick check, ask a model to play a first-time user and paraphrase the screen.
cards.phrase: review this copy as a first-time user would: paraphrase what each message means and what you'd do next, and flag anything ambiguous

cards.name: Content audit
cards.desc: Pull every string in a flow into one list and review it against the word list, voice chart and patterns here: duplicates, inconsistent terms, missing states. Useful before a redesign and an easy job to hand to a model.
cards.phrase: audit these strings: flag inconsistent terms, off-voice lines, missing empty/error/loading states and anything over length, then suggest fixes in a table

cards.name: Appalachian old-time
cards.desc: Fiddle and clawhammer banjo playing dance tunes and old ballads carried over from the British Isles. Modal melodies, plain voices, no polish. The source of most of what follows on this page.
cards.phrase: Appalachian old-time folk: fiddle and clawhammer banjo in unison, modal melody, a plain unvarnished voice, recorded close and dry on a porch

cards.name: Bluegrass
cards.desc: Acoustic string band music played fast and clean: banjo rolls, mandolin chop on the offbeat, fiddle and dobro taking turns on breaks. No drums; the bass and mandolin keep time.
cards.phrase: traditional bluegrass: fast three-finger banjo rolls, mandolin chop on the offbeat, fiddle and dobro breaks, upright bass, high lonesome three-part harmony, no drums

cards.name: Americana
cards.desc: A catch-all for modern roots music that borrows from country, folk, blues and rock. Usually a band with acoustic and electric guitars, warm and slightly worn, with the song and the story at the center.
cards.phrase: Americana: strummed acoustic guitar and organ over a loose backbeat, pedal steel swells, a weathered storytelling vocal, warm analog production

cards.name: Cosmic Americana
cards.aka: cosmic country, psychedelic country, western noir
cards.desc: Country songcraft played inside a huge reverb. Tremolo guitar, pedal steel and organ hang in the air like a night sky over the desert; harmonies sound far away. The lane that Lord Huron lives in.
cards.phrase: cosmic Americana: country songwriting drenched in reverb, tremolo electric guitar and pedal steel swells, distant layered harmonies, a wide-open night-sky feeling

cards.name: Alt-country
cards.desc: Country songs played by people raised on punk and indie rock. Twang and pedal steel, but ragged, loud in places, and suspicious of Nashville gloss.
cards.phrase: alt-country: country instrumentation played with indie-rock looseness, jangly slightly distorted electric guitar, pedal steel, a ragged honest vocal

cards.name: Cowboy ballad
cards.aka: western song, gunfighter ballad, singing cowboy
cards.desc: Story songs of the old West sung by a smooth baritone over a loping clip-clop rhythm, with Spanish-tinged guitar and harmony "ooh"s behind. Often tragic, always cinematic.
cards.phrase: classic cowboy ballad: loping clip-clop rhythm, Spanish-tinged nylon guitar, a smooth baritone telling a tragic story of the old West, harmony "ooh"s behind

cards.name: Spaghetti western score
cards.desc: The 1960s Italian take on the Western: twangy reverb guitar, a lonely whistle, mariachi trumpet, wordless choir, whip cracks and church bells. Operatic, dusty and slightly absurd.
cards.phrase: spaghetti western score: twangy reverb-soaked electric guitar, a lonely whistled melody, mariachi trumpet, wordless choir and galloping rhythm, sun-bleached drama

cards.name: Outlaw country
cards.desc: 1970s country that walked out on Nashville production: long hair, small bands, honest songs. Telecaster twang, a steady train beat and a gruff baritone.
cards.phrase: outlaw country: stripped-down band, twangy Telecaster, steady train-beat drums, a gruff unpolished baritone, 1970s Texas grit

cards.name: Honky-tonk
cards.desc: Country for dance halls and jukeboxes: a two-step shuffle, crying steel guitar, fiddle fills and a tinny barroom piano behind songs about drinking and heartbreak.
cards.phrase: honky-tonk country: two-step shuffle, crying pedal steel, fiddle fills, a tinny barroom piano and a twangy heartbroken vocal

cards.name: Murder ballad
cards.desc: Old story songs where someone dies, usually by the river. Minor modes, droning banjo, hushed voices, and a slow tale that ends badly. A deep vein in Appalachian music and in modern folk-noir.
cards.phrase: southern gothic murder ballad: sparse fingerpicked guitar and droning banjo in a minor mode, a hushed haunted vocal, a slow story that ends badly

cards.name: Laurel Canyon folk-rock
cards.desc: Folk songs plugged into a California band: 12-string jangle, piano, stacked harmonies and warm 1970s tape. Sunny on the surface and bittersweet underneath.
cards.phrase: Laurel Canyon folk-rock: jangly 12-string guitars, piano, stacked three-part harmonies, sunny but bittersweet, warm 1970s analog production

cards.name: Indie folk
cards.desc: Acoustic songs recorded with indie-rock ears: fingerpicking, reverb-rich rooms, banjo and glockenspiel, and big gang-vocal choruses. Ranges from hushed and wintry to stomping festival anthems.
cards.phrase: indie folk: fingerpicked acoustic guitar in a reverberant room, soaring layered harmonies, stomps and handclaps in the chorus, earnest and wistful

cards.name: Chamber folk
cards.desc: Intimate folk songs dressed with a small classical ensemble: string quartet, harp, woodwinds. Quiet, literary, beautifully arranged.
cards.phrase: chamber folk: intimate acoustic guitar and a delicate string quartet arrangement, harp and woodwinds, a quiet literate vocal

cards.name: Psych folk
cards.aka: freak folk, acid folk, wyrd folk
cards.desc: Folk that wandered into the woods and found something strange: drones, hand drums, recorders, wavering voices and songs that drift instead of resolving.
cards.phrase: psychedelic folk: droning acoustic textures, hand percussion and recorder, a wavering otherworldly vocal, pastoral and slightly uncanny

cards.name: Gospel & spirituals
cards.desc: Music of the Black church and its descendants: a lead voice called back by the choir, Hammond organ, handclaps on 2 and 4, building to a shout. Underneath almost every American genre.
cards.phrase: gospel: Hammond organ and piano, handclaps on two and four, a powerful lead vocal answered by a full choir, building to a joyful shout

cards.name: Delta blues
cards.desc: Solo voice and guitar from the Mississippi Delta: slide on a resonator, a foot stomping time, moaning vocals, twelve bars bent to the singer's will.
cards.phrase: raw Delta blues: solo slide guitar on a resonator, a foot-stomp rhythm, a moaning untrained voice, scratchy 1930s recording

cards.name: Celtic folk
cards.desc: Jigs, reels and airs from Ireland and Scotland: fiddle and whistle on an ornamented tune, bodhrán and bouzouki driving underneath, or a slow air sung alone.
cards.phrase: Celtic folk: fiddle and tin whistle playing a lively jig in 6/8, bodhrán frame drum, bouzouki rhythm, ornamented melody

cards.name: Sea shanty
cards.desc: Work songs for hauling ropes: one voice calls a line, a rough chorus roars back, feet stomp the time. Built to be sung by people who are not singers.
cards.phrase: sea shanty: a lead singer calls each line and a rough chorus of voices answers, foot stomps and concertina, bold and rhythmic

cards.name: Cajun & zydeco
cards.desc: Dance music from south Louisiana. Cajun is accordion and fiddle in waltzes and two-steps; zydeco is its Creole cousin, with rubboard and R&B drive.
cards.phrase: Cajun two-step: diatonic accordion and fiddle in unison, scraped rubboard and triangle, hollered vocals in Louisiana French

cards.name: Roots reggae
cards.desc: Jamaican music built on the offbeat: a guitar skank on 2 and 4 (or every "and"), deep melodic bass, and the one-drop beat where the kick lands on 3, not 1.
cards.phrase: roots reggae: one-drop drums, offbeat guitar skank, deep melodic bass, organ bubble, laid-back and warm

cards.name: Afrobeat
cards.desc: Lagos in the 1970s: interlocking funk guitars, a huge horn section, polyrhythmic drums and songs that run fifteen minutes. Different from modern Afrobeats pop.
cards.phrase: Afrobeat: interlocking funky guitars, polyrhythmic drums and percussion, a big horn section riffing, long hypnotic groove

cards.name: Flamenco
cards.desc: Andalusian song, guitar and dance. Fierce rasgueado strums, palmas handclaps, cajón, Phrygian melodies and raw, wailing singing.
cards.phrase: flamenco: rasgueado guitar strums, palmas handclaps and cajón, Phrygian melodies, raw impassioned singing

cards.name: Fado
cards.desc: Lisbon's song of longing. A single dramatic voice with a twelve-string Portuguese guitar and a classical guitar, slow and mournful, built around the feeling of saudade.
cards.phrase: fado: twelve-string Portuguese guitar and classical guitar, a mournful dramatic vocal full of longing, slow and intimate

cards.name: Mariachi
cards.desc: Trumpets and violins in bright unison, strummed vihuela and guitarrón bass, and a singer who sounds like an opera tenor at a wedding. Gritos (joyful shouts) optional but encouraged.
cards.phrase: mariachi: bright trumpets and violins in harmony, strummed vihuela and guitarrón bass, a proud soaring vocal with gritos

cards.name: Cumbia
cards.desc: A swaying dance rhythm from Colombia's coast that spread across Latin America. The güiro scrapes a steady pattern, the bass lopes, and an accordion or organ carries the tune.
cards.phrase: cumbia: steady scraped güiro, loping bass, accordion or organ melody, a swaying dance groove

cards.name: Klezmer
cards.desc: Eastern European Jewish wedding music: a clarinet that laughs and sobs, violin and accordion, oom-pah bass, and dances that speed up until somebody falls over.
cards.phrase: klezmer: wailing clarinet with bends and sobs, violin and accordion, oom-pah tuba, a freylekhs dance rhythm in the freygish mode

cards.name: Gamelan
cards.desc: Indonesian ensembles of tuned bronze metallophones and gongs. Interlocking parts shimmer because paired instruments are tuned slightly apart. Debussy heard it in Paris in 1889 and never got over it.
cards.phrase: Balinese gamelan: shimmering interlocking bronze metallophones with beating tuning, gong cycles, kendang drums

cards.name: Surf rock
cards.desc: Early-60s California instrumentals: a Fender guitar soaked in spring reverb, rapid tremolo picking and pounding drums. The template for every "twang" sound since.
cards.phrase: surf rock: twangy Fender guitar drenched in spring reverb, rapid tremolo picking, driving drums, instrumental

cards.name: Rockabilly
cards.desc: Country meets rhythm and blues in a Memphis studio: slapped upright bass, a hollow-body guitar, and a hiccuping vocal with slapback echo on it.
cards.phrase: rockabilly: slapped upright bass, twangy hollow-body guitar, slapback echo on a hiccuping vocal, Sun Studio 1956

cards.name: Garage rock
cards.desc: Teenagers with fuzz pedals and cheap organs, recorded loud and fast. Revived in the 2000s with the same rawness and better haircuts.
cards.phrase: garage rock: fuzzed-out guitars, cheap combo organ, crashing drums, a raw shouted vocal, recorded loud and fast

cards.name: Psychedelic rock
cards.desc: Rock that tried to sound like an altered state: phased and backwards guitars, swirling organ, drones and long jams. Modern neo-psych keeps the haze with cleaner drums.
cards.phrase: psychedelic rock: phased guitars, swirling organ, backwards tape effects, dreamy vocals, hazy 1967 production

cards.name: Heartland rock
cards.desc: Big-hearted rock about small towns and open roads: chiming guitars, Hammond and piano, straight driving eighths and a raspy voice singing to the back row.
cards.phrase: heartland rock: chiming guitars, Hammond organ and piano, driving straight eighths, a raspy anthemic vocal about small towns and open roads

cards.name: Desert noir
cards.desc: Slow, cinematic songs that sound like a motel sign buzzing at 2 a.m. in Arizona: baritone twang guitar with deep tremolo, mariachi trumpet, brushes and a low voice.
cards.phrase: desert noir: slow baritone twang guitar with deep tremolo and reverb, distant mariachi trumpet, brushed drums, a low cinematic vocal

cards.name: Desert rock
cards.desc: Heavy, hypnotic riffs played through down-tuned fuzz in the California desert. Repetition is the point; the heat haze is in the guitar tone.
cards.phrase: desert rock: down-tuned fuzz riffs, hypnotic repetition, heat-haze guitar tone, hazy vocals floating on top

cards.name: Dream pop
cards.desc: Soft, shimmering songs where texture matters more than words: chorused guitars, synth pads, slow drum machines and a breathy voice half lost in reverb.
cards.phrase: dream pop: shimmering chorused guitars, soft synth pads, a breathy reverb-soaked vocal, slow and hazy

cards.name: Shoegaze
cards.desc: Walls of distorted, pitch-bent guitar so loud and blurred that the vocals become one more texture. Named for players staring at their effects pedals.
cards.phrase: shoegaze: a wall of distorted pitch-bending guitars, vocals buried in the mix, washes of reverb, loud and blurry

cards.name: Post-rock
cards.desc: Long instrumental pieces that build from near silence to an enormous wall of sound. Tremolo-picked guitars, glockenspiel, swelling strings, very few words.
cards.phrase: post-rock: instrumental, a long crescendo from quiet tremolo-picked guitars to a cathartic wall of sound, cinematic

cards.name: Post-punk
cards.desc: Punk's energy pointed somewhere colder: melodic bass up front, angular chorused guitar, mechanical drums and a baritone that refuses to emote.
cards.phrase: post-punk: driving melodic bass up front, angular chorused guitar, mechanical drums, a cold baritone vocal

cards.name: Indie rock
cards.desc: Guitar bands from the 2000s indie boom: jangly interlocking guitars, tight drums, a casual voice and production that sounds a little homemade even when it isn't.
cards.phrase: indie rock: jangly interlocking guitars, tight bright drums, a casual earnest vocal, 2000s indie production

cards.name: Grunge
cards.desc: Quiet verses that explode into sludgy distorted choruses. Anguished vocals, drop-D riffs and early-90s Seattle rain in the guitar tone.
cards.phrase: grunge: quiet clean verses that explode into sludgy distorted choruses, anguished vocals, raw early-90s production

cards.name: Krautrock
cards.desc: 1970s German bands who swapped blues for repetition: a steady motorik beat, droning synths and grooves that run forward like an autobahn.
cards.phrase: krautrock: hypnotic motorik beat, repetitive bass, droning analog synths, long and forward-driving

cards.name: Doo-wop
cards.desc: Street-corner vocal groups: a falsetto lead, a bass voice singing nonsense syllables, close harmony "oohs", triplet piano and the I–vi–IV–V changes.
cards.phrase: 1950s doo-wop: a vocal group with a falsetto lead and a bass voice singing nonsense syllables, triplet piano, I–vi–IV–V changes

cards.name: Wall of Sound pop
cards.desc: Pop records stacked with everything at once: doubled pianos and guitars, castanets, strings, timpani, all poured into an echo chamber until it sounds like one huge instrument.
cards.phrase: 1960s girl-group pop with a Wall of Sound: layered pianos and guitars, castanets, strings and timpani, huge echo-chamber reverb

cards.name: Motown soul
cards.desc: Detroit's hit factory: tambourine on every beat, a busy melodic bass line, vibes and horn stabs, gospel-rooted leads and call-and-response backups.
cards.phrase: Motown soul: four-on-the-floor tambourine and snare, a busy melodic bass line, horn stabs, call-and-response backing vocals, bright 1965 mix

cards.name: Southern soul
cards.desc: Grittier than Motown: a tight rhythm section in Memphis or Alabama, Hammond organ, punchy horns and a singer pleading from the bottom of their heart.
cards.phrase: Southern soul: a tight rhythm section, Hammond organ, punchy horn section, a raw pleading vocal, warm 1968 analog recording

cards.name: Disco
cards.desc: Dance music built on a four-on-the-floor kick with open hi-hats on the offbeats, an octave-jumping bass, string sweeps and scratchy funk guitar.
cards.phrase: disco: four-on-the-floor kick, open hi-hats on the offbeat, octave-jumping bass, lush string sweeps, chicken-scratch guitar

cards.name: Synth-pop
cards.desc: Pop songs played on analog synths and drum machines: sequenced arpeggios, gated snares, glossy pads and a cool, emotive singer.
cards.phrase: 80s synth-pop: analog synth arpeggios, drum machine with a gated-reverb snare, glossy pads, a cool emotive vocal

cards.name: City pop
cards.desc: Late-70s and 80s Japanese pop made for driving through Tokyo at night: slap bass, Rhodes, bright brass and immaculate studio gloss. Rediscovered online in the 2010s.
cards.phrase: Japanese city pop: slap bass, Rhodes electric piano, bright brass, glossy late-70s production, a breezy nighttime-city mood

cards.name: Yacht rock
cards.desc: Smooth late-70s LA soft rock made by session aces: jazzy Rhodes chords, clean guitar, a sax solo and a soft blue-eyed soul voice.
cards.phrase: yacht rock: smooth jazzy chords on Rhodes, clean session guitar, saxophone solo, a soft blue-eyed soul vocal, polished late-70s LA production

cards.name: 80s power ballad
cards.desc: A slow song that starts on piano or clean guitar and ends with exploding drums, distorted guitars, a key change and a singer belting to the cheap seats.
cards.phrase: 80s power ballad: soft piano opening, explosive drums and distorted guitars in the chorus, a belted climactic key change, huge reverb

cards.name: Bedroom pop
cards.desc: Pop recorded at home on a laptop: soft clean guitar, cheap synths, drum machines and a quiet double-tracked voice that sounds like it's trying not to wake anyone.
cards.phrase: bedroom pop: lo-fi home recording, soft clean guitar and cheap synths, a quiet intimate double-tracked vocal

cards.name: Neo-soul
cards.desc: Late-90s soul with hip-hop drums laid way behind the beat, warm Rhodes chords, round bass and a jazzy, conversational voice.
cards.phrase: neo-soul: warm Rhodes chords, drums laid way behind the beat, round bass, a jazzy relaxed vocal

cards.name: Baroque pop
cards.desc: Pop songs arranged like small classical pieces: harpsichord, string quartet, French horn and lush layered harmonies. Melancholy and ornate.
cards.phrase: baroque pop: harpsichord and string quartet, French horn, lush layered harmonies, melancholy and ornate

cards.name: Modern R&B
cards.desc: Spacious late-night R&B: deep sub bass and crisp 808s, airy pads, silky stacked vocals and ad-libs panned around the head.
cards.phrase: modern R&B: deep sub bass and crisp 808s, airy synth pads, silky stacked vocals and ad-libs, intimate and spacious

cards.name: Ambient
cards.desc: Music meant to be "as ignorable as it is interesting" (Brian Eno): beatless pads and drones, sparse piano, field recordings and long reverb tails that evolve slowly.
cards.phrase: ambient: beatless, slowly evolving pads and drones, sparse piano notes, long reverb tails, calm and spacious

cards.name: Synthwave
cards.desc: A 2010s love letter to 80s movie soundtracks: pulsing analog arpeggios, gated drums, neon saw leads. The music for night drives that never happened.
cards.phrase: synthwave: pulsing analog synth arpeggios, gated-reverb snare, neon saw leads, retro 1980s night-drive mood

cards.name: House
cards.desc: Chicago club music from the mid-80s: four-on-the-floor kick around 122 BPM, offbeat open hats, warm chord stabs, a rolling bassline and a soulful vocal sample.
cards.phrase: deep house: four-on-the-floor kick, offbeat open hi-hats, warm chord stabs, rolling bassline, 122 BPM

cards.name: Techno
cards.desc: Relentless, hypnotic machine music: a hard kick on every beat, 909 hats, repeating synth lines that mutate slowly. Detroit invented it; Berlin built warehouses for it.
cards.phrase: techno: relentless four-on-the-floor kick, hypnotic 909 hi-hats, a repetitive modular synth line, dark warehouse atmosphere, 132 BPM

cards.name: Drum and bass
cards.desc: Chopped breakbeats at 170-plus BPM over deep rolling sub bass. Liquid DnB adds lush pads and soul samples; jungle keeps it raw and ragga.
cards.phrase: drum and bass: rapid chopped breakbeats at 174 BPM, deep rolling sub bass, atmospheric pads

cards.name: Trip-hop
cards.desc: Slow, smoky music from 90s Bristol: dusty sampled breakbeats, deep bass, cinematic strings, vinyl crackle and a melancholy singer.
cards.phrase: trip-hop: a slow dusty breakbeat, deep bass, cinematic sampled strings, vinyl crackle, a smoky melancholy vocal

cards.name: Lo-fi hip-hop
cards.desc: Mellow instrumental beats for studying: lazy swung drums, jazzy Rhodes chords, vinyl crackle and tape wobble, around 80 BPM.
cards.phrase: lo-fi hip-hop: lazy swung boom-bap drums, jazzy Rhodes chords, vinyl crackle and tape wobble, a mellow study mood, 80 BPM

cards.name: Boom bap
cards.desc: The sound of 90s New York rap: hard sampled kick ("boom") and snare ("bap"), a chopped soul or jazz loop and scratched hooks.
cards.phrase: boom-bap hip-hop: hard-hitting sampled kick and snare, a chopped soul loop, scratched hook, 90 BPM, golden-era New York

cards.name: Trap
cards.desc: Southern hip-hop built on booming 808 bass that slides between notes, rapid rolling hi-hat triplets and a half-time snare. Dark, minor and huge in the low end.
cards.phrase: trap: booming 808 bass slides, fast rolling hi-hat triplets, half-time snare, a dark minor-key melody, 140 BPM

cards.name: Dub
cards.desc: Reggae taken apart at the mixing desk: bass and drums up front, everything else thrown into tape echo and spring reverb, instruments dropping in and out.
cards.phrase: roots dub: deep bass up front, one-drop drums, offbeat skank thrown into tape echo and spring reverb, instruments dropping in and out

cards.name: Chillwave
cards.desc: Hazy late-2000s bedroom electronica: filtered synths, washed-out drum machines and a nostalgic summer feeling, like a VHS of a beach holiday.
cards.phrase: chillwave: hazy filtered synths, washed-out drum machine, nostalgic summer mood, lo-fi warmth

cards.name: Vaporwave
cards.desc: Slowed-down 80s smooth jazz, muzak and corporate jingles, chopped and drowned in reverb. Ironic, eerie and oddly beautiful.
cards.phrase: vaporwave: slowed-down 1980s smooth-jazz and mall-muzak samples, chopped loops, heavy reverb, eerie nostalgia

cards.name: Folktronica
cards.desc: Acoustic guitar, plucked strings and found sounds cut into glitchy electronic beats. Warm and organic, made on a laptop.
cards.phrase: folktronica: plucked acoustic and found-sound samples cut into glitchy electronic beats, warm and organic

cards.name: Big band swing
cards.desc: Dance orchestras of the 1930s and 40s: sax, trumpet and trombone sections trading riffs over walking bass and a swinging ride cymbal.
cards.phrase: big-band swing: brass and sax sections trading riffs, walking bass, a swinging ride cymbal, 1940s ballroom

cards.name: Bebop
cards.desc: Small-group jazz built for listening, not dancing: fast virtuosic horn lines, complex chord changes, a busy ride cymbal and walking bass.
cards.phrase: bebop: fast virtuosic sax and trumpet lines, complex chord changes, walking bass and a busy ride cymbal

cards.name: Cool & modal jazz
cards.desc: Relaxed, spacious jazz: muted trumpet, a soft tenor, brushes and open piano voicings that sit on one mode instead of racing through chords.
cards.phrase: cool modal jazz: muted trumpet, relaxed tenor sax, brushed drums, spacious piano voicings, late-night 1959

cards.name: Film noir jazz
cards.desc: Slow, smoky jazz for rain-slick streets: tenor sax over brushes and upright bass, a vibraphone hanging in the dark, menace in the minor chords.
cards.phrase: film noir jazz: a slow smoky tenor saxophone, brushed drums, upright bass, vibraphone, a rain-slick city at night

cards.name: Bossa nova
cards.desc: Rio in the late 50s: gentle syncopated nylon guitar, soft percussion, jazz chords and a voice barely above a whisper.
cards.phrase: bossa nova: gentle syncopated nylon-string guitar, soft brushed percussion, light flute, a near-whispered vocal

cards.name: Minimalism
cards.desc: Short repeating patterns that shift slowly against each other, pulsing piano and marimba, a steady hypnotic pulse. Every modern film score borrows from it.
cards.phrase: minimalist composition: interlocking repeating piano and marimba patterns that shift gradually, a hypnotic steady pulse

cards.name: Romantic orchestral
cards.desc: The big emotional orchestra: sweeping strings, warm horns, expressive rubato and swells that rise and break like weather.
cards.phrase: lush Romantic-era orchestral: sweeping strings, warm French horns, expressive rubato, big emotional swells

cards.name: Impressionist
cards.desc: Shimmering piano and harp, whole-tone and pentatonic colors, blurred pedal and chords that float without needing to resolve. Music like watercolor.
cards.phrase: impressionist: shimmering piano and harp, whole-tone and pentatonic colors, blurred pedal, a watercolor mood

cards.name: Baroque
cards.desc: Harpsichord continuo, crisp string ensembles and interlocking counterpoint over a steady motor rhythm. Ornate and mathematical.
cards.phrase: baroque: harpsichord continuo, a crisp string ensemble, interlocking counterpoint, steady motor rhythm

cards.name: Sacred choral
cards.desc: A cappella choir with pure straight tone, slow suspensions that ache before they resolve, and the long reverb of a stone church.
cards.phrase: sacred choral: an a cappella choir with pure straight tone, slow suspensions, cathedral reverb

cards.name: Epic trailer
cards.desc: Movie-trailer music: low brass braams, pounding taiko, racing string ostinatos and a choir rising to a huge hybrid climax with synth risers and impacts.
cards.phrase: epic trailer music: low brass braams, pounding taiko, a staccato string ostinato, a rising choir, huge hybrid orchestral climax

cards.name: Western film score
cards.desc: Classic Hollywood Westerns: soaring brass themes in open fifths, galloping strings and snare, and wide orchestration that sounds like big sky.
cards.phrase: classic Hollywood Western score: soaring open-fifth brass themes, galloping strings and snare, wide-open Americana orchestration

cards.name: Horror score
cards.desc: Dissonant string clusters, low drones, prepared piano, whispers and sudden stingers. Built to make you lean away from the screen.
cards.phrase: horror score: dissonant string clusters, low drones, sudden stingers, unsettling prepared piano, creeping dread

cards.name: Chiptune
cards.desc: Music made with (or imitating) old game-console sound chips: square-wave leads, a triangle-wave bass, a noise channel for drums, and fast arpeggios faking chords.
cards.phrase: chiptune: 8-bit square-wave lead, triangle-wave bass, noise-channel drums, upbeat NES game soundtrack

cards.name: Strummed acoustic guitar
cards.desc: The steel-string acoustic strummed with a pick: the backbone of folk, country and singer-songwriter music. Say how it's strummed (driving eighths, lazy downstrokes, palm-muted) to steer the feel.
cards.phrase: a strummed steel-string acoustic guitar driving the rhythm

cards.name: Fingerpicked guitar
cards.desc: Thumb alternates bass notes while fingers pick melody on top, so one guitar sounds like two. The sound of intimate folk, from Mississippi John Hurt to Bon Iver.
cards.phrase: gently fingerpicked acoustic guitar, an alternating thumb bass under a picked melody

cards.name: 12-string guitar
cards.desc: Six pairs of strings, some tuned an octave apart, so every chord rings with a natural chorus shimmer. Big and chiming when strummed.
cards.phrase: a chiming 12-string guitar with natural octave shimmer

cards.name: Nylon-string guitar
cards.desc: Soft, round and warm with a quick decay. Bossa nova, flamenco, classical and the clip-clop of cowboy ballads all use it.
cards.phrase: a warm nylon-string guitar, soft and round

cards.name: Clawhammer banjo
cards.desc: Banjo struck downward with the back of a fingernail, with the thumb catching the high drone string. Rhythmic and percussive: "bum-ditty, bum-ditty". Old-time music's heartbeat.
cards.phrase: clawhammer banjo with a percussive bum-ditty rhythm and a ringing high drone string

cards.name: Three-finger banjo
cards.desc: Fast rolling patterns picked with thumb and two fingers wearing metal picks: a constant cascade of bright notes. If you hear it, you're in bluegrass.
cards.phrase: fast bright three-finger bluegrass banjo rolls

cards.name: Fiddle
cards.desc: The violin played folk-style: double stops, slides, drones and shuffle bowing. It can carry a dance tune or cry behind a ballad.
cards.phrase: a fiddle with slides and double stops, bowing a lonesome melody

cards.name: Mandolin
cards.desc: Small, bright and pairs-strung. Plays the offbeat "chop" in bluegrass, fast tremolo on held notes, and sparkly fills in folk-rock.
cards.phrase: bright mandolin, tremolo-picked on the held notes

cards.name: Upright bass
cards.desc: Plucked acoustic bass with a woody thump. Walks in jazz, plays root-fifth in country, and gets slapped for rockabilly.
cards.phrase: a woody upright bass playing a walking line

cards.name: Dobro
cards.desc: An acoustic guitar with a metal cone, played flat with a steel slide. Nasal, singing and bluesy; it slides between notes the way a voice does.
cards.phrase: a nasal singing dobro, slid with a steel bar

cards.name: Pedal steel
cards.desc: A table-like guitar played with a bar, with pedals that bend notes inside chords. Its swells and cries are the sound of country heartbreak and cosmic Americana.
cards.phrase: pedal steel swelling and crying behind the vocal

cards.name: Autoharp
cards.desc: A zither with chord bars: press a button and strum, and every string in that chord rings. Shimmery and sweet; Maybelle Carter and June Carter Cash played it.
cards.phrase: a shimmering strummed autoharp

cards.name: Appalachian dulcimer
cards.desc: A long narrow box laid across the lap, with a melody string over drones. Gentle, modal and old; Joni Mitchell wrote "Blue" on one.
cards.phrase: a gentle Appalachian dulcimer playing a modal melody over its own drone

cards.name: Hammered dulcimer
cards.desc: A trapezoid of strings struck with small hammers. Bright, ringing, a little like a piano with no dampers. Common in Celtic, Appalachian and Eastern European music.
cards.phrase: a ringing hammered dulcimer with sustained sparkling notes

cards.name: Harmonica
cards.desc: Reedy, breathy and expressive, with bends that wail like a voice. Folk players use it on a neck rack between verses; blues players push it through an amp.
cards.phrase: a wailing harmonica with bent notes between verses

cards.name: Accordion
cards.desc: Bellows-driven reeds with a wheezy, nostalgic sound. Central to Cajun, Tex-Mex, polka, French musette and sea shanties.
cards.phrase: a wheezy nostalgic accordion

cards.name: Washboard & spoons
cards.desc: Kitchen percussion: a washboard scraped with thimbles, spoons clacked on the knee. Pure jug band and zydeco.
cards.phrase: scratchy washboard and spoons percussion

cards.name: Telecaster twang
cards.desc: A bright, snappy, cutting electric guitar sound with a quick attack. Country leads, bent double stops and slapback echo.
cards.phrase: a bright twangy Telecaster with slapback echo

cards.name: Tremolo baritone guitar
cards.aka: twang baritone, Duane Eddy sound, western guitar
cards.desc: A low, twangy electric guitar played through an amp's pulsing tremolo and a big spring reverb. Instantly Western, instantly cinematic.
cards.phrase: a low twangy baritone electric guitar through pulsing amp tremolo and deep spring reverb

cards.name: Fuzz guitar
cards.desc: A guitar pushed into square-wave distortion: buzzy, thick and woolly. 60s garage, stoner rock and shoegaze all live here.
cards.phrase: a buzzy woolly fuzz guitar riff

cards.name: Jangle guitar
cards.desc: Clean, bright, chorused electric guitar playing ringing arpeggios. The sound of 60s folk-rock and 80s college rock.
cards.phrase: bright jangly clean electric guitar arpeggios with a touch of chorus

cards.name: Rhodes electric piano
cards.desc: Struck metal tines through a pickup: a warm, bell-like piano that barks when hit hard. Soul, jazz fusion, neo-soul and lo-fi chords.
cards.phrase: warm bell-like Rhodes electric piano chords

cards.name: Wurlitzer
cards.desc: An electric piano with reeds instead of tines: reedier, more nasal and growly than a Rhodes, often through its built-in tremolo.
cards.phrase: a reedy Wurlitzer electric piano with gentle tremolo

cards.name: Hammond organ
cards.desc: A tonewheel organ shaped with drawbars and spun through a rotating Leslie speaker. Swells, growls, gospel pads and rock stabs.
cards.phrase: a Hammond B3 organ through a swirling Leslie speaker

cards.name: Honky-tonk piano
cards.desc: An upright piano slightly out of tune with itself (or with tacks in the hammers), so every note jangles. Saloons, honky-tonks and ragtime.
cards.phrase: a jangly out-of-tune honky-tonk upright piano

cards.name: Grand piano
cards.desc: The full-range acoustic piano. Specify the character: bright concert grand, intimate close-miked felt piano, or a warm old upright in a room.
cards.phrase: an intimate close-miked felt piano with soft hammers and audible pedal noise

cards.name: Mellotron
cards.desc: A 60s keyboard that plays tape loops of real flutes, strings and choirs, slightly wobbly and eerie. The flute sound is "Strawberry Fields Forever".
cards.phrase: wobbly vintage Mellotron flutes

cards.name: Analog synth bass
cards.desc: A fat, squelchy bass from an analog synthesizer, its filter snapping shut on every note. Funk, synth-pop, synthwave and "Stranger Things".
cards.phrase: a fat squelchy analog synth bass

cards.name: Synth pad
cards.desc: Soft sustained synthesizer chords with a slow attack, filling the space behind everything else. Name it warm, glassy, dark or airy.
cards.phrase: a warm slow-attack analog synth pad holding chords underneath

cards.name: Brushed drums
cards.desc: Drums played with wire brushes: soft swishes and taps instead of cracks. Instantly intimate; jazz ballads, folk and late-night country.
cards.phrase: soft brushed drums with gentle swishes on the snare

cards.name: Floor toms
cards.desc: A beat built on the low toms instead of the snare: rolling, thunderous and primal. Indie folk anthems and war-drum builds love it.
cards.phrase: rolling thunderous floor toms instead of a snare backbeat

cards.name: TR-808
cards.desc: The 1980 Roland drum machine: a booming sine kick that doubles as a bass note, snappy snare, ticking hats and cowbell. Hip-hop and trap run on it.
cards.phrase: booming 808 kick and bass with ticking hi-hats

cards.name: String section
cards.desc: Violins, violas, cellos and basses playing together: lush sustained chords, swells, pizzicato or tense tremolo. The quickest way to make something cinematic.
cards.phrase: a lush string section swelling under the chorus

cards.name: Solo cello
cards.desc: Closest instrument to a human voice: warm, dark and singing. One cello reads as grief, intimacy or longing.
cards.phrase: a solo cello singing a slow, mournful line

cards.name: Harp
cards.desc: Plucked strings with a soft attack and long ring. Glissandos say "magic", "dream sequence" or "once upon a time".
cards.phrase: a harp glissando opening into gentle arpeggios

cards.name: French horn
cards.desc: A round, noble brass voice that can be heroic in a theme or soft and distant in a pad. The sound of frontier vistas and Spielberg sunsets.
cards.phrase: warm French horns playing a noble open-fifth theme

cards.name: Muted trumpet
cards.desc: A trumpet played through a mute, small and buzzy and lonesome. Late-night jazz, noir and the far end of a desert.
cards.phrase: a lonesome muted trumpet in the distance

cards.name: Tenor saxophone
cards.desc: Breathy and husky at low volume, honking and wild when pushed. Noir, soul solos, 80s rock and smooth jazz.
cards.phrase: a breathy smoky tenor saxophone

cards.name: Clarinet
cards.desc: Woody and agile: dark and hollow in the low register, sweet in the middle, shrill on top. Klezmer, New Orleans jazz and pastoral scoring.
cards.phrase: a woody clarinet line with a playful lilt

cards.name: Flute & whistle
cards.desc: Airy, pure and breathy. A concert flute floats; a tin whistle dances an Irish jig.
cards.phrase: an airy breathy flute melody

cards.name: Timpani
cards.desc: Tuned orchestral drums: thunderous rolls building tension, booming hits on the downbeat of a climax.
cards.phrase: a timpani roll swelling into a booming hit

cards.name: Celesta & glockenspiel
cards.desc: Small metal bars struck by hammers (glockenspiel) or a keyboard (celesta). Twinkling, innocent, a little magic: music boxes, snowfall, childhood.
cards.phrase: a twinkling celesta melody like a music box

cards.name: Harmonium
cards.desc: A wheezy pedal- or hand-pumped reed organ: drones, hymns and something ancient in a farmhouse parlor.
cards.phrase: a wheezy drone of harmonium chords

cards.name: Pipe organ
cards.desc: Massive, sacred, overwhelming: pipes from sub-bass rumble to piercing high stops, in a building made to make it bigger.
cards.phrase: a massive cathedral pipe organ

cards.name: Whistling
cards.desc: A human whistle carrying the tune: lonely on a prairie, carefree on a porch. Morricone made it the sound of the West.
cards.phrase: a lonely whistled melody carrying across open space

cards.name: Musical saw
cards.desc: A handsaw bent and bowed, singing in a wavering, ghostly voice somewhere between a theremin and a soprano.
cards.phrase: a wavering ghostly musical saw

cards.name: Theremin
cards.desc: An electronic instrument played without touching it, gliding between pitches with heavy vibrato. 1950s sci-fi, flying saucers, the uncanny.
cards.phrase: a gliding vibrato-heavy theremin

cards.name: Music box
cards.desc: A tiny metal comb plucked by a turning cylinder: delicate, mechanical, nostalgic, and creepy in the right film.
cards.phrase: a delicate wind-up music box melody

cards.name: Toy piano
cards.desc: Small metal rods struck by plastic hammers: plinky, out of tune and charming, or deeply unsettling.
cards.phrase: a plinky out-of-tune toy piano

cards.name: Vibraphone
cards.desc: Metal bars with motorized resonators that add a soft pulsing tremolo. Cool jazz, noir, lounge and dreamy indie.
cards.phrase: mellow vibraphone with a slow pulsing tremolo

cards.name: Kalimba
cards.desc: Metal tines plucked by the thumbs on a wooden box: soft, round, bell-like and hypnotic.
cards.phrase: a soft bell-like kalimba pattern

cards.name: Church bells
cards.desc: Huge bronze bells tolling in the distance, with their strange, clashing overtones. Weddings, funerals, high noon.
cards.phrase: distant church bells tolling

cards.name: Stomps & claps
cards.desc: Feet on a wooden floor and hands clapping in time, the drum kit of indie folk choruses and shanty halls.
cards.phrase: foot stomps on a wooden floor and handclaps on the backbeat

cards.name: Tambourine & shaker
cards.desc: Jingles and shakers that add shimmer and drive without weight. Soul records put a tambourine on every beat; folk records shake an egg.
cards.phrase: a tambourine shaking on every beat

cards.name: Choir "oohs"
cards.desc: Wordless sustained voices behind everything: "ooh" for warmth, "aah" for heaven. Used as a pad, they make a track feel bigger and more human.
cards.phrase: wordless choir "oohs" swelling behind the chorus

cards.name: Very slow
cards.desc: Under 60 BPM. Funeral marches, ambient pieces and the slowest ballads. At this speed you feel each beat arrive.
cards.phrase: a very slow tempo, around 55 BPM, every beat given room

cards.name: Ballad tempo
cards.desc: 60 to 76 BPM. Love songs, slow waltzes, slow-dance country. About a resting heartbeat.
cards.phrase: a slow ballad tempo, around 70 BPM

cards.name: Walking pace
cards.desc: 76 to 100 BPM. Unhurried, conversational, easy to sway to. Much of folk, soul and lo-fi sits here.
cards.phrase: an unhurried walking tempo, around 88 BPM

cards.name: Mid-tempo
cards.desc: 100 to 120 BPM. The default for pop and rock: alive but not rushing.
cards.phrase: a steady mid-tempo groove, around 110 BPM

cards.name: Dance tempo
cards.desc: 118 to 130 BPM. House, disco and most club music live in this narrow band because it matches how people dance.
cards.phrase: a danceable tempo, 124 BPM

cards.name: Uptempo
cards.desc: 130 to 160 BPM. Punk, bluegrass breakdowns, surf, fast country. Energy and urgency.
cards.phrase: a driving uptempo beat, around 150 BPM

cards.name: Breakneck
cards.desc: Over 160 BPM. Bebop, drum and bass, hardcore punk, fiddle contests. Often felt in half time so it doesn't exhaust the listener.
cards.phrase: a breakneck tempo, around 180 BPM

cards.name: 4/4 common time
cards.aka: common time, four on the floor (one feel of it)
cards.desc: Four beats to a bar, the default for nearly all pop, rock and dance music. Count "1-2-3-4", with weight on 1 and 3 and the snare usually on 2 and 4.
cards.phrase: in 4/4 time

cards.name: 3/4 waltz
cards.desc: Three beats to a bar: "OOM-pah-pah". Waltzes, country ballads, many folk songs and lullabies. Instantly old-fashioned and swaying.
cards.phrase: a swaying 3/4 waltz rhythm

cards.desc: Two big beats, each split into three: "ONE-and-a TWO-and-a". Rolling and lilting. Irish jigs, sea songs, "House of the Rising Sun", many ballads.
cards.phrase: a rolling 6/8 rhythm

cards.name: 12/8 slow blues
cards.desc: Four beats each split into triplets. The slow-blues and doo-wop ballad feel, heavy and swaying with a constant triplet underneath.
cards.phrase: a heavy 12/8 slow-blues triplet feel

cards.name: 2/4 two-beat
cards.desc: Two beats to a bar: bass on one, chord on two. Marches, polkas, bluegrass and early country.
cards.phrase: a bouncing two-beat feel, bass on one and chord on two

cards.desc: Five beats to a bar, usually felt as 3+2. Lopsided but hypnotic. "Take Five" and the "Mission: Impossible" theme.
cards.phrase: an off-kilter 5/4 rhythm felt as 3+2

cards.desc: Seven quick beats grouped 2+2+3 (or 3+2+2). Feels like it stumbles forward. Balkan folk, prog rock and modern indie.
cards.phrase: a lurching 7/8 groove grouped 2+2+3

cards.name: Free time
cards.aka: rubato, ad lib, out of time
cards.desc: No steady beat: the performer stretches and pushes the tempo with the phrase, like speech. Intros, a cappella ballads, solo piano and old field recordings.
cards.phrase: performed in free time, rubato, no steady beat

cards.name: Straight eighths
cards.desc: Eighth notes exactly even, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4. The plain, driving rock and pop default.
cards.phrase: a straight-eighths rock beat, kick on one and three, snare on two and four

cards.name: Swing
cards.desc: Each pair of eighth notes is played long-short ("doo-ba, doo-ba"), with the ride cymbal leading. The lilt of jazz and big band.
cards.phrase: swung eighth notes, a lilting jazz swing feel on the ride cymbal

cards.name: Shuffle
cards.desc: A heavier cousin of swing: the long-short triplet bounce driven by the snare and a boogie bass line. Blues, early rock'n'roll and honky-tonk.
cards.phrase: a bouncing blues shuffle with a boogie bass line

cards.name: Train beat
cards.desc: Brushes or sticks chugging on the snare in steady eighths with accents on 2 and 4, like wheels on a track. Country's engine, from Johnny Cash to outlaw.
cards.phrase: a chugging country train beat on the snare

cards.name: Boom-chick
cards.desc: Bass note on the beat ("boom"), chord strum on the offbeat ("chick"), alternating root and fifth. Country, bluegrass guitar and the Carter Family.
cards.phrase: an alternating boom-chick guitar pattern, bass note then strum

cards.name: Texas two-step
cards.desc: A brisk dance-hall shuffle: quick-quick-slow-slow on the floor, walking bass and a snare tick on the offbeats.
cards.phrase: a brisk Texas two-step shuffle for the dance floor

cards.name: Four on the floor
cards.desc: Kick drum on every quarter note. The heartbeat of disco, house, techno and stadium-indie choruses.
cards.phrase: a four-on-the-floor kick on every beat

cards.name: Half-time
cards.desc: Snare moves from 2 and 4 to beat 3, so the music feels half as fast while everything else keeps moving. Heavy and spacious; trap and big final choruses.
cards.phrase: a heavy half-time feel with the snare on three

cards.name: Motorik
cards.desc: A steady, endless eighth-note beat with almost no fills, like driving on an open highway. Krautrock, post-punk and The War on Drugs.
cards.phrase: a steady unbroken motorik beat that never fills

cards.name: Bo Diddley beat
cards.desc: The "shave and a haircut, two bits" rhythm on tom-toms and maracas, a clave pattern brought into rock'n'roll.
cards.phrase: a Bo Diddley beat on tom-toms and maracas

cards.name: Gallop
cards.desc: A long-short-short "da-da-DUM" figure like hooves: Western scores, cavalry charges and heavy metal.
cards.phrase: a galloping long-short-short rhythm like hooves

cards.name: Stomp-clap
cards.desc: Kick or foot stomp on every beat with handclaps on 2 and 4, played by a whole room. The 2010s indie-folk anthem beat.
cards.phrase: a communal stomp-clap beat, stomps on every beat and claps on two and four

cards.name: Bossa nova groove
cards.desc: Soft brazilian syncopation: bass on 1 and 3, a rim click pattern that anticipates the beat, and guitar chords pushed ahead of the bar.
cards.phrase: a gentle bossa nova groove with a syncopated rim click

cards.name: One drop
cards.desc: Reggae's signature beat: nothing on beat 1, kick and rim together on 3. It leaves a hole where you expect the downbeat.
cards.phrase: a reggae one-drop beat, kick and rim together on three

cards.name: Son clave
cards.desc: A five-hit pattern across two bars (three in one, two in the other) that anchors salsa, rumba and much Latin music.
cards.phrase: a 3-2 son clave pattern on wood block

cards.name: Breakbeat
cards.desc: A syncopated funk drum pattern with ghost notes, the kind sampled from soul records to build hip-hop, jungle and big beat.
cards.phrase: a syncopated funk breakbeat with ghost notes on the snare

cards.name: Behind the beat
cards.desc: Snare and fills land a hair late, so the groove feels relaxed and heavy. Neo-soul, lo-fi and classic soul pockets. Compare "on top of the beat", which pushes and feels urgent.
cards.phrase: drums sitting lazily behind the beat, a relaxed deep pocket

cards.name: Major
cards.desc: Bright, settled, resolved. The sound of most pop, hymns, nursery rhymes and campfire songs.
cards.phrase: in a bright major key

cards.name: Natural minor
cards.desc: Darker and sadder than major, because of its flat third, sixth and seventh. Ballads, laments, most "dark" anything.
cards.phrase: in a melancholy minor key

cards.name: Dorian
cards.desc: Minor with a raised sixth: sad but hopeful, a bit jazzy or Celtic. "Scarborough Fair", "Oye Como Va", lots of Irish tunes.
cards.phrase: in Dorian mode, minor but with a hopeful raised sixth

cards.name: Mixolydian
cards.desc: Major with a flat seventh: bright but bluesy and unresolved. Bluegrass, Celtic reels, classic rock and "Sweet Home Alabama".
cards.phrase: in Mixolydian mode, major with a bluesy flat seventh

cards.name: Phrygian
cards.aka: Spanish Phrygian (with major third: Phrygian dominant)
cards.desc: Minor with a flat second, a half step above home that sounds Spanish, Middle Eastern or menacing. Flamenco, surf rock, metal.
cards.phrase: in Phrygian mode with a dark Spanish flat second

cards.name: Lydian
cards.desc: Major with a raised fourth: dreamy, floating, wondrous. Film scores use it for flying, space and magic.
cards.phrase: in Lydian mode, dreamy and floating with a raised fourth

cards.name: Harmonic minor
cards.desc: Minor with a raised seventh, which leaves an exotic gap of three half steps. Gothic, Middle Eastern, klezmer-adjacent, neoclassical metal.
